2. The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures
3. The Lankavatara King's Request
4. The Meaning of the One Hundred and Eight Phrases
The Lankavatara Sutra is devoted specifically to the essential gateway of the Tathagata's mind-ground; it is an exceedingly important treasure for practice. This sutra has three translations:
1. Liu Song
Gunabhadra (

), whose translation is the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra, in four fascicles. It is also called the four-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Song translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Song translation."

(Liu Song, 420-479 CE) The first dynasty of the Southern Dynasties during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period — Song. Because its rulers were surnamed Liu, it is called Liu Song to distinguish it from the Song dynasty later founded by Zhao Kuangyin.
2. Northern Wei
Bodhiruci (?

), whose translation is the Sutra of Entering Lanka, in ten fascicles. It is also called the ten-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Wei translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Wei translation."
(Northern Wei, 386-534 CE) The first dynasty of the Northern Dynasties during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period — Wei.
3. Tang
Siksananda (

), whose translation is the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka, in seven fascicles. It is also called the seven-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Tang translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Tang translation."

This Tang translation was made by Siksananda at the command of Empress Wu Zetian. Since the Lankavatara Sutra is "the mysterious pivot of the mind-measure of all Buddhas, the wondrous key to the treasure-caves of all sutras," while Gunabhadra's, terse and archaic in wording, had not circulated widely, and Bodhiruci's was marred by many errors (
chuǎn

, erroneous), she took the Sanskrit original from the palace and asked Siksananda to retranslate it from the original, consulting the two earlier versions and "examining the essential meanings of the three versions." Thus the seven-fascicle Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka came into being. Compared with the first two, the Tang rendering is fluent in phrase and clear in meaning.

(Mind-measure) When the mind gives rise to false imagining and takes all manner of measure of outer objects, this is the mind-measure of ordinary beings; the mind-measure genuinely realized by the Tathagata is far removed from all objects and from all grasping, and dwells in no-mind. This sutra says:
"Who sees all conditioned dharmas / from grasp and grasping free — / that mind-measure of no-mind / is mind-measure to me."

(Mysterious pivot) The hub for grasping the profound meaning of the Way. (Wondrous key) The wondrous key to attaining the Way; "key" means a key. (Examining the essential meanings of the three versions) Thoroughly investigating the essential meaning expounded by the three versions of the sutra (two Chinese translations and one Sanskrit original).

Among these three Chinese translations, the four-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra (the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra) was entrusted by Bodhidharma, the first patriarch of Chan, to the second patriarch Huike, with the words:
"In the land of Han I see no other sutra; let the worthy one practice according to this and naturally attain deliverance from the world."

This is the supreme treasure for transmitting the lamp and sealing the mind; patriarch after patriarch handed it down as the mind-dharma, and possessing great power to gather and transform beings, it circulated most widely. Except for the first chapter, "The Lankavatara King's Request," taken from the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka, the sutra text in the remaining chapters ("No Gate Is the Dharma Gate," "The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures," "The Meaning of the One Hundred and Eight Phrases," "The Storehouse Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousnesses," "The Realm of the Storehouse Consciousness," "No-Self and the Tathagatagarbha," "Awakening to the Mind's Own Manifestation," "The Great Skillful Means Dharma Gate," and "The Mark of Self-Realized Noble Wisdom") is taken from this translation. When passages from the other two translations are quoted, the Sutra of Entering Lanka is abbreviated as the Wei translation, and the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka as the Tang translation.
The Lankavatara Sutra — this is the method by which Śākyamuni Buddha himself proclaimed the perfect realization of Buddhahood he had attained (
"the Dharma of the noble wisdom realized by himself"
). Yet the text is abstruse and hard to read. In Su Dongpo's words (Preface to the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra):
"The meaning of the Lankavatara is ever
(zhé, namely)

profound and subtle, while its wording is terse and archaic. Readers may not even be able to punctuate the sentences — how much less can they set aside the text to grasp the meaning, and forget the meaning to awaken the mind?"

(Translation: In the Lankavatara, the meaning is profound and subtle, while the wording is terse and archaic. Readers may not even be able to punctuate it — how much less set aside the text to grasp the meaning, and forget the meaning to awaken the mind?)

(Profound and subtle, miǎo) Deep and refined. (Punctuating sentences) Books in ancient times had no punctuation marks. When reciting, one paused according to the meaning, or also marked the book with circles and dots at the pauses; this was called "punctuating sentences." Such "sentences" were often shorter than what grammar today calls a sentence.
To understand the sutra more easily and deeply, first read
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
and
The True Nature of All Dharmas
so as to gain a comprehensive understanding of mind, self-nature, tathagatagarbha, and the true nature of all dharmas.

blocks.text: 1. No Gate Is the Dharma Gate

inline.s: Question: Master Mazu said that the Lankavatara Sutra teaches:
"The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; no gate is the dharma gate."
What does this sentence mean?

Answer: "The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence" means the Lankavatara Sutra takes mind as its essential doctrine. The entire Lankavatara Ratna Sutra has only one chapter, and its chapter title is: The Mind of All Buddha-Speech. "The mind of all Buddha-speech": all Buddha-speech teaches only this mind. That is to say, all Buddhas proclaim this mind. For

one's own mind is Buddha; all realms are merely what karma evokes and what mind alone manifests. Whether one is in birth-and-death or in nirvana depends entirely on a single turn of mind, and there is no other dharma.
The mind is so important that all Buddhas proclaim it. Master Hanshan said:
"Because
(since)
this sutra points directly to the storehouse consciousness of sentient beings as the tathagatagarbha, revealing the states that appear before us in daily use,
causing one to follow along and observe the mind's own manifestation, and instantly realize the self-realized noble wisdom of all Buddhas
, therefore it is named 'the mind of Buddha-speech.'"
(Notes from the Pavilion for Contemplating the Lankavatara Precious Sutra)
(Only one chapter in the whole) According to Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra:
"This sutra has forty fascicles. This
(the Lankavatara Sutra that reached our land)
is only one tenth of it."
(The mind of all Buddha-speech) The Tang translation says:
"the mind taught by all Buddhas."

(The consciousness-store is the tathagatagarbha) The consciousness-store and the tathagatagarbha are two states of one body. See the chapter "The Storehouse Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousnesses."

(The mind's own manifestation) "Direct perception" means intuitively knowing that something exists without conceptual thought — direct knowing. (Knowing by inference is "inferential cognition.") Awakening to the mind's own manifestation is like a mirror reflecting objects: knowing the states manifested by one's own mind without conceptual calculation. This sutra says:
"Simply awaken to the mind's own manifestation, and false imagining does not arise; one is peaceful
(same as "steady")
and happy, and worldly affairs cease forever."
The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:

"The Buddha said: 'Simply awaken to the mind's own manifestation, and false imagining does not arise; one is peaceful and happy, and worldly affairs cease forever.' To be peaceful and happy is to be tranquil, wondrous, and constant; for worldly affairs to cease forever is for grasping to be cut off. One may be said to have met with a perfect treasure trove, to have suddenly cut off all seeking, to have reached the nirvana of everlasting bliss, beyond which there is nowhere further to go. At the boundary between ordinary beings and sages, one is as if arrived home; as the reliance of the deluded and the awakened, one has fathomed the root. The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says: 'The vajra treasury lacks nothing.'"
Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra says:
"Because
(since)
the mind's own manifestation is such that sage and ordinary being are not established and all is negated, thereby revealing
(and thus displaying)
the ultimate meaning of enlightenment within birth and death.'"
Patriarch Bodhidharma's Dharma Gate of Pacifying the Mind says:

"Whoever has a mind that discriminates and calculates the mind's own manifestation — all of it is a dream. If one understands that the mind is quiescent and extinguished, with no place for any thought, this is called right enlightenment."
Master Hanshan also said:
"The chapter "The Mind of Buddha-Speech":
this sutra points directly to the quiescent one mind as its essence, and takes entry by realization of self-realized noble wisdom as its aim
(Supplement to the Lankavatara)
(The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; no gate is the dharma gate) The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp records:
(Mazu)

One day he addressed the assembly: All of you, each believe that your own mind is Buddha; this mind is the Buddha-mind. Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China in person and transmitted the supreme teaching of the one mind, causing you to open to awakening. He also cited passages from the Lankavatara Sutra to seal the mind-ground of sentient beings, fearing that you might be inverted and not believe in this dharma of the mind, which each of you possesses. Therefore the Lankavatara Sutra says:
the Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; 'no' gate is the dharma gate.

It also says: One who seeks the dharma should seek nothing; outside the mind there is no other Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no other mind. Not grasping good, not rejecting evil, relying on neither purity nor defilement
(hù)

, realizing the emptiness of the nature of offenses — thought after thought unattainable, because without self-nature. Therefore the three realms are mind only, and the myriad phenomena are all sealed by the one dharma."
(The myriad phenomena are all sealed by the one dharma)

The myriad phenomena are all stamped with the imprint of the one dharma. (The one dharma seal) Also called the one true-nature seal, or the seal of the true nature of all dharmas. A dharma seal is the seal of the Buddhadharma, the seal of truth passed down from Buddha to Buddha; it is the criterion of the Buddhadharma, and whatever does not accord with it is not Buddhadharma. The Mahayana teachings take the true nature of all dharmas as their foundation; apart from this, it is the teaching of Mara. (The true nature of all dharmas) "True nature" means the actual state of affairs; "the true nature of all dharmas" means the actual state of affairs of all dharmas. The Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
"What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever."
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says:
"All dharmas are like illusions, and the Tathagata, amid them, by the power of skillful means, is unstained and unattached."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"The bodhisattva mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as they truly are — not inverted, not moved, not retreating, not turning."
(See
The True Nature of All Dharmas
in full.)

(Noble wisdom) The Tathagata's wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma realm — the wisdom that awakens to "all dharmas are originally unborn"; also called the pure dharma-realm wisdom. This sutra says:

"Mahamati, one whose mark of the ultimate self-realized noble wisdom is such that he does not calculate or attach to any mark of dharma, gains the body of the samadhi of illusion, and advances and brings forth conduct at the stage of all Buddhas."
It also says:

"The Buddha told Mahamati: What former sages knew, they transmitted to one another — that false imagining has no nature. The bodhisattva mahasattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, observes with self-realization, not relying on another, free from the views of false imagining, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage; this is called the mark of self-realized noble wisdom."

No gate is the dharma gate" — "no gate" does not mean that there is no gate. The "no" here is not the "no" of existence and non-existence; it is the true nature of all dharmas that transcends existence and non-existence — originally there is not a single thing. The "gate" here means a path, a key. "No gate is the dharma gate" means:
taking "no" as the path of practice.

In other words, by the principle of the true nature of all dharmas, one shatters the dream of ignorance and perfectly accomplishes the Buddha Way. Then what is used to shatter it? The mind is used to shatter it. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence." In the Lankavatara Sutra, this method of practice, "no," is taught everywhere, and summed up it is:

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two selves are both relinquished; the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are entirely transcended; one realizes self-realized noble wisdom and enters the Tathagata's stage.
— This is the main content of the Lankavatara Sutra.

blocks.text: 2. The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures

inline.s: The main content of the Lankavatara Sutra is:

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two selves are both relinquished; the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are entirely transcended; one realizes self-realized noble wisdom and enters the Tathagata's stage.
This sutra says:
"The five dharmas and the three self-natures, together with the eight kinds of consciousness, and the two kinds of no-self, comprise the Mahayana
(encompass all of the Great Vehicle)
(Mahayana) Short for Mahayana; rendered in Chinese as the Great Vehicle.
(The five dharmas)

All dharmas can be summed up in five: mark, name, discrimination, right wisdom, and suchness. 1. Mark: the myriad phenomena, whose forms each differ. 2. Name: positing various names based on those marks, in order to express them. 3. Discrimination: thinking about and distinguishing the marks and names of all things, whereby size, height, beauty and ugliness, right and wrong, and so on appear. 4. Right wisdom: the unstained mind and mental factors, far from discrimination, regarding name and mark as mutually external, free from permanence and annihilation, knowing in accordance with principle. 5. Suchness: the realm realized by right wisdom, the essence of true suchness in which mind and object are both quiescent.

The relations among the five dharmas are: based on "mark" one establishes "name"; based on "name" one thinks and calculates ("discrimination"); by "right wisdom" one is free from "discrimination" and realizes "suchness." Among these, "discrimination" goes from delusion into delusion, sinking lower and lower; "right wisdom" goes from awakening into awakening, advancing higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage. In the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka,

"the Buddha said: Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva, relying on the teachings of the sages, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet, he observes with self-realization, not awakened by another, free from the views of discrimination, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage. Such practice is called the mark of conduct of self-realized noble wisdom."
(The three natures)

That is, the three self-natures: 1. The self-nature of dependent arising: all dharmas arise depending on various conditions, have no substantial reality, and are merely illusory; hence the self-nature of dependent arising. 2. The self-nature of false imagining: sentient beings are deluded and do not understand that all dharmas are originally empty; they falsely calculate regarding their own bodies and all dharmas, grasping each as truly existent; hence the self-nature of false imagining. 3. The self-nature of perfect accomplishment: the tathagatagarbha mind (the mind in the state of tathagatagarbha) is limpid and ever quiescent, perfectly accomplished; hence the self-nature of perfect accomplishment.
The Tang translation says:
"Ignorance, craving, and karma — the various minds arise depending on them; thereby I understand this as the nature of dependent arising
(the self-nature of dependent arising)
. Falsely discriminating things as existent is what the deluded mind pursues; these distinctions are entirely nonexistent, yet delusion falsely counts them as existent
(the self-nature of false imagining)

. When the mind is bound by conditions, it arises in sentient beings; if conditions are far removed, I say nothing is seen. Having departed from all conditions, the marks discriminated by itself no longer arise in the body; this I call
(means)
no going. What arises in the minds of sentient beings — the grasping and the grasped — all that is seen is without mark; foolish people falsely discriminate, revealing the alaya
(the consciousness-store)
. The supreme storehouse consciousness, free from grasped and grasper, I call true suchness
(the self-nature of perfect accomplishment — the tathagatagarbha)

(Translation: Craving (clinging) born of ignorance, and karma — the various minds arise depending on them; thereby I understand that this is the self-nature of dependent arising. Falsely discriminating dharmas as existent is what the deluded mind pursues; in reality these myriad phenomena are without distinction (the true nature of all dharmas), yet the deluded mind falsely counts them as existent — this is the self-nature of false imagining. When the mind is bound by conditions, it arises in sentient beings; if conditions are far removed, I say nothing is seen. Having departed from all conditions, the marks discriminated by itself no longer arise in the body; this I call no going. What arises in the minds of sentient beings — the grasped and the grasping — all that is seen is in reality without mark, yet foolish people falsely discriminate various marks, and so the one mind becomes the evolving consciousnesses (the consciousness-store). The supreme storehouse consciousness, free from grasping and grasped, I call the self-nature of perfect accomplishment — the tathagatagarbha.)

(Revealing the alaya) Among the eight consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mental, manas, and alaya), the alaya is principal, and the other seven are all derived from it; therefore sutras and treatises often use it to represent the totality of the eight consciousnesses — the consciousness-store.
(The self-nature of perfect accomplishment) The tathagatagarbha. This sutra says:
"Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva should be well versed in the three self-natures. What are the three self-natures? They are the imagined self-nature
(the self-nature of false imagining)
, the self-nature of dependent arising, and the accomplished self-nature
(the self-nature of perfect accomplishment)

. Mahamati, the self-nature of false imagining arises from marks. Mahamati said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, how does the self-nature of false imagining arise from marks?' The Buddha told Mahamati: 'The marks of the things of dependent arising, and the marks of things as they appear in activity — attachment to these gives rise to two kinds of self-nature of false imagining. These are established by the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: namely, attachment to the marks of names, and attachment to the marks of things. Attachment to the marks of names means attachment to inner and outer dharmas. Attachment to the marks of things means attachment to the general and particular marks of just those inner and outer dharmas. These are called the two kinds of marks of the self-nature of false imagining. Whatever arises depending on a support or a condition is called dependent arising. What is the self-nature of accomplishment? It is freedom from the false imagining of the marks of names and the marks of things, what is attained by noble wisdom, and the realm reached by the conduct of self-realized noble wisdom; this is called the self-nature of accomplishment,
the tathagatagarbha mind
The Tang translation says:

"Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva should well know the marks of the three self-natures. What are the three? They are: the self-nature of false imagining, the self-nature of dependent arising, and the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. Mahamati, the self-nature of false imagining arises from marks. How does it arise from marks? It is because one gives rise to attachment depending on the appearance of the various kinds of things of dependent arising. Mahamati, that attachment to the marks of things gives rise to two kinds of false imagining, which are proclaimed by all Tathagatas, namely: attachment to the marks of names, and attachment to the marks of things. Mahamati, attachment to the marks of things means attachment to inner and outer dharmas; attachment to the marks of names means attachment to the general and particular marks within those inner and outer dharmas. These are called the two kinds of marks of the self-nature of false imagining. Mahamati, what arises from a support and a condition is the nature of dependent arising. What is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the true suchness reached by self-realized noble wisdom, free from all discrimination of the marks of names and the marks of things. Mahamati,
this is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment, the tathagatagarbha mind

The relations among the three self-natures are: when the one mind is deluded about the self-nature of dependent arising of all dharmas and falsely grasps all dharmas as truly existent, it turns the tathagatagarbha into the eight consciousnesses (the consciousness-store); this is the self-nature of false imagining (the consciousness-store), and so one falls from Buddhahood into being a sentient being. When the one mind awakens to this self-nature of dependent arising and realizes the dharma of non-arising, it restores the eight consciousnesses (the consciousness-store) to the tathagatagarbha; this is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (the tathagatagarbha), and so one goes from being a sentient being to Buddhahood.

Consciousness (the one mind) has two states, delusion and awakening. The state of delusion is the sentient being (among the ten dharma realms, all except the Buddha are called sentient beings); the state of awakening is the Buddha. Awakening is the original state of consciousness, called the storehouse consciousness, also named the tathagatagarbha; delusion is the state of ignorance in which consciousness flows through birth and death, called the evolving consciousnesses, also named the consciousness-store. Practice means returning to the source, restoring the evolving consciousnesses (the consciousness-store) to the storehouse consciousness (the tathagatagarbha).

(The ten dharma realms) Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four noble realms.
(The eight consciousnesses)
Eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, mental consciousness, manas consciousness, and alaya consciousness. (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
in full.)
(The two selves)

"The self of persons" and "the self of dharmas," also called the two graspings, self-grasping and dharma-grasping. The self of persons (self-grasping): a person is a false combination of the five aggregates, arising when conditions gather and ceasing when conditions disperse; there is no real self-entity, yet sentient beings falsely grasp it as a truly existing self-entity. Breaking the self of persons, one ends segmental birth-and-death and escapes the round of rebirth. The self of dharmas (dharma-grasping): whether Buddhadharma or worldly dharma, all are falsely established depending on conditions and exist in mutual opposition; none has independent existence, yet sentient beings falsely grasp all dharmas as having truly existing essence and function. Breaking the self of dharmas, one ends transformational birth-and-death and perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. The Diamond Sutra says:
"If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata names him a true bodhisattva."

(The five aggregates) Also called the "five shadows." The five aggregates are: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, form refers to matter and is called "form-dharma"; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called "mind-dharma." Form is the body; the remaining four are the mind. Master Yinguang said:

"The five shadows are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Form is the body that is the karmic reward one has evoked; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the illusory, false mind that arises on contact with objects. Through these illusory body-and-mind dharmas, one gives rise to delusion and creates karma with respect to the objects of the six dusts."
(From the Essence of Master Yinguang's Writings) The Nirvana Sutra says:

"At the time of death, relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot compose himself. All the good and evil of his life appear before him. After the warmth has gone, the past five aggregates cease and the present intermediate existence arises. After entering the womb, the present intermediate existence ceases and the future five aggregates arise. It is like a lamp arising and darkness ceasing, a lamp ceasing and darkness arising, continuous without interruption."
The Heart Sutra says:
"Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, when practicing deeply the prajna paramita, illuminated the five aggregates as all empty and crossed beyond all suffering and distress."

(Segmental birth-and-death) Sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the good and evil karma they have evoked, all have a limited lifespan and a differentiated body; hence the name "segmental birth-and-death." One who ends segmental birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. (Transformational birth-and-death) The sages among the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and have ended segmental birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the path, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shift between delusion and awakening differs; the passage from the earlier into the later is just like one round of birth-and-death, so it is called "transformational birth-and-death." One who ends transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
(The two dharmas of existence and non-existence)

Existing dharmas and non-existing dharmas. Existing dharmas refer to the myriad phenomena of the world, all things. Non-existing dharmas refer to things that do not exist, such as turtle hair and rabbit horns. The "existence" here means that the mark exists; the "non-existence" means that the mark does not exist. Existence and non-existence are both spoken in relation to each other: non-existence is spoken in relation to existence, and existence in relation to non-existence. Since all dharmas are nothing whatsoever and originally not a single thing exists, to speak of existence or non-existence is entirely false view. (See
The True Nature of All Dharmas
in full.) The Wei translation says:

"Those of false views debate the arising of dharmas and falsely imagine existence and non-existence. If one knows there is nothing born, one also knows there is nothing ceasing. Seeing the world as all empty and quiescent, such a one does not fall into existence or non-existence."
Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra says:

"Therefore this verse praises the Buddha as 'free from both existence and non-existence.' How profound! The two views of existence and non-existence are thorns in the dharmakaya. What is called self-realized noble wisdom is nothing else: one merely knows this and is free from this, and no real dharma is to be attained at all. This is indeed the ultimate doctrine of this sutra. A practitioner who knows this may be said to practice without practicing and realize without realizing. If for a single thought practice and realization are not forgotten, one falls back into this again — how much more so if one takes discriminating words and letters as attainment! If the observer observes in this way, he may be said to know the true nature of dharmas.'"

(Turtle hair and rabbit horns) This is only an analogy to illustrate the principle and should not be clung to one-sidedly; moreover, in the regions where the Buddha taught there were no green-haired turtles. And the so-called "green-haired turtle" is in fact a turtle on whose back algae grow, appearing as green filaments, which in the water merely look like turtle hair. ("Non-existence" means that the mark does not exist) The "mark" spoken of here means the manifestation of things in the dream of ignorance, which differs from the "mark" of daily life and natural science. Take air: daily life and natural science hold that it is colorless and without mark, but in Buddhadharma it has a mark, because its existence (within the dream of ignorance) can be determined by various means — only the naked eye cannot see it. In fact it has density, weight, cold and heat, motion and stillness; all of these are marks.
(Self-realized noble wisdom)
The Tathagata's wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma realm — the wisdom that awakens to "all dharmas are originally unborn"; also called the pure dharma-realm wisdom. This sutra says:

"Mahamati, one whose mark of the ultimate self-realized noble wisdom is such that he does not calculate or attach to any mark of dharma, gains the body of the samadhi of illusion, and advances and brings forth conduct at the stage of all Buddhas."
It also says:

"The Buddha told Mahamati: What former sages knew, they transmitted to one another — that false imagining has no nature. The bodhisattva mahasattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, observes with self-realization, not relying on another, free from the views of false imagining, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage; this is called the mark of self-realized noble wisdom."
(The Tathagata's stage)
The stage of Buddhahood.

blocks.text: 3. The Lankavatara King's Request

inline.s: The sutra passage is taken from the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka)

blocks.text: The Assembly of Sages

inline.s: [Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Lanka on the peak of Mount Malaya by the seashore, together with a great assembly of bhikshus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.]

This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. At that time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Lanka on the peak of Mount Malaya by the seashore, together with a great assembly of bhikshus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.

(Thus have I heard) This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. "Thus have I heard" engenders faith, proving that this sutra was indeed spoken by the Buddha and that the record is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, he instructed Venerable Ānanda: when compiling the sutras, place the phrase "Thus have I heard" at the head of every sutra, to prove it was truly spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of other paths. The "I" is Ānanda, the compiler of the sutras, referring to himself. Ānanda was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment. Later he left home to follow the Buddha and became his attendant, famed for never forgetting what he heard and for being foremost in learning. When Ānanda left home, the Buddha had already taught the Dharma for twenty years, so he asked the Buddha to repeat all that had been taught before; he also attained the samadhi of self-realization of the dharma-nature, by which he could comprehend all dharmas in samadhi. Therefore after the Buddha's parinirvana, when Venerable Mahakashyapa assembled the sutra collection in the great stone cave of Magadha, five hundred arhats gathered, and the assembly urged Ānanda to ascend the seat and repeat the sutras. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:

"I and Ānanda and others, at the place of King of Emptiness Buddha, simultaneously brought forth the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Ānanda always delighted in much learning, while I always strove diligently. Therefore I have already attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, while Ānanda protects and upholds my Dharma, and will also protect the Dharma-treasury of future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to accomplishment the assembly of bodhisattvas."

(At one time) At that time — the time when the Buddha taught this sutra, when teacher and disciples were in accord in the Way and the capacities of beings and the teaching met. The Tathagata's teaching of the Dharma reaches humans and gods, and its compilation and transmission spread throughout the world; because years, months, and days cannot be made to agree, "at one time" records it. (Teacher and disciples) Teacher and student, master and disciple. (The capacities of beings and the teaching meeting) "Capacity" is the root-capacity of the listeners; "teaching" is the Buddha's bestowal of teaching. Root-capacities differ, so the Buddha, according to their capacities, bestows teachings of greater or lesser depth. "The capacities of beings and the teaching meeting" means that the roots of the listeners at the assembly and the Buddha's teaching respond and accord. (Buddha) Short for "Buddha," here meaning Śākyamuni Buddha. "Buddha" is a Sanskrit sound, rendered in Chinese as "the Awakened One." Inwardly awakened, one is without any false thoughts; outwardly awakened, one is unstained by the six dusts.

(Great bhikshu) "Bhikshu" is the general term for one who has left home and received the complete precepts; males are called "bhikshus," females "bhikshunis." A "great bhikshu" is a bhikshu of lofty virtue and senior years. (Great bodhisattva) Those from the first ground upward are great bodhisattvas. (Great bhikshu) "Bhikshu" is the general term for one who has left home and received the complete precepts; males are called "bhikshus," females "bhikshunis." A "great bhikshu" is a bhikshu of lofty virtue and senior years. (Great bodhisattva) Those from the first ground upward are great bodhisattvas.

[These bodhisattva mahasattvas had all already comprehended the five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and no-self, and were well aware of the meaning that realms are the mind's own manifestation. They sported in the boundless powers of the samadhis and spiritual penetrations of perfect ease, and according to the minds of sentient beings manifested various forms, skillfully taming them. All Buddhas poured water on their crowns with their own hands. They all came to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, and the bodhisattva mahasattva Mahamati was foremost among them.]

These great bodhisattvas had all comprehended the five dharmas, the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two no-selves, and understood the principle that realms are the mind's own manifestation. With the boundless powers of the samadhis and spiritual penetrations of perfect ease, they sported in the three realms, and according to the minds of sentient beings manifested corresponding forms to skillfully tame and deliver them. All Buddhas with their own hands poured water on their crowns. They all came to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, and the bodhisattva mahasattva Mahamati was foremost among them.

(Sporting) When Buddhas and bodhisattvas sport in spiritual penetrations, transforming people as their own delight, this is called "sporting." (Skillful means) The devices, methods, or words adopted to guide and teach sentient beings. (Manifesting various forms) Displaying various bodily forms. As the Universal Gateway Chapter says:
"This Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva has accomplished such merit and virtue, and with various forms travels through all lands, delivering sentient beings."
(Foremost) The leading position in the assembly is called foremost. Sometimes one person is foremost, sometimes several.

blocks.text: The Holy Wisdom Which Attests the Dharma

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One, having spoken the Dharma in the palace of the Dragon King, after seven days came forth from the great sea. Immeasurable hundreds of millions of Brahma gods, Shakra, world-protectors, and hosts of dragons and devas came to welcome the Buddha. Then the Tathagata raised his eyes and beheld the great city of Lanka upon Mount Malaya, and straightway smiled, saying: All the Tathagatas of the past, Arhats and fully and perfectly Enlightened Ones, all preached in this very city the Dharma of the Holy Wisdom they themselves had realized — not the realm of the speculative, perverse views of the heterodox, nor the cultivation of the two vehicles. Now I too shall reveal this Dharma to King Ravana.

At that time the World-Honored One, having taught the Dharma in the palace of the Dragon King, came forth from the great sea after seven days. The great Brahma king, Shakra, and the four world-protecting kings, leading immeasurable billions of devas and dragons, came to welcome the Buddha. Then the World-Honored One looked about and beheld the great city of Lanka upon Mount Malaya, and straightway smiled, saying: In times past all the Buddhas, without exception, proclaimed in this very city the Dharma they themselves had realized as Holy Wisdom — which is not the realm of the speculative, perverse views of the heterodox, nor the cultivation of the two vehicles. Now I too shall reveal to King Ravana this Dharma of the Holy Wisdom realized by oneself (the method whereby Śākyamuni Buddha himself perfectly realized Buddhahood).

[Shakra, world-protectors, and the hosts of dragons and devas] Brahma: the great Brahma king. Shakra: Indra, lord of the Trayastrimsha heaven. World-protectors: the four heavenly kings. The hosts of dragons and devas: the eight classes of devas and dragons. [The Holy Wisdom realized by oneself] The method of cultivation whereby the Buddha himself realized Holy Wisdom (Buddhahood). [Holy Wisdom] The wisdom that rightly illumines the ultimate truth and is free from false discrimination is called Holy Wisdom. The Tang translation says:

“Mahamati, the great bodhisattva, relying on the holy teachings, engages in no discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, he contemplates self-awakening, not awakened by another, free from the view of discrimination, ascending ever higher until he enters the Tathagata stage. Such cultivation is called the course of the self-realized Holy Wisdom.”

[Tathagata, Arhat, fully Enlightened] Tathagata, Arhat, and fully and perfectly Enlightened One are three of the Buddha's ten epithets. Tathagata: riding the path of Suchness, he passes from cause to fruit and realizes perfect enlightenment. Arhat: worthy of the offerings of humans and devas. Fully and perfectly Enlightened One: the true, universal, and equal enlightenment — that is, the Buddha's enlightenment. [The two vehicles] The sravaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle. Those who awaken through cultivating the Dharma of the four noble truths are collectively the sravaka vehicle; those who awaken through cultivating the twelve links of dependent arising are collectively the pratyekabuddha vehicle.
“Now I too shall reveal this Dharma to King Ravana.”
: Now I too shall reveal to King Ravana this Dharma of the Holy Wisdom realized by oneself (revealing the Dharma the Buddha himself realized as Holy Wisdom). This is the center of this sutra.

blocks.text: Requesting the Buddha to Speak the Dharma

inline.s: At that time Ravana, king of the yakshas, through the Buddha's spiritual power heard the Buddha's voice and knew from afar that the Tathagata had come forth from the dragon palace, surrounded by Brahma, Shakra, world-protectors, devas, and dragons. Seeing the waves of the sea, he contemplated the great ocean of the alaya-consciousness of his own assembly; as the wind of the objective world stirred, the waves of the evolving consciousness arose. Filled with joy, he proclaimed aloud in his city: I shall go to the Buddha and beg him to enter this city, that I and all the devas and humans may in the long night obtain great benefit.

At this time Ravana, king of the yakshas, through the Buddha's spiritual power heard the Buddha's voice and knew from afar that the World-Honored One had come forth from the dragon palace, surrounded by the great Brahma king, Shakra, the four world-protecting kings, and hosts of devas and dragons. Seeing the great sea surging with waves, he reflected that the ocean of the alaya-consciousness of the gathered assembly likewise rose in waves under the blowing of the wind of the objective world, becoming the ocean of the evolving consciousness. Thereupon he rejoiced, and proclaimed aloud within his city of Lanka: I shall go to see the World-Honored One and beg him to enter this city and preach the wondrous principle that causes the waves of the evolving consciousness of all beings to subside and the ocean of mind to become clear — that I and all the devas and humans may in the long night of ignorance obtain great benefit.
[Alaya-consciousness] The fundamental nature (the Tathagata-garbha).
[Evolving consciousness] The nature of consciousness. (Regarding self-nature, fundamental nature, and the nature of consciousness, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha

Having spoken these words, accompanied by his retinue, he rode in a palace of flowers to the place of the World-Honored One. Having arrived, he descended from the palace, circled to the right three times, and offered music and song in worship of the Tathagata. The instruments he held were all of great blue indra-gems, inlaid with lapis lazuli and other jewels, and wrapped in priceless fine garments. Their sound was exquisite, the notes harmonious; and he spoke a gatha praising the Buddha:
Having spoken these words, King Ravana and his retinue rode
in a palace of flowers (a palace adorned with wondrous flowers) and went forward

to the place of the World-Honored One. Upon arriving, he descended from the palace and circled to the right three times, offering music and dance in worship of the World-Honored One. The instruments he held were all of great blue indra-gems, inlaid with lapis lazuli and other jewels, and wrapped in priceless fine garments. Their sound was exquisite, the notes harmonious and elegant. And in this he spoke a gatha praising the Buddha:
[Ji (
ji
) le]
Music and dance.
The treasury of Mind's self-nature, without self, freed from the defilement of views; the knowledge of realized wisdom — O Buddha, please proclaim it for us.
The wondrous principle of mind and self-nature — without self and free from discrimination and clinging — is what the self-realized Holy Wisdom knows; may the Buddha proclaim it for us.

[Treasury of Dharma] The teaching of the Buddha; because the teaching contains and stores many meanings, it is called the treasury of Dharma. [No-self] No self of persons and no self of dharmas (see the note on “the two selves” later). [Defilement of views] As for “view” (an opinion or standpoint), it is clinging and discrimination. When clinging and discrimination arise, that is called the defilement of views.

Good dharmas are his body; the realized wisdom is his ever-bliss. Sovereign of free transformation, may he enter the city of Lanka. The Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the past have all dwelt within this city. This host of yakshas, of one mind, longs only to hear the Dharma.

Gathering good dharmas as his own practice, he attains Holy Wisdom and abides forever in bliss; O great World-Honored One, sovereign of free transformation, may you enter the city of Lanka and preach for us this most wondrous Dharma. The Buddhas and great bodhisattvas of the past have all dwelt within this city. This host of yakshas, of one mind, longs only to hear the Dharma.
[Good dharmas]

Dharmas that are reasonable and beneficial; thus the five precepts and the ten good actions are the good dharmas of the world, while the three studies and the six perfections are the good dharmas of the world-transcending.
At that time Ravana, king of Lanka, having praised the Buddha with the tone of the Dutaka melody, again spoke a verse in song:
At that time Ravana, king of Lanka, having praised the Buddha with the Dutaka melody, again spoke a verse in song:
[Dutaka melody]
A certain rhythmic cadence used in singing and in praise.

The World-Honored One abode seven days in the sea, then came from the dragon palace and calmly rose to this shore. I, with my maidens, the yaksha train, and Sukasrana the wise among the host, all came by their spiritual power to the Tathagata's place. Each descended his flower-palace, bowing to the world's honored one; and again by the Buddha's awesome might, each before the Buddha declared his own name:

The World-Honored One dwelt for seven days in the ocean of Magadha; then he came forth from the dragon palace and calmly rose to this shore. I, with my maidens, the yaksha retinue, and Sukasrana, the wisest in the assembly, all by their spiritual power came before the World-Honored One. Each descended from his flower-palace and bowed in homage to the world's honored one (the World-Honored One); and again, through the Buddha's awesome might, each declared his own name before the Buddha:
[Maidens]
Palace women.

I am the rakshasa king, ten-headed Ravana; now have I come to the Buddha's place. O Buddha, receive me and all beings dwelling in the city of Lanka. The countless Buddhas of the past all ascended the jewel-mountain's summit, abode in Lanka's city, and preached the Dharma self-realized. So should the World-Honored One abide upon that jewel-adorned hill, mid a bodhisattva throng, and speak the pure Dharma. We today, with the dwellers of Lanka, of one mind together, long to hear the wordless self-realized Dharma.

I am the rakshasa king, ten-headed Ravana; today I have come before the Buddha. O Buddha, receive me and all beings in the city of Lanka. The countless Buddhas of the past all ascended to the summit of Lanka, dwelt in the city of Lanka, and preached the Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom. The World-Honored One should likewise abide in the city of Lanka adorned with countless jewels, surrounded by the host of bodhisattvas, preaching this pure Dharma. We today, with the great assembly in the city of Lanka, of one mind together, long to hear the wordless Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom.
[The jewel-mountain's peak] The summit of Mount Lanka. The Entry of Lanka Sutra, in the chapter on the Buddha's Invitation, says:

“That mountain was formed of manifold precious substances, the gems inlaid one with another, radiant and blazing, like a mountain of gold illumined by a hundred thousand suns. Moreover, there were countless gardens of flowers and fragrant trees, all groves of jewel-perfumed forests; the gentle breeze struck them, swaying the branches and stirring the leaves, and a hundred thousand subtle fragrances were at once diffused while a hundred thousand subtle sounds arose together. The layered crags wound in and out, and everywhere were the halls of sages, the chambers of spirits, and stone chapels, formed of countless gems, transparent within and without, so that the light of sun and moon could no longer appear — all these were places where the immortals and sages of old, contemplating the Dharma of reality as it is, attained the Way.”
[Self-realized Dharma] The Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom.

I mind the Buddhas of all times, the countless Ones, round whom bodhisattvas throng, preaching the Lanka's words. This Entry-Lanka scripture, praised by the Buddhas gone — O Buddha, as the supreme of old, unfold it to the assembly. I beg you, for the countless yaksha host your pity's due, to enter that jewel-adorned city and this wondrous Door renew.

I call to mind all the countless Buddhas of the ages past, preaching the Lanka Sutra surrounded by hosts of bodhisattvas. This Entry of Lanka scripture was praised by the Buddhas of old; O Buddha, like the Buddhas of the past, do you also unfold it for the assembly. I beg the Buddha, out of compassion for the countless yaksha host, to enter the city of Lanka adorned with many jewels, and speak this Door of the wondrous Dharma.

Wondrous is this city of Lanka, adorned with jewels of many kinds; its walls are not of earth and stone, its nets all treasures fine. This yaksha host once made offerings to the Buddha, their cultivation free from all faults, their realization ever clear. Yaksha men and women thirst for the Great Vehicle, themselves believing in Mahayana, and glad that others abide in it.

Wondrous is this city of Lanka, adorned with jewels of many kinds; its walls are not of earth and stone, and its nets are all formed of precious gems. This yaksha host once made offerings to the Buddha, and their cultivation was free from all faults, and their realization ever clear. Yaksha men and women, thirsting for the Great Vehicle, themselves believed in the Great Vehicle and were glad to let others believe in it.
[Mahayana] An abbreviation of Mahayana, rendered in Chinese as the Great Vehicle.

We pray the supreme of the world, for the rakshasa host and the jar-eared retinue, to come to the city of Lanka. In the past, the future, and the present I have diligently made offerings to the Buddhas; I long to hear the self-realized Dharma, the ultimate and Great Vehicle's path. May the Buddha, pitying me and this yaksha host, with all the sons of the Buddha, enter this city of Lanka. My palace, my maidens, and all my garlands, and my delightful garden of no-sorrow — may the Buddha in compassion receive them. Toward the Buddhas and bodhisattvas I withhold nothing, even my own body in service — we pray you receive them in compassion.

We pray the supreme of the world (the World-Honored One), for the rakshasa host and the jar-eared retinue and others, to come to the city of Lanka. In the past, the future, and the present I have diligently made offerings to the Buddhas; I long to hear the Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom, the ultimate path of the Great Vehicle. May the Buddha pity me and this yaksha host, together with the great bodhisattvas, and enter this city of Lanka. My palace, my maidens, and all my garlands, and my lovely garden of no-sorrow — I offer all to the Buddha; may the Buddha pity us and receive them. Toward the Buddhas and bodhisattvas I withhold nothing, even my own body in tender service — we pray the World-Honored One, out of compassion, to receive it.
[Jar (
weng
) eared] A description of the rakshas' ears being as large as jars.

blocks.text: The Buddha Accepts the Invitation

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One, having heard these words, told him: O yaksha king, the great teachers (the Buddhas) of past ages, all pitying you, accepted your invitation, went to the jewel-mountain and preached the self-realized Dharma; the Buddhas of the future shall do likewise. This is the dwelling place of those who cultivate the deep contemplation and abide in the bliss of the Dharma in this very life; I and the bodhisattvas, pitying you, accept your invitation. Having spoken these words, he remained silent.

At that time the World-Honored One, having heard these words of King Ravana, told him: O yaksha king, all the great teachers (the Buddhas) of past ages, pitying you, accepted your invitation, went to the jewel-mountain of Lanka and preached the Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom; so too shall the Buddhas of the future. This is the dwelling of those who cultivate deep contemplation and abide in the bliss of the Dharma in this very life; I and the bodhisattvas, out of pity for you, accept your invitation. Having spoken, the World-Honored One remained silent.
[Abiding in the bliss of the Dharma in this very life]
Cultivating meditative concentration, free from all false thinking, body and mind quiescent, one receives in this very life the bliss of Dharma-joy and abides in it steadfast.

At that time King Ravana offered the Buddha the wondrous flower-palace upon which he had ridden. The Buddha sat upon it, and the king and the bodhisattvas went before and behind to lead and follow; countless maidens sang and praised, making offerings to the Buddha, and they went to that city. Upon arriving at that city, King Ravana and his retinue made manifold superior offerings. The boys and girls among the yaksha host offered the Buddha a net of jewels. King Ravana made an offering of a precious garland and hung it upon the neck of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas. Then the World-Honored One and the bodhisattvas, having received the offerings, each in brief set forth the profoundly deep Dharma of the self-realized realm.

At that time King Ravana offered the Buddha the wondrous flower-palace on which he had ridden. The Buddha sat upon it, and King Ravana and the bodhisattvas went before and behind to lead and follow; countless maidens sang and praised, making offerings to the Buddha, and they went to the city of Lanka. Upon arriving, King Ravana and his retinue made manifold superior offerings. The boys and girls among the yaksha host offered a net of jewels to the Buddha. King Ravana offered a precious garland and hung it on the neck of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas. Then the World-Honored One and the bodhisattvas, having received the offerings, each in brief set forth for King Ravana and his retinue the profoundly deep Dharma of the self-realized realm.

blocks.text: Urging Mahamati to Question

inline.s: At that time King Ravana and his retinue made further offerings to the bodhisattva Mahamati, and exhorted him, saying:
At that time King Ravana and his retinue again made offerings to the bodhisattva Mahamati, and exhorted him, saying:

Now I invite the great one to ask the World-Honored One of the self-realized wisdom-realm of all the Tathagatas. I, with the yaksha host and these bodhisattvas, of one mind long to hear — therefore we all urge you. You are a cultivator, the most excellent in speech; therefore we revere you and urge you to ask the Dharma. The pure self-realized Dharma ultimately enters the Buddha-stage, free from the heterodox and the two vehicles, and from all their faults.

Now I respectfully invite the great being to question the World-Honored One concerning the realm of self-realized Holy Wisdom of all the Tathagatas. I, with the yaksha host and these bodhisattvas, with one mind long to hear — therefore we all urge you. You are the most excellent in speech among cultivators; therefore we revere you and urge you to ask the Dharma. The pure Dharma of self-realized Holy Wisdom ultimately enters the Buddha-stage, free from the heterodox, the two vehicles, and all their faults.

blocks.text: The King of Lanka Awakens

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One, by his spiritual power, transformed within that mountain countless jewel-mountains, all adorned with the wonderful gems of the devas, in the hundreds of thousands of millions. On each mountain appeared a Buddha-body; before each Buddha was King Ravana and his assembly; and all the lands in the ten directions appeared within them. In each land there was a Tathagata; before each Buddha was King Ravana with his retinue; and in the Asoka garden of the great city of Lanka, such adornment was in every way without difference. In each there arose the bodhisattva Mahamati to ask, and the Buddha revealed the realm of self-realized wisdom. Having spoken this sutra with a hundred thousand subtle sounds, the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all vanished into the sky and were seen no more.

At that time the World-Honored One, by his spiritual power, transformed within the mountain of Lanka countless Lanka-mountains, all adorned with the wonderful gems of the devas, by the hundreds of thousands of millions. On each mountain appeared a Buddha-body; before each Buddha was King Ravana with his assembly; and all the lands in the ten directions appeared within them. In each land there was a Tathagata; before each Buddha was King Ravana with his retinue; and in the Asoka garden of the great city of Lanka, such adornment was in every way the same. In each arose the bodhisattva Mahamati to ask, and the Buddha revealed to the great assembly the realm of self-realized Holy Wisdom. Having spoken this sutra with a hundred thousand subtle sounds, the Buddha and the bodhisattvas all vanished into the sky and were seen no more.

King Ravana saw only himself abiding in his own palace, and reflected: Who was it that spoke? Who heard the words? What was seen? Who was the seer? The Buddha, the cities, the multitude of jewels, mountains and forests — where are these things now? Were they made in a dream? Conceived by magic? Like the Gandharva city? Seen through a film over the eyes? Deceived by a mirage? Like the stone woman's child in a dream? Like the turning wheel of fire of smoke and flame? And he reflected again:
All dharmas are of such a nature — they are but the realm of one's own mind's discrimination.

Deluded common beings cannot understand this. There is no seer, and nothing seen; there is no speaker, and nothing spoken; seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are all discrimination. As when one sees as before one cannot see the Buddha; when no discrimination arises then one does see him.

At that time King Ravana saw only himself abiding in his own palace, and reflected: Who was it just now speaking the Dharma? Who was hearing? What was seen? Who was the seer? The Buddha, the cities, the multitude of jewels, mountains and forests — where are these things now? Were they made in a dream? Conceived by magic? Like the Gandharva city? The flowers in the sky seen by a diseased eye? A thirsty deer deceived by a mirage? Like the stone woman dreaming she bore a child? Like the turning wheel of fire of smoke and flame? And he reflected again: All dharmas are of such a nature; they are but the realm manifested by one's own mind's discrimination. Deluded and inverted common beings cannot understand this truth. In reality there is no seer, and nothing seen; no speaker, and nothing spoken; seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are all the realm manifested by one's own mind's discrimination. If one sees as one did just now, one cannot see the Buddha; when no discrimination arises, then one does see the Buddha.
[The Gandharva city]

Musicians are called gandharvas; they can conjure up palaces and towers for people to behold, so these conjured towers are called the Gandharva city. Mirage-like phantasms such as the sea mirage are also called the Gandharva city.

[The mirage] The vapor produced beneath the blazing sun; from afar it seems to be water, and a thirsty deer longs to drink and so runs after it, but in the end it cannot be had — it is used as a simile for illusion. [The turning fire-wheel] In darkness, when a torch is whirled, it is mistaken for a single wheel of fire — a simile for a false appearance. [Flowers in the sky] A diseased eye wrongly sees flowers in empty space — a simile for an optical illusion. [The nature of all dharmas is thus] The self-nature of all dharmas is like this. Here “self-nature” refers to the inherent, immutable, unchanging nature (essence) of each dharma. [As one sees as before one cannot see the Buddha; when no discrimination arises then one does see him] The Diamond Sutra says:
“All that has form is false and vain; if one sees all forms as non-form, then one sees the Tathagata.”

At that time the king of Lanka at once awakened, freed from all defilement, realized that it is only one's own mind, and abode in non-discrimination. Through the power of the roots of goodness planted in former times, he obtained vision of all dharmas in accordance with reality, not awakened by reliance on another. He could observe skillfully with his own wisdom, forever free from all speculative wrong interpretations, abiding in the great cultivation, a teacher of cultivators, manifesting various bodies. He was adept in skillful means, and knew the signs of advancement upon each stage; he always delighted to be free from mind, will, and consciousness, cut off the view of threefold continuity, free from the attachments of the heterodox, self-awakened within, entered the Tathagata-garbha, and advanced toward the Buddha-stage.

At that time the king of Lanka at once awakened, free from all defilement, realized that the realm is merely what one's own mind manifests, and abode in the wisdom of non-discrimination. Through the power of the roots of goodness planted in former times, he obtained vision of all dharmas in accordance with reality (seeing that all dharmas are illusory appearances), not awakened by reliance on another. He could observe skillfully with his own wisdom, forever free from all speculative wrong interpretations, abiding in the great cultivation, a teacher of cultivators, manifesting various bodies. He was adept in skillful means, and knew the signs of advancement upon each stage; he always delighted to be free from mind, will, and consciousness, cut off the view of threefold continuity, free from the attachments of the heterodox, self-awakened within, entered the Tathagata-garbha, and advanced toward the Buddha-stage.

[Vision in accordance with reality] To know that all dharmas are illusory appearances — “in the midst of seeming arising and ceasing, one sees only non-arising” — this is vision in accordance with reality; whereas sentient beings “in the midst of serene non-arising, wrongly see arising and ceasing.” (See
The Reality of All Dharmas

.) [The stages] That is, the ten stages. In the fifty-two stages of a bodhisattva's cultivation, the tenth group of ten is called the ten stages; upon these ten stages one gradually opens the Buddha-realm and accomplishes the all-knowing wisdom, already within the sage's position, whence they are also called the “ten sages.” [Mind, will, consciousness] Gathering up is called mind; reflecting is called will; distinguishing is called consciousness. Of “mind, will, and consciousness,” mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the alaya-consciousness), will refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas-consciousness), and the consciousness refers to the sixth consciousness. [Free from mind, will, and consciousness] Free from the operation of the consciousness-mind. (Regarding the operation of the consciousness-mind, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha

, the section on “The Operation of the Consciousness-Mind.”) [Threefold continuity] The continuity of the world, the continuity of beings, and the continuity of karma. The continuity of the world means that because beings, deluded, continually create karma, their world of retribution is continually established; the continuity of beings means that because beings have not cut off birth and death, their five aggregates are continually and provisionally conjoined, so beings are continually constituted; the continuity of karma means that because beings continually create karma, the bitter retribution of their evil karma is continually established. [The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of conditioning, and the aggregate of consciousness; these five gather and arise together, so they are called the “five aggregates”; and because they can cover over one's true nature, causing one to be deluded and inverted and to create all karmas, they are also called the “five coverings.” Of these, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called the “dharma of form”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, conditioning, and consciousness pertain to spirit and are called the “dharmas of mind.” These are the five great constituents of body and mind. Of them the aggregate of form is the physical body, while the other four aggregates (feeling, perception, conditioning, consciousness) are the mind. [The Tathagata-garbha] The fundamental nature. (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha

He heard a voice in the sky and within the palace, saying: Excellent, O king! As you have learned, all cultivators should so learn, should so see, and all Tathagatas should be so seen. If one sees all dharmas otherwise, that is a view of annihilation. You should forever be free from mind, will, and consciousness; you should diligently contemplate all dharmas; you should cultivate inner practice, not adhere to outward views, nor fall into the two vehicles nor into the phrases and meanings the heterodox cultivate, their seen realms, nor the samadhi-dharmas that should be attained.

He heard a voice issuing from the sky and within the palace, saying: Excellent, O king! As you have learned, all cultivators should so learn, should so see, and all Tathagatas should be so seen. If one sees otherwise than this, that is a view of annihilation. You should forever be free from mind, will, and consciousness; you should diligently contemplate all dharmas; you should cultivate inner practice, not adhere to outward views, nor fall into the two vehicles nor into the phrases and meanings the heterodox cultivate, their seen realms, nor the samadhi-dharmas they should attain.

You should not delight in frivolous talk and jesting; you should not give rise to the views of the Vedas; you should not cling to the ease of kingship; nor should you dwell in the six concentrations and the like. If you can be thus, this is the practice of one who cultivates in accordance with reality: he can overthrow other doctrines, can break evil views, can abandon all clinging to the view of self, can with wondrous wisdom turn the consciousness upon which he relies, can cultivate the bodhisattva's path of the Great Vehicle, and can enter the Tathagata's realm of self-realization.

You should not delight in frivolous talk and jesting; you should not give rise to the views of the Vedas; you should not cling to the ease of the kingly position; nor should you dwell in the six concentrations and the like. If you can be thus, this is the practice of one who cultivates in accordance with reality — he can overthrow other evil doctrines, break evil views, abandon all clinging to the view of self, with wondrous wisdom turn the consciousness upon which he relies, cultivate the bodhisattva's path of the Great Vehicle, and enter the Tathagata's realm of self-realization.

[The views of the Vedas] The sayings of the four Veda books, which the heterodox Brahmins revere as spoken by Brahma. [The six concentrations] The four dhyanas of the form realm, plus the intermediate concentration and the not-yet-attained concentration. [The four dhyanas] Four concentrations, cultivating which one can be born into the four dhyana heavens of the form realm: the first dhyana, the second dhyana, the third dhyana, and the fourth dhyana.

You should thus diligently cultivate and study, causing the Dharma you have obtained to become ever purer. Skillfully cultivate samadhi and samapatti; do not cling to the realms of the two vehicles and the heterodox as supreme bliss. As the ordinary cultivator discriminates, the heterodox cling to the view of self, holding to the appearance of self, and grasping at the reality of the qualities; the two vehicles see dependent arising from ignorance, and vainly discriminate within the emptiness of self-nature.

You should thus diligently cultivate and study, causing the Dharma you have obtained to become ever purer. Skillfully cultivate samadhi and samapatti; do not cling to the realms of the two vehicles and the heterodox as supreme bliss. As the ordinary cultivator discriminates, the heterodox cling to the view of self, holding to the appearance of self, and wrongly cling to the qualities as real and so grasp at them. The two vehicles wrongly cling to the flow of the twelve links of dependent arising, beginning with ignorance conditioning formations, as real, and vainly discriminate within the emptiness of self-nature.
[Samadhi]

In Chinese it is rendered: fixed concentration. It means concentrating the mind in a single state. When a cultivator's six senses contact the six sense-objects, if he can refrain from giving rise to mind, from moving a thought, from discriminating, from clinging — that is called “fixed concentration,” which is entering the state of “samadhi.” [Samapatti] In Chinese: equal holding. Free from both drowsiness and agitation is “equal”; keeping the mind focused on a single object is “holding.” It means that one who seeks perfect enlightenment, with the pure enlightened mind, knows that the nature of mind and the sense-objects all arise from transformation, and so gives rise to transformative practice to eliminate all transformations. [Agitation] Swaying. The mind-thoughts waver and cannot be subdued. [Quality (guna)] It means: primary substance.

[The twelve links of dependent arising] The twelve links explain the process of the wandering of beings through birth and death. The twelve links are: ignorance (the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion are the root of birth and death), conditioning (creating various karmas), consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering the womb), name-and-form (the embryo having only a physical form, the six senses not yet complete), the six sense-entrances (the embryo growing into a human form with the six senses such as the eye), contact (on leaving the womb, contact with the external world), feeling (on contact with the external world, feeling of pleasure and pain arises), craving (toward objects, craving arises), grasping (pursuit and creation), becoming (the karmic cause that will draw on future retribution), birth (again receiving a future body of the five aggregates), aging and death (the future body gradually grows old and dies). Its process of wandering through birth and death is: ignorance conditions conditioning; conditioning conditions consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense-entrances; the six sense-entrances condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; birth conditions aging and death. Contemplating the twelve links of dependent arising is the method of cultivation of the pratyekabuddha.

King of Lanka, this Dharma is supreme and is the path of the Great Vehicle; it can cause one to accomplish self-realized Holy Wisdom, and to receive a superior life among the various realms of existence. King of Lanka, this Great Vehicle practice breaks the film of ignorance, extinguishes the waves of consciousness, and does not fall among the evil practices of the heterodox. King of Lanka, the heterodox practitioner clings to self and composes various wrong doctrines, and cannot proclaim the two meanings of freedom from clinging and the seeing of the nature of consciousness. Excellent! King of Lanka, your having first seen the Buddha and pondered this meaning — such pondering is itself seeing the Buddha.

King of Lanka, this Dharma is supreme and is the path of the Great Vehicle; it can cause one to accomplish self-realized Holy Wisdom, and to receive a superior and marvelous life among the various realms of existence. King of Lanka, this Great Vehicle practice breaks the film of ignorance, extinguishes the waves of consciousness, and does not fall among the evil practices of the heterodox. King of Lanka, the heterodox practitioner clings to self and composes various wrong doctrines, and cannot proclaim the two meanings of freedom from clinging and the seeing of the nature of consciousness. Excellent! King of Lanka, your having first seen the Buddha and pondered this meaning — such pondering is itself seeing the Buddha.

[The various realms of existence] All realms of existence. Among “existence” there are the distinctions of the three existences, the four existences, the seven existences, the nine existences, and the twenty-five existences. [The nature of consciousness] That is, the element of consciousness. It is said that in a former kalpa the bodhisattva Maitreya, at the place of the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp, left the home life and cultivated the samadhi of mind-only consciousness; only when the Buddha Dipamkara appeared did he accomplish the supreme, wondrous, complete samadhi of consciousness-mind, understanding that all the lands of the Tathagatas, pure or impure, existent or non-existent, are all manifestations of the transformations of one's own mind, and so awakened into perfect penetration. Therefore he said: I contemplate that the ten directions are only consciousness; the consciousness-mind is perfectly bright, and I have attained the tolerance of non-arising — this is the foremost. [The element of consciousness] The nature of consciousness has no source; it arises because the six senses connect with the six sense-objects. When senses and objects mutually arise, discriminating [consciousness] wrongly arises. Sentient beings, confounded, merely follow discrimination and do not know that the nature of consciousness is clear, that it pervades the whole Dharma-realm, that following the minds of beings and according to karma it manifests — and because senses and objects are boundless, consciousness too is inexhaustible, containing and emitting the emptiness of the ten directions — how could it have a place? Therefore it is called the element of consciousness.

At that time King Ravana again thought: May I once more behold the Tathagata. The Tathagata, the World-Honored One, is free and at ease in all contemplation, beyond the dharmas of the heterodox; he can teach the realm of self-realized Holy Wisdom, surpassing all the works of the transformations in response; he abides in the Tathagata's fixed concentration and enters the bliss of samadhi. Therefore he is called the great teacher of contemplation, and also the great compassionate one: he can burn up the firewood of afflictions and discriminations completely, surrounded by the host of the sons of the Buddha, pervading into the minds of all beings, present everywhere, possessed of all knowledge, forever free from all discrimination of things and signs. Now I long to behold again the Tathagata's great spiritual power; because of seeing it, the unattained are attained, the attained do not regress, and freed from all discriminations, abiding in the bliss of samadhi, one grows and fulfills the Tathagata's stage of knowledge.

At that time King Ravana again thought: May I once more behold the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One is free and at ease in all contemplative practices, beyond the dharmas of the heterodox; he can teach the realm of self-realized Holy Wisdom, and surpasses all the matters of the one who transforms in response and that which is transformed; he abides in the Tathagata's fixed concentration and enters the bliss of samadhi. Therefore he is called the great teacher of contemplation and the great compassionate one. He can burn up the firewood of afflictions and discriminations completely; surrounded by the host of the sons of the Buddha, he pervades into the minds of all beings, is present everywhere, possessed of all knowledge, forever free from all discrimination of things and signs. Now I long to behold again the World-Honored One's great spiritual power; because of seeing it, the unattained are attained, the attained do not regress, and freed from all discriminations, abiding in the bliss of samadhi, one grows and fulfills the Tathagata's stage of knowledge.

At that time the World-Honored One, knowing that the king of Lanka was about to realize the tolerance of non-arising, out of compassion manifested his body, causing the objects of transformation to return as before. Then the ten-headed king saw what he had formerly seen: countless mountain-cities, all adorned with jewels; in each city was a Tathagata, an Arhat, fully and perfectly Enlightened, adorned with the thirty-two marks; and he saw his own body standing before each Buddha, each surrounded by Mahamati and the yakshas, preaching the Dharma practiced by the self-realized wisdom; and he also saw the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions — such matters were all without any difference.

At that time the World-Honored One, knowing that the king of Lanka was about to realize the tolerance of non-arising, out of compassion manifested his body, causing the scene just vanished to reappear. Then the ten-headed king of Lanka again saw what he had just seen: countless mountain-cities of Lanka, all adorned with many jewels; in each city was a Buddha adorned with the thirty-two marks, and he saw his own body standing before each Buddha; each Buddha was surrounded by Mahamati and the yakshas, preaching the Dharma practiced by the self-realized wisdom; and he also saw that the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions were all such a scene, without any difference.

[The forbearance of non-arising dharmas] Abbreviated as non-arising forbearance: when true wisdom abides in the principle that “all dharmas originally never arose, and so also never cease,” one no longer falls back.
