The True Characteristics of All Dharmas
; with that, the scripture becomes easy to understand.

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the whole assembly, observing with the eye of wisdom and not with the eye of flesh; like a lion king springing forward and looking back, he rejoiced and laughed aloud. From between his brows, from his thighs, flanks, waist, and neck, and from his shoulders and arms, within the swastika marks, from each and every pore there poured forth immeasurable beams of wondrous light, like a rainbow trailing its radiance, like the sun spreading its light, and like the fierce blaze of the fire at the end of a kalpa. Then in the sky, Brahma, Shakra, and the four heavenly kings, seeing from afar the Tathagata seated like Mount Sumeru on the summit of Mount Lanka, rejoiced and laughed aloud.

At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the assembled audience, observing with the eye of wisdom and not with the eye of flesh; like a lion king springing forward and looking back, he rejoiced and laughed aloud. From between his brows, from his thighs, flanks, waist, and neck, and from his shoulders and arms, within the swastika marks, from each and every pore there poured forth immeasurable beams of wondrous light, like a rainbow trailing its radiance, like the sun spreading its light, and like the fierce blaze of the fire at the end of a kalpa. Then in the sky, the great king Brahma, Shakra, the four heavenly kings, and others, seeing from afar the Tathagata seated like Mount Sumeru, rejoiced and laughed aloud on the summit of Mount Lanka.
[Springing forward] swift and full of momentum. [Looking back (
xi

)] turning around to look back. [The “virtue” mark] The shape of the swastika (wan). This is an auspicious emblem handed down in India; in Sanskrit its name is shrivatsa-lakshana, that is, the auspicious ocean-of-clouds mark. The masters Kumarajiva and Xuanzang translated it as the “virtue” mark; in Wei times, in the Commentary on the Ten Stages Sutra, Bodhiruci translated this word as the “wan” mark. [The fire of a kalpa] One of the three great disasters: the great conflagration that occurs during the kalpa of destruction, burning up to the first dhyana heaven, so that everything is reduced to ashes. [Brahma, Shakra, the four heavenly kings] [Mount Sumeru]

At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the assemblies of gods reflected thus: “The Tathagata, the World-Honored One, is sovereign over the Dharma — for what reason has he rejoiced and laughed aloud? Why has he emitted light, remained silent and unmoved, abided in the realm of his own realization and entered into the bliss of samadhi, and, like a lion king, looked all around and gazed upon Ravana, recalling the true Dharma?”

At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the heavenly assemblies reflected thus: The World-Honored One is sovereign over all dharmas — for what reason has he rejoiced and laughed aloud? For what reason has he emitted light, remained silent and unmoved, abided in the realm of his own realization and entered the bliss of samadhi, and, like a lion king, looked all around, observing the thought of the true Dharma in the mind of King Ravana?

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati, having first received the invitation of King Ravana, and further knowing the mind of the assembly of bodhisattvas, and observing that all future sentient beings delight in clinging to words and phrases, grasping the meaning in dependence on words and so producing confusion, and seizing upon the practices of the hearers and the non-Buddhist teachers —

At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati, having first received the request of King Ravana, and further knowing the minds of the various bodhisattvas in the assembly, and observing that all future sentient beings wholly delight in clinging to words and phrases, grasping the meaning in dependence on words and so producing confusion, and seizing upon the practices of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhist teachers —
[Grasping the meaning in dependence on words] Seeing the finger and not the moon.

Some had this thought: “The World-Honored One has already left behind the realms of the consciousnesses — for what reason has he rejoiced and laughed aloud?” To sever their doubt, Mahamati asked the Buddha; the Buddha then said: “Well said, Mahamati! Well said, Mahamati! You observe the world, pitying sentient beings, who in the three times are bound by wrong views, and wish to cause them to awaken and so ask me. Those of great wisdom, for the benefit of self and others, are able to ask thus.”

They had this thought: The World-Honored One has already left behind the realms of the consciousnesses — for what reason has he rejoiced and laughed aloud? The bodhisattva Mahamati asked the Buddha in order to sever their doubts, and the Buddha then said: “Well said, Mahamati! Well said, Mahamati! You observe the world, pitying sentient beings, who in the three times are bound by wrong views, wishing to cause them to awaken, and so ask me. The great wise ones, for the benefit of self and others, are able to ask in this way.”

[The three times] The past time, the present time, and the future time. Whatever dharma has already arisen and ceased is called the “past time”; what has arisen but not yet ceased is called the “present time”; and what has not yet arisen, not yet come forth, is called the “future time.”

Mahamati, this king of Lanka once asked the past Tathagatas, the Arhats, the Fully Awakened, about the meaning of the two kinds; now he wishes to ask again, and in the future it will be so as well. The characteristics that distinguish these two kinds of meaning — all the hearers and all the non-Buddhist teachers are unable to fathom them.

Mahamati, this king of Lanka once asked the past Buddhas about the meaning of the two kinds; now he also wishes to ask, and in the future likewise will ask. The characteristic of distinction between these two kinds of meaning — all the hearers and all the non-Buddhist teachers are unable to fathom it.
[The meaning of the two kinds] The meaning of Dharma and non-Dharma.

At that time, the Tathagata, knowing that the king of Lanka wished to ask this meaning, said to him: “King of Lanka, since you wish to ask me, you should ask quickly. I will explain it for you one by one, fulfilling your wish and causing you joy; so that with wisdom you may reflect and contemplate, be apart from all discrimination, well know the stages, cultivate the antidotes, realize the true meaning, enter the bliss of samadhi, be received by the Tathagatas, abide in the bliss of shamatha, and be far from the faults of the samadhi of the two vehicles — abiding in the grounds of the bodhisattvas of Immovability, Good Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud,
and truly know that all dharmas are without a self.

Then in the great jeweled lotus palace, with the water of samadhi I shall sprinkle the crown of your head, and once more display countless lotuses surrounding you, with countless bodhisattvas abiding therein, and with the assembled multitudes gazing upon one another in turn — a realm such as this is inconceivable.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the king of Lanka wished to ask this meaning of the two kinds, said to him: “King of Lanka, since you wish to ask me, you should ask quickly. I will explain it for you one by one, fulfilling your wish and causing you joy; so that with wisdom you may reflect and contemplate, be apart from all discrimination, well know the stages, cultivate the antidotes, realize the true meaning, enter the bliss of samadhi, be received by the Tathagatas, abide in the bliss of shamatha, and be far from the faults of the samadhi of the two vehicles — abiding in the grounds of Immovability, Good Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud, and truly know that all dharmas are without a self. You shall, in the great jeweled lotus palace, receive from the Buddhas the sprinkling of the crown with the water of samadhi, and be surrounded by countless lotus seats, with countless bodhisattvas seated upon them, gazing upon you and the great multitudes in turn — a realm such as this is inconceivable.”

[Shamatha] Translated into Chinese as “cessation” (zhi); that is, the meaning of stilling all stray thoughts. [The grounds of Immovability, Good Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud] The eighth, ninth, and tenth of the ten grounds. [The assembly] The great multitude gathered together.

King of Lanka, when you set forth one expedient practice and abide in the ground of cultivation, you will also set forth immeasurable other expedient practices. You will surely obtain the inconceivable matter spoken of above and stand in the Tathagata's position, taking form in response to beings. What you shall attain — all the hearers and all the non-Buddhist teachers, Brahma, Shakra, and the heavenly beings, have never seen.

King of Lanka, when you set forth one expedient practice and abide in the ground of cultivation, you will also set forth immeasurable other expedient practices. You will surely obtain the inconceivable matter spoken of above and stand in the Tathagata's position, taking form in response to beings. What you shall attain — all the hearers and all the non-Buddhist teachers, the great king Brahma, Shakra, and the four great heavenly kings, have never seen.

At that time, the king of Lanka, having received the Buddha's permission, straightway on the summit of the jewel mountain, pure and luminous like a great lotus, rose from his seat, surrounded by the assembly of heavenly maidens; and he conjured up immeasurable flowers of various colors, various colored scents, incense powders and fragrant ointments, banners, canopies, colored umbrellas, crowns, pendants, necklaces, and other superb and wonderful ornaments of adornment never seen or heard of in the world.

At that time, the king of Lanka, having received the Buddha's permission, straightway on the summit of the jewel mountain, pure and luminous like a great lotus, rose from his seat, surrounded by the assembly of heavenly maidens; and conjuring forth immeasurable flowers of various colors, various colored scents, incense powders and fragrant ointments, banners, curtains, and flower canopies, crowns, pendants, and necklaces, and other superb and wonderful ornaments of adornment never seen or heard of in the world.

xian
)] The curtain on a carriage.

And again he conjured up all the various immeasurable musical instruments of the realm of desire, surpassing those belonging to all the world of gods, nagas, gandharvas, and the rest. And again he conjured up the musical instruments formerly seen in the Buddha lands of the ten directions. And again he conjured up a great jeweled net covering all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. And he displayed various supremely fine garments and raised banners as an offering.

Once more he conjured up all the various immeasurable musical instruments of the realm of desire, surpassing those belonging to all the world of gods, nagas, gandharvas, and the rest. Once more he conjured up the musical instruments formerly seen in the Buddha lands of the ten directions. Once more he conjured up a great jeweled net covering all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. He displayed various supremely fine garments and raised banners as an offering.

Having done these things, he rose into the sky to the height of seven tala trees, and in the sky again rained down various clouds of offerings, and made music, descending from the sky. He then sat upon the summit of the jewel mountain, luminous and shaped like a great lotus and second only to the sun in brightness, and with joy and reverence spoke thus: “I now wish to ask the Tathagata the two meanings. These two meanings I have already asked of the past Tathagatas, the Arhats, the Fully Awakened, and those Buddha World-Honored Ones have already explained them to me. I now also wish to ask this meaning; I pray only that the Tathagata will proclaim it to me. World-Honored One, it is the nirmita Tathagata who speaks these two meanings, not the fundamental Buddha. The fundamental Buddha speaks of the realm of the bliss of samadhi, not of what is carried out by false discrimination. Well done! The World-Honored One is sovereign over the Dharma; I pray only that in compassion he speak these two meanings, which all the Buddha's children long to hear.”

The king of Lanka, having done these things, rose into the sky to the height of seven tala trees, and in the sky again rained down various clouds of offerings, played all kinds of music, and descended from the sky. He then sat upon the summit of the jewel mountain, luminous, shaped like a great lotus, and second only to the sun in brightness, and with joy and reverence spoke thus: “I now wish to ask the Tathagata the two meanings. These two meanings I have already asked of the past Buddhas, and those Buddhas have already explained them to me. I now also wish to ask this meaning; I pray only that the World-Honored One will proclaim it to me. World-Honored One, it is the nirmita Buddha who speaks these two meanings, not the Dharma-body Buddha. The Dharma-body Buddha speaks of the realm of the bliss of samadhi, not of what is carried out by false discrimination. Well done! The World-Honored One is sovereign over all dharmas; I pray only that in compassion he speak these two meanings, which all the Buddha's children long to hear.”

[Seven tala trees high] The tala tree is a tall tree; hence to measure the height of a thing one often says “seven tala trees” or “seven tala trees high,” meaning seven times the height of a tala tree. The Lotus Sutra says: “Seated on a throne of seven treasures, rising into the sky seven tala trees high.” [The nirmita Tathagata] The nirmita Buddha — a Buddha body conjured by transcendental power (the responsive body). [The fundamental Buddha] The Dharma-body Buddha. [The three bodies] The Dharma body, the reward body, and the responsive body. The Dharma body, also called the self-nature body or the Dharma-nature body, is the ever-abiding, unceasing true nature originally possessed by everyone; only, we sentient beings are deluded and it does not manifest, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The reward body is formed from the Buddha's wisdom and merit; there is the distinction between the reward body enjoyed by oneself and the reward body enjoyed by others: the reward body enjoyed by oneself is the body in which the Buddha enjoys the bliss of the inner realization of the Dharma, while the reward body enjoyed by others is the body manifested by the Buddha in teaching the Dharma to the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The responsive body, also called the nirmita body or the transformation body, is the Buddha body manifested in response to the karmic conditions of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the king: “You should ask me, and I will explain for you.”
At that time, the World-Honored One told the king of Lanka: “You should ask me, and I will explain it for you.”

Then the yaksha king, wearing again various jeweled crowns and necklaces and various ornaments to adorn his body, spoke thus: “The Tathagata always says: Even the Dharma should be given up, how much the more what is not the Dharma. How then can one give up these two kinds of Dharma? What is Dharma? What is non-Dharma? If the Dharma should be given up, why are there two? If there are two, then one falls into the characteristic of discrimination. To say dharmas have essence or have no essence, are real or not real — all of these are discrimination, and one cannot know the characteristic of non-difference of the alaya-consciousness; such views abide like a hairy circle, and are not the realm of pure wisdom. The Dharma-nature being thus, how can it be given up?”

At that time, the yaksha king, wearing again various jeweled crowns, necklaces, and ornaments to adorn his body, spoke thus: “The Tathagata always says: Even the Dharma should be given up, how much the more what is not the Dharma. How can one give up these two kinds of Dharma? What is Dharma? What is non-Dharma? If the Dharma should be given up, why are there two? If there are two, then one falls into the characteristic of discrimination. To say dharmas have essence or have no essence, are real or not real — all of these are discrimination, and one cannot know the characteristic of non-difference of the store-consciousness; such views abide like a hairy circle, and this is confusion and inversion, not the realm of pure wisdom. The Dharma-nature (the true characteristic of all dharmas) being thus, how can it be given up?”
[Unable to know the characteristic of non-difference of the alaya-consciousness] Mr. Tam Shek-wing's new translation of the Sanskrit original of the Lankavatara Sutra says:
“This is a failure to cognize the non-discriminating characteristic of the store-consciousness.”

[A hairy circle] It is the same as a flower in the sky — the misconception of a diseased eye, used as a metaphor for an illusion. The Yogacarabhumisastra says: “As with an eye, if there are such defects as a cataract, then such morbid phenomena as a circle of hairs appear and are to be seen.”

Then the Buddha said to the king of Lanka: “King of Lanka, do you not see that dharmas such as a jar are impermanent and decaying, and that ordinary people falsely produce discrimination within them? Why do you not now thus know the characteristic of distinction of Dharma and non-Dharma? This is what ordinary people discriminate, not the insight of realization. Ordinary people fall into various characteristics; they are not those who realize. King of Lanka, as when a palace or garden is burned and you see various flames — the nature of fire is one, but the flames that issue forth, owing to the strength of the fuel, are long and short, large and small, each different. Why do you not now thus know the characteristic of distinction of Dharma and non-Dharma?”

Then the Buddha said to the king of Lanka: “King of Lanka, do you not see that dharmas such as a jar are impermanent and decaying, and that ordinary people falsely produce discrimination within them? Why do you not now thus know the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma? This characteristic of distinction is what ordinary people discriminate, not the insight of realization. Ordinary people fall into various characteristics; they are not those who realize with sage wisdom. King of Lanka, as when fire burns a palace and garden and you see various flames — the nature of fire is one, but because of the strength of the fuel the flames that issue forth differ as long and short, large and small (this metaphor illustrates that the essence is one while the characteristics are many). Why do you not now thus know the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma?”

King of Lanka, as a single seed gives rise to the sprout, the stem, the branches, the leaves, and the flowers and fruits, with immeasurable differences. Thus it is with external dharmas, and thus also with internal dharmas. That is, with ignorance as condition, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields and all dharmas arise, and in the three realms one takes rebirth in the various destinies, with suffering and bliss, good and bad, speech and silence, conduct and rest, each different. Again, as with the various consciousnesses, though their characteristic is one, in accordance with the realm there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, defiled and pure, good and evil. King of Lanka, not only do the dharmas above have differences, but also, when practitioners cultivate the practice of contemplation, what their own wisdom carries out likewise sees characteristics of difference — how much the more so for Dharma and non-Dharma, which have manifold distinctions and discriminations? King of Lanka, as for the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma, know that it is all on account of the discrimination of characteristics.

King of Lanka, as a single seed, when sprouting, when growing a stem, when putting forth branches, when growing leaves, when blooming, and when bearing fruit — all these characteristics have immeasurable differences among themselves (this is a metaphor that the essence is the same while the characteristics are a thousandfold different). Thus it is with external dharmas, and thus also with internal dharmas. That is, with ignorance as condition, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields and all dharmas arise; and so in the three realms one takes rebirth in the various destinies, with suffering and bliss, good and bad, speech and silence, conduct and rest, each different. Again, as with the various consciousnesses, though their characteristic is one, in accordance with the realm there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, defiled and pure, good and evil. King of Lanka, not only do the dharmas above have differences, but also, when practitioners cultivate the practice of contemplation, what their own wisdom carries out likewise sees characteristics of difference — how much the more so for Dharma and non-Dharma, which have manifold distinctions and discriminations? King of Lanka, as for the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma, know that it is entirely on account of discriminating characteristics.

[Aggregates, elements, and sense-fields] The five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense-fields. [The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness — the five great constituent elements that form a person's body. [The eighteen elements] Together called the six sense organs (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental objects), and the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness), which collectively are the “eighteen elements.” [The twelve sense-fields] The six sense organs plus the six sense objects are together called the twelve sense-fields. “Field” means that from which things arise; from the six sense organs and six sense objects arise the six consciousnesses. Then the six sense organs, six sense objects, and six consciousnesses form the eighteen elements. [As for the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma, know that it is all on account of discriminating characteristics] As for the characteristic of distinction between Dharma and non-Dharma, know that it is entirely on account of discriminating characteristics. Because when the king of Lanka asked he said: “All of these are discrimination — this is confusion and inversion, not the realm of pure wisdom.” Therefore, when the Buddha answered, he said that as regards the essential nature of all dharmas all are equally empty — where is there any difference? But as regards their characteristics, the differences are a thousand millionfold.

King of Lanka, what is Dharma? It is what the two vehicles and the non-Buddhist teachers, with false discrimination, say has a real existence and the like as the cause of the various dharmas. Such dharmas should be given up and abandoned; one should not discriminate and grasp their characteristics within them. If one sees the Dharma-nature of one's own mind, then there is no clinging. Things such as a jar are taken by the foolish; originally they have no essence. Those who practice contemplation, by means of vipashyana observing truly, are said to abandon the dharmas.

King of Lanka, what is Dharma? It is what the two vehicles and the non-Buddhist teachers, with false discrimination, say has a real existence and the like as the cause of the various dharmas. Such dharmas should be given up and abandoned; one should not discriminate and grasp their characteristics within them. If one sees the Dharma-nature of one's own mind, then there is no clinging. Things such as a jar are taken by the foolish; originally they have no essence. Those who practice contemplation, by means of vipashyana observing truly, are said to abandon the dharmas.
[Vipashyana] Translated into Chinese as “contemplation” (guan). Whenever one undertakes contemplation, one must simultaneously cultivate cessation (shamatha).

King of Lanka, what is non-Dharma? It is knowing that all dharmas are without self-nature and without characteristics, forever apart from discrimination. Those who see truly, whether such a realm exists or does not — toward it they do not even stir; this is called abandoning non-Dharma.

King of Lanka, what is non-Dharma? It is knowing that all dharmas are without self-nature and without characteristics, forever apart from discrimination. Those who are able to see truly, toward such a realm of existence or non-existence, do not stir their minds; this is called abandoning non-Dharma.
[Without self-nature] Having no real entity.

There is furthermore a non-Dharma — the horns of a hare, the child of a barren woman, and the like — which have neither self-nature nor characteristics, and cannot be discriminated, but are said to have names only in accordance with worldly convention. They are not like things such as a jar, which can be grasped and clung to, because they are not taken by the consciousness; such discrimination should also be abandoned. This is called abandoning Dharma and abandoning non-Dharma. King of Lanka, what you asked before, I have now finished explaining.

There is furthermore a non-Dharma — the horns of a hare, the child of a barren woman, and the like — which have neither essence nor characteristics, and cannot be discriminated, but are said to have names only in accordance with worldly convention. They are not like things such as a jar, which can be grasped and clung to, because they are not taken by the consciousness; such discrimination should also be abandoned. This is called abandoning Dharma and abandoning non-Dharma. King of Lanka, the question you asked before — “even the Dharma should be given up, how much the more what is not the Dharma” — I have now finished answering.

This is to say: all dharmas have no essence, but as regards characteristics they can be divided into two kinds: those that have characteristics (that which has a corresponding thing, such as a jar) are called Dharma; those that do not even have characteristics (that which has a name only without the thing, such as a hare's horn or a barren woman's child) are called non-Dharma.
[A barren woman] A woman who is unable to bear children.

King of Lanka, you say: “I have already asked this meaning of the past Tathagatas, and those Tathagatas have already explained it to me.” King of Lanka, you say: “The past is merely discrimination, and so too is the future; I am the same as them.” King of Lanka, those Buddha-Dharmas are all apart from discrimination, having gone beyond all the eloquence of discrimination; they are not like the characteristic of form, but are to be realized by wisdom alone — and for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, the Tathagata preaches the Dharma, and is called the Tathagata by reason of the wisdom that is without characteristics. Therefore the Tathagata has wisdom as his essence. Because wisdom is his body, he cannot be discriminated, cannot be discriminated as an object, cannot be discriminated by the characteristic of self, person, or sentient being. Why cannot he be discriminated? Because the mind-consciousness, depending on a realm, arises and grasps the characteristics of color and form. Therefore he is apart both from that which discriminates and from that which is discriminated.

King of Lanka, you say: “I have already asked this meaning of the past Tathagatas, and those Tathagatas have already explained it to me.” King of Lanka, you say: “The past is merely discrimination, and the future too is discrimination; I am the same as them.” King of Lanka, those Buddha-Dharmas are all apart from discrimination, having gone beyond all the eloquence of discrimination; they are not like the characteristic of form (not like the characteristic of the form-object which the eye can see), but are to be realized by wisdom alone (only to be realized by wisdom). For the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, the Tathagata preaches the Dharma, and is called the Tathagata by reason of the wisdom that is without characteristics. Therefore the Tathagata has wisdom as his essence. Because wisdom is his body, he cannot be discriminated as that which discriminates, cannot be discriminated as that which is discriminated, cannot be discriminated by the characteristic of self, person, or sentient being. Why cannot he be discriminated? Because the mind-consciousness, depending on a realm, arises and grasps the characteristics of color and form. Therefore he is apart both from that which discriminates and from that which is discriminated.
[Eloquence of discrimination] Words that are not practical or real.

King of Lanka, as sentient beings painted in colors upon a wall have no awareness, so too are all sentient beings in this world — they are entirely like this. There is no karma and no retribution; the dharmas too are like this — nothing heard, nothing spoken.

King of Lanka, as sentient beings painted in colors upon a wall have no awareness, so too are all sentient beings in this world. There is also no karma and no retribution; the dharmas too are like this — nothing heard, nothing spoken.

King of Lanka, the sentient beings of the world are like things conjured; ordinary people and non-Buddhist teachers cannot understand it. King of Lanka, those able thus to see are said to have right view; if one sees otherwise, it is called the view of discrimination. Because of discrimination, one grasps at duality.

King of Lanka, the sentient beings of the world are like things conjured up by a magician; ordinary people and non-Buddhist teachers cannot understand this principle. King of Lanka, those able thus to see are said to have right view; if one sees otherwise, it is called the view of discrimination. Because of discrimination, one grasps at duality.

[Because of discrimination, one grasps at duality] Because of discrimination, one grasps at duality, for example: good and bad, impure and pure, increasing and decreasing, adverse and favorable, arising and ceasing, and so on.

King of Lanka, as someone sees his image in water and a mirror, sees his shadow in a lamp and the moon, and hears his echo in a mountain valley, and then produces discrimination and gives rise to grasping. This too is the same — Dharma and non-Dharma are merely discrimination. Because of discrimination, one cannot give up, but only further increases all falsehood and does not reach still extinction. Still extinction is what is called the one object; the one object is the supreme samadhi,
from which arises the self-realized sage wisdom, with the tathagata-garbha as its realm.

King of Lanka, as someone sees his image in water and a mirror, sees his shadow in a lamp and the moon, and hears his echo in a mountain valley, and then produces discrimination and gives rise to grasping. This too is the same — Dharma and non-Dharma are merely discrimination. Because of discrimination, one cannot give up, but only further increases all falsehood and does not reach still extinction. Still extinction is what is called the one object — to be one with the true characteristic of all dharmas (gathering the characteristics back into the nature); the one object is the supreme samadhi, from which arises the self-realized sage wisdom, with the tathagata-garbha as its realm.

[The sentient beings of the world are like things conjured] The sentient beings of the world are like things conjured up by a magician. [The one object] The object that is not two — that is, the meaning of “not two” in the term “the gate of the not-two”: there is no good and bad, impure and pure, increasing and decreasing, adverse and favorable, arising and ceasing, and so on. [Not-two] The one real principle (the true characteristic of all dharmas), equal like Thusness; hence the dharmas have no mutual distinction — this is called not-two. The Heart Sutra says: “These dharmas are empty in characteristic: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.” When a bodhisattva awakens to the one real, equal principle, he is said to enter the gate of the not-two. [The gate of the not-two] The gate of the not-two Dharma. The principle of not-two is the standard of the Buddha's Way, hence it is called “Dharma”; the sages enter through it, hence it is called “gate.” Buddhism has eighty-four thousand gates of Dharma, but the gate of the not-two stands above all the gates of Dharma and can directly see the Sage's Path.
The sutra passages of the following chapters are all taken from the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra.

blocks.text: 4. The Meaning of the One Hundred and Eight Phrases
Mahamati Praises the Buddha

inline.s: Mahamati Bodhisattva, in verse,
praised
the World-Honored One
's
contemplation of stillness (the Muni's contemplation of stillness)
there is
dharma
and no dharma
both
are
left behind;
teaching
sentient beings
to be forever free of all illusion.

At that time, the bodhisattva Mahamati and the bodhisattva Mati, together traveling through all the Buddha lands, relying on the Buddha's transcendental power, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees on the ground, pressed their palms together in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse:
At that time, together with Mati Bodhisattva, who
had roamed
through all the Buddha lands,
the
Mahamati Bodhisattva
relying on the Buddha's
mighty
spiritual
power and empowerment,
rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, pressed his palms together in reverence, and praised the Buddha in verse:

[Baring the right shoulder] When wearing the kashaya, one bares the right shoulder and covers the left shoulder. Originally this was a gesture of respect in ancient India, which Buddhism adopted — that is, when a monk meets the Buddha or greets a master, he must bare the shoulder, signifying that he is ready for labor and service under command.
The world is apart from arising and ceasing, like a flower in the sky; / Wisdom attains neither existence nor non-existence, / And so arouses the great compassionate heart.
Though the World-Honored One abides in the
worldly
world, he is far from the
birth and death of
all dharmas;
with wondrous wisdom he does not cling to existence or non-existence, and in compassion arouses the great compassionate heart.
Because
the birth and death of
all dharmas is like a flower in the
sky,
all are illusions; the Tathagata's wondrous wisdom clings neither to existence nor to non-existence.
Mourning that sentient beings from beginningsless time struggle in pain within the realm of illusion and do not awaken,
he therefore arouses the great compassionate heart, eagerly wishing to save them.
“The world is apart from arising and ceasing, like a flower in the sky” is the
emptiness
that emerges from the mud unstained; “wisdom attains neither existence nor non-existence, and so arouses the great compassionate heart” is the coincident practice of emptiness and compassion.

[A flower in the sky] A flower in the sky (in ancient usage the same as “flower”), a metaphor for an illusion. A person with a diseased eye sees a flower in the sky; the sky originally has no flower, it is only the diseased eye's
illusory vision.
The Perfect Awakening Sutra says:

“Falsely taking the four elements as one's own body, and the shadow of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind — as when a diseased eye sees a flower in the sky, and a second moon.”
The Transmission of the Lamp says:
“With a single cataract in the eye, the flowers of the sky fall in confusion.”

[The four elements] All tangible matter in the world is composed of the four elements — earth, water, fire, and wind — hence they are called “great” — the great earth-element, the great water-element, the great fire-element, the great wind-element. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth, and wind has movement. [The shadow of the six sense-objects] The six sense organs and six sense objects interacting produce the discriminating, clinging, deliberating mind; this deliberating mind is called the shadow of the six sense-objects — the phantom image that appears when the six sense organs are conditioned by the six sense objects.
All dharmas are like illusions, far from the mind-consciousness; / Wisdom attains neither existence nor non-existence, / And so arouses the great compassionate heart.
The World-Honored One,
knowing
that dharmas are like illusions,
thereby
is far from
the
mind-consciousness; with wondrous wisdom he does not cling to existence or non-existence, and in compassion arouses the great compassionate heart.

[Mind, intention, and consciousness] “Mind” has the meaning of accumulation, that is, the eighth consciousness (the alaya-consciousness); “intention” has the meaning of deliberation, that is, the seventh consciousness (the manas-consciousness); “consciousness” has the meaning of discrimination, that is, the sixth consciousness. [Being far from mind-consciousness]

To be far from mind, intention, and consciousness. The later text says: “Being apart from mind, intention, and consciousness, the bodhisattva gradually transforms the body and obtains the Tathagata's body.”
[Being apart from mind, intention, and consciousness] To leave behind the functioning of the mind-consciousness. (As for the functioning of the mind-consciousness, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagata-Garbha
, the section on “the process of the functioning of the mind-consciousness.”)
Far from annihilation and permanence — the world is always like a dream; / Wisdom attains neither existence nor non-existence, / And so arouses the great compassionate heart.
The World-Honored One is far from annihilation
and
permanence,
all
because the world is always
like a
dream; with wondrous wisdom he does not cling to existence or non-existence, and in compassion arouses the great compassionate heart.
[The two views of annihilation and permanence] The view of annihilation and the view of permanence. The view of annihilation is the wrong view that falsely holds that after a person dies
everything is nothing (holding that after the five aggregates cease in this life, they do not arise again);
the view of permanence falsely holds that body and mind abide forever (
holding that the five aggregates are
a permanently
enduring entity
Knowing that person and dharma are without self, / Afflictions and the realm of the knowable too, / Ever pure and without characteristics — / Thus he arouses the great compassionate heart.
Realizing
that person and dharma
both are

without self — afflictions and the realm of wisdom are not truly existing — with wondrous wisdom he does not cling to existence or non-existence, and in compassion arouses the great compassionate heart.
[Eryang] a Sanskrit transliteration, also written Eryan. A free rendering is

the realm of wisdom. The Treasury of the Śrīmālā Sutra (Shengman Baoku) says: “Eryan is called the mother of wisdom, for wisdom is born from it, and so it is also named the realm of wisdom.” [Shengman Baoku] is also written
Treasury of the Śrīmālā Sutra
. Composed by Jizang of the Sui dynasty (549-623
years
), it is
the
most exhaustive commentary on the Śrīmālā Sutra.
“All things are without nirvāṇa, there is no Buddha that attains nirvāṇa, and no nirvāṇa that a Buddha attains.”
Nirvāṇa
is likewise an affair within a dream
there is
no nirvāṇa
of the
Buddhas,
there are
no
Buddhas
that
enter
nirvāṇa.
[No nirvāṇa for all things]
this is an inverted construction, used to heighten the emphasis. Its meaning is: there is no nirvāṇa for anything at all.
The World-Honored One understood deeply that the ten dharma-realms are but a dream of ignorance, and so nirvāṇa and the Buddha
too
are all illusions; there is no real nirvāṇa, no real Buddha who enters nirvāṇa, and no real event of a Buddha entering nirvāṇa
at all
. In the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra the Buddha says:
“Samsara and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike the aspect of flowers in the sky.”
“Far from awareness
and the object of awareness, whether there is or whether there is not, both of these are wholly abandoned.”
The World-Honored One
is far from awareness and its object,
regardless of
whether dharmas exist
or
do not
exist,
these
two are both far removed.
“The Muni, in still contemplation, is thus far from arising; this is called non-grasping, and pure in the present world and the world beyond.”
Reverently
following
the World-Honored One’s
still contemplation,
he is
far from all
illusory forms
such a wondrous dharma
is named non-grasping; pure in the present world and the world beyond
forever
pure.
[Still contemplation] all dharmas are originally still
, without arising or ceasing
. The Avataṃsaka Sutra says:
“Contemplating the still dharma, one extinguishes all stupidity and darkness.”
The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says:

“To know illusion is already to leave it, no further expedient is needed; to leave illusion is already to awaken, and there is no gradation either.” Hence the patriarchs say: “When the wild mind does not rest, this very rest is bodhi.”

blocks.text: Mahāmati Opens the Inquiry

inline.s: Above, Mahāmati’s verse of praise to the Buddha says: “Whether there is or whether there is not, both of these are wholly abandoned.” This is the non-dual dharma-gate, wherein existence and non-existence are both abandoned.
The abandonment of both existence and non-existence is the essential purport of this sutra.

Because what Mahāmati asks below are all dharmas of existence and non-existence (all names, marks, and false imagining), the World-Honored One therefore answers: all of these are negated. This is to cause one to abandon them and let go of them. If one can fully abandon them and let go, that is self-realized noble wisdom.

[The non-dual dharma-gate] non-dual means no duality. The real aspect of all dharmas, all things equally as they truly are, without distinction between one and another, is called non-dual. When a bodhisattva awakens to this principle that all is one, real and equal, it is called the “non-dual dharma-gate.” (For the real aspect of all dharmas, see in detail
the Real Aspect of All Dharmas
article)

“At that time, the bodhisattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha in verse, announced his own name: My name is Mahāmati, who is versed in the Great Vehicle; now with the one hundred and eight meanings, I respectfully ask the most honored of the honored.”
At that time, the bodhisattva Mahāmati
having
praised the Buddha in verse
and finishing
then
announced his own name: My name is Mahāmati, who is versed in the Great Vehicle; now
with
the one hundred and eight meanings,
I reverently
seek instruction
from
the World-Honored One (the most honored of the honored).
Thus what the bodhisattva Mahāmati is about to ask is
the one hundred and eight meanings

, and below he asks in one breath more than a hundred questions, which in fact is to lead toward the exposition of the one hundred and eight meanings; and the World-Honored One’s series of replies finally also come down to expounding the one hundred and eight meanings.
[The most honored of the honored]
the Buddha is
the most honored
among
the honored

, and so the Buddha is called the “most honored of the honored.” [Now with the one hundred and eight meanings, I respectfully ask the most honored of the honored] the “one hundred and eight meanings” are the principles of the “one hundred and eight phrases.” The “one hundred and eight phrases” spoken of here are precisely what the World-Honored One speaks below, and what all Buddhas speak, namely the phrases: “non-arising phrase, arising phrase; eternal phrase, impermanent phrase.
and so on. They are actually one hundred and three phrases; the number one hundred and eight is chosen as a round figure.

The meaning of the ‘one hundred and eight phrases’ is: no marks — within all marks, abandoning all marks. The Tang translation says: ‘Mahāmati! The Buddhas teach the Dharma in order to purify the two kinds of obstacles, the obstructing delusion and the obstructing knowledge,
and thus lead beings to abide progressively
among the one hundred and eight markless dharmas
in
it.” “

[The two kinds of obstacles, the obstructing delusion and the obstructing knowledge] the obstructing delusion and the obstructing knowledge, also called the affliction-obstacle and the knowable-obstacle. [The two obstacles] the affliction-obstacle and the knowable-obstacle. The affliction-obstacle is also called the delusion-obstacle; it refers to afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, which cause sentient beings to revolve through birth and death within the three realms, thereby obstructing the work of nirvāṇa, and so it is called the “affliction-obstacle.” The knowable-obstacle is also called the knowledge-obstacle; it refers to the ignorance and wrong views of sentient beings, which cover over the understanding of wisdom and make it not keen, thereby obstructing the work of bodhi, and so it is called the “knowable-obstacle.” [No marks] within all marks, abandoning all marks. The Diamond Sutra says:
“To abandon all marks, this is called being a Buddha.”
[Clinging to marks] the Diamond Sutra says:
“All that has marks is all false and vain.”
To cling to marks is to take the marks as real, and then to give rise to discrimination (reflective calculation).

Since the “one hundred and eight meanings” are: no marks — within all marks, abandoning all marks. Therefore all discriminations are negated (arising and non-arising, eternal and impermanent, and so on; every kind of discrimination is a mistake) and all should be abandoned. So, the true aim of Mahāmati’s inquiry is not that the World-Honored One should answer these questions one by one, but that the World-Honored One should thereby expound the “one hundred and eight meanings.” Below, although Mahāmati in one breath raises more than a hundred questions, asking everywhere about all dharmas of the world and beyond the world, the World-Honored One does not answer his questions one by one, but only says that all these are without self-nature, and even wittily retorts that he has not asked comprehensively enough; finally it comes down to expounding the “one hundred and eight phrases,” and this is the true point —
“I shall speak to you of the realm of self-realization.”

For the realm of self-realization is precisely to abandon marks, to be far from every kind of discrimination; and Mahāmati’s questions are all views of discrimination, all clinging to marks. The Diamond Sutra says:
To abandon all marks
, this is called being a Buddha.”
The Tang translation says:
“Mahāmati, the great bodhisattvas, relying on the sacred teachings, have no discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet, they observe self-realization, not awakened by another,
abandon the views of discrimination
, and advance higher and higher, entering the stage of the Tathāgata. Practicing thus is called the course of self-certified noble wisdom.”

“The World-Understander, hearing the verse they spoke, observed all the assembly, and said to the Buddha’s children: You who are Buddha’s children, now you may all freely ask, and I shall speak for you the realm of self-realization.”
The World-Honored One (the World-Understander), having heard the verse spoken by the bodhisattva Mahāmati, observed the whole assembly
, and seeing that the time had matured
, said to
them
You
who
are
Buddha’s
children
, may all
freely at will
raise
your
questions, and I
shall
proclaim for you
the realm of the Tathāgata’s
self-realization.
The point is set forth:
the realm of the Tathāgata’s
self-realization
— this is the central topic of this sutra.

[World-Understander] one of the ten titles of the Buddha; because the Buddha understands all things in the world and beyond the world, he is called the “World-Understander.” [Buddha’s children] refers to those who, trusting in the Buddha’s teachings, take up his family enterprise, and seeking to become Buddhas so that the Buddha-seed is never cut off
— this is an epithet of honor for the bodhisattvas
It also refers to the Buddha’s disciples and Buddhist believers.
“At that time, the bodhisattva Mahāmati, relying on the Buddha’s permission, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, asked in verse:
At that time, the bodhisattva Mahāmati, relying on the Buddha’s permission, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined in reverence, asked in verse:
[Permit] the “permit” in “relying on the Buddha’s permission” means to grant permission (to hear and then to grant).
How is thought purified? How does thought increase? How is delusion seen? How does delusion increase?”
How
is
the false
thought
purified? Why
do
false thoughts instead increase
How
are
stupidity and confusion
clearly seen?
Why would
stupidity and confusion instead
increase
[How (yún hé)] in what way, why, how, and in what manner.
“Why do Buddha-lands transform, with marks and with all the heterodox teachers? How is the state of no-reception reached? Why is it called no-reception?
Why do
Buddha-lands
manifest forth all kinds of marks, and all
kinds
of heterodox teachers? How is the stage of no-reception reached? For what reason is it called no-reception?

[Heterodox teachers] those who establish a path outside Buddhism are called heterodox teachers, that is, the wrong teachings outside the truth. [No-reception] not receiving further existence (having done with birth and death, no longer receiving a body in a future life).
Why is it called Buddha’s child? To what place does liberation reach? Who is bound and who is freed?”
For what reason is it called Buddha’s child? When one cultivates the path and attains liberation, to what place will one go? Who is bound? Who is liberated?
What is the realm of meditative concentration? Why are there three vehicles? I beg that you explain.”
What is the state of meditative concentration like? Why are there three vehicles? I beg the World-Honored One to explain this for us.

[The three vehicles] the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. The Śrāvaka vehicle is also called the lesser vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle is also called the great vehicle.
“From what does dependent origination arise? How does the creator and the created come about? How is the explanation of both-and-different stated? How does it increase?”

All dharmas arise by dependent origination — so from what does this dependent origination itself arise? Since all dharmas arise from causes and conditions, why is there still a creator and a created? Why is it said “both exist and do not exist, neither exist nor not exist” (the explanation of both-and-different)? And why does it again go on increasing into all sorts of doctrines?

[The explanation of both-and-different] when describing the existence of things, there are four basic statements: it exists, it does not exist, both exist and do not exist, neither exists nor does not exist. [The four emptiness concentrations] this is the highest concentration of ordinary beings; after the body ends, one may be reborn in the four heavens of the formless realm, but one still cannot leave the three realms. [The concentration of extinction] this is a concentration of the world-transcending path, able to cut off delusion and be done with birth and death, and to escape the round of rebirth. [The thoughtless concentration] this is the meditation that the heterodox teachers cultivate in order to obtain the reward of the heaven of no-thought
a kind of meditation that extinguishes all thought whatsoever
of

the mind. After the body ends, one may be reborn in the heaven of no-thought, with a life span of five hundred kalpas; and when that life span is nearly spent, within the concentration the thought of awareness arises again, and one falls back into the round of rebirth. So although the thoughtless concentration can, within the concentration, keep thought from arising — like a fish in ice or a dormant insect — it cannot cut off delusion and attain the world-transcending noble fruit.

In these ten stages one gradually opens the Buddha-realm and accomplishes the wisdom of all species, and this already belongs to the noble stage, so it is also called the “ten noble ones.”

[Icchantika] an abbreviation of icchantika, meaning one for whom it is extremely difficult to become a Buddha.

[The two truths] the ultimate truth and the conventional truth. The ultimate truth, also called the truth of highest meaning or the noble truth of supreme meaning, is the real principle seen by noble wisdom, that is, the content of dharma-nature inwardly realized, beyond words. The conventional truth, also called the worldly truth or the truth of mundane convention, is the worldly matters and marks that ordinary beings see.

Why is the world like an illusion, like a dream, like the city of the gandharvas, like the heat-haze, and like the moon in water?

[The city of the gandharvas] that is, the city of the gandharvas, a metaphor for an illusion. The performers of the western regions are called gandharvas, and they conjure up by illusion a city, which vanishes in an instant; this is called a city of the gandharvas. And a mirage over the sea is also called a city of the gandharvas. [The heat-haze] also called the blaze of the sun, it is the vapor produced under the scorching sun; seen from afar it looks like water, a thirsty deer longs to drink and ultimately cannot, and this is used as a metaphor for an illusion.
Illusion, dream, the city of the gandharvas, the heat-haze, and the moon in water are five of the ten great-vehicle similes.

[The ten great-vehicle similes] the various great-vehicle scriptures often use ten similes — illusion, the heat-haze, the moon in water, empty space, an echo, the city of the gandharvas, a dream, a shadow, an image in a mirror, and a transformation — to set forth the principle of “emptiness.”

Why are Buddha-lands shaped like sun and moon, like Sumeru and the lotus, lands with the excellent marks of lions, lying on their sides or inverted, like Indra’s net, or all made of precious jewels, like the konghou or the waist-drum, shaped like various flowers, or beyond the light of sun and moon — thus and so, immeasurable?

Why are Buddha-lands of such different shapes? Some are like sun and moon, some like Mount Sumeru or a lotus, some bear the marks of a lion, some are like vessels — tilted or inverted, facing up or lying across — some are like the thousand pearls of Indra’s net reflecting one another, some are like various precious jewels, some are like the konghou or the waist-drum, some are shaped like various flowers, some are beyond the light of sun and moon: why are there such immeasurable Buddha-lands?
[Konghou (
kōng hóu

)] The name of an ancient plucked stringed instrument. [Mount Sumeru] Translated into Chinese as “Wondrous High Mountain.” The mountain is broad above and below and narrow in the middle. It is formed of the four treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal — and so is called “wondrous”; no other mountain can compare with its height, and so it is called “high”; hence the name “Wondrous High,” and it is the king of mountains. This mountain is the center of a small world. The Four Heavenly Kings dwell on its four sides halfway up, the Trāyastriṃśa gods at its summit; at its base are seven ranges of golden mountains encircled by seven seas of perfumed water; beyond the golden mountains lies the salty sea, and beyond the salty sea the great Iron Ring Mountain; the four great continents lie in the four directions of this salty sea.

[Sugata] One of the ten epithets of the Tathāgata. Shan means good, shi means to go: the Buddha cultivates the right path, enters nirvāṇa, and goes toward a good destination, and so is named “Sugata.” [Teacher of Gods]
That is,

one of the ten epithets of the Tathāgata: among the gods and humans of the six destinies there is none who does not take the Buddha as their teacher, and so he is called “Teacher of Gods and Humans.”

[Siddhānta] That is, the four siddhāntas. The Chinese meaning of “siddhānta” is “universal bestowal.” “Xi” means universal; “tan” is the abbreviation of the Sanskrit dāna, which also means giving. The “four siddhāntas” are four methods of universal bestowal. The Buddha bestows them universally upon beings by four methods, so that all beings may complete the Buddha-path; this is called the “four siddhāntas.” First, the worldly siddhānta: at the beginning the Buddha follows the ordinary sentiments of the world, proclaiming shallow and near-at-hand matters and principles, so that hearers may rejoice and accept them in faith. Second, the siddhānta of each individual: the Buddha examines the faculties of beings and the depth or shallowness of their capacities, and speaks the dharma each one needs, so that beings may arouse right faith and increase their roots of goodness. Third, the therapeutic siddhānta: to those with much anger he teaches the contemplation of compassion; to those with much delusion he teaches the contemplation of causes and conditions; to those with many hindrances he teaches the contemplation of Buddha-recitation — thus he universally bestows various medicines of dharma to remove the grave illnesses of beings. Fourth, the siddhānta of the first meaning: the Buddha, seeing that the faculties and conditions of beings are already ripe, speaks for them the real nature of all dharmas, so that beings may together awaken and enter the path of the noble ones. [Delusion of views] The delusion of views is confusion and error in understanding, comprising the five wrong views: the view of a body, the extreme view, the wrong view, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and observances.
Those most excellent sons, the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas — from what cause a hundred transformations? How is it that a hundred have no reception?
The pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas and other Buddha-sons — from what cause is there transformation birth-and-death? Why again is there no reception?

[The two deaths] Fragmentary birth-and-death and transformation birth-and-death. [Fragmentary birth-and-death] For beings in the three realms and six paths, because of good and evil karma, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have divisions, and so their birth-and-death is called “fragmentary birth-and-death.” One who ends fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformation birth-and-death] For the sages of the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended fragmentary birth-and-death, in the course of cultivating the path deluded thought gradually ceases and realization gradually increases; the passage of this delusion and awakening is different in each period, and the moving from the earlier period into the later is just like one passage through birth-and-death — its change is wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable, and so it is called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who ends transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit. [No reception] Entering nirvāṇa and receiving no further becoming

[Six penetrations] The penetration of the divine eye, the penetration of the divine ear, the penetration of knowing others’ minds, the penetration of remembering past lives, the penetration of miraculous movement, and the penetration of the exhaustion of outflows. Worldly people can at most attain the first five, while supramundane persons (those who have ended fragmentary birth-and-death) alone can possess all six. [Seventh stage] The seventh of the ten stages, the Stage of Traveling Far. The bodhisattva cuts off the subtle manifesting forms of all karmic fruits, brings forth supreme practices, broadly transforms beings, perfects the pāramitā of skillful means, and accumulates provisions for traveling far, and so it is called the “Stage of Traveling Far.”

All the questions above were asked at random. For the purpose of the bodhisattva Mahāmati in raising these questions was not truly to obtain answers to them, but to cause the World-Honored One thereby to proclaim the one hundred eight meanings. All these questions are dharmas of existence and non-existence, which must be abandoned in order to enter the self-awakened noble wisdom. Therefore the World-Honored One’s answers below all simply cause one to be free of this and abandon this — all of them are not. If one fully accomplishes this freedom and abandonment, that is the self-awakened noble wisdom.

dharma-gate. The Tang translation says:
“At that time
the World-Honored One, having heard his request for the supreme dharma-gate of the wondrous mind of all Buddhas of the Great Vehicle
, addressed him, saying: ‘Well done! Mahāmati, listen! Listen! As you have asked, I shall speak in due order.’”
Therefore what the bodhisattva Mahāmati requested was in truth the supreme dharma-gate of the Great Vehicle’s wondrous
mind of all Buddhas
— the gate of signlessness. [Knower of the World] One of the ten epithets of the Buddha: because the Buddha understands all things within and beyond the world, he is named “Knower of the World.”
Birth and non-birth, nirvāṇa, emptiness, and the moment — all come down to the absence of self-nature
Birth and non-birth, nirvāṇa, space, and the moment — all the marks of the dependent and principal distinctions of the ten dharma-realms — are ultimately without self-nature.
[Absence of self-nature] All dharmas have no real substance of their own; they are all illusion. (See
The Real Nature of All Dharmas
.) [All come down to the absence of self-nature] Ultimately all are without self-nature.

All come down to the absence of self-nature” — this is the World-Honored One’s summary answer to Mahāmati’s more than one hundred questions! In what follows, the unspoken implication each time the World-Honored One repeats Mahāmati’s question is precisely this: all come down to the absence of self-nature — these are all illusions, which the self-awakened noble wisdom must abandon; why then do you still think and calculate within them? Hence at the end of his reply the World-Honored One says: “Far from all faults of views, the siddhāntas are apart from words.” From this we know that the World-Honored One’s overall answer to Mahāmati’s more than one hundred questions concerning various views is: all come down to the absence of self-nature, far from all faults of views, the siddhāntas are apart from words.

[Ten dharma-realms] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary destinies; the last four are the four noble ones. [Dependent and principal] The dependent reward and the principal reward. Worldly lands, houses, vessels, and the like, which are the support of the body, are called the “dependent reward”; the body of a being, falsely assembled from the five aggregates, which is what past karma has brought about, is called the “principal reward.”
The Buddha’s pāramitās, the Buddha-sons and śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas and the various heterodox, and the formless practices — all such matters as these.

The various pāramitās of the bodhisattvas in the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-sons and śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas and the various heterodox, and the formless practices — all such matters as these are ultimately without self-nature.

[Pāramitā] Also written pāramitā. It means “reaching the other shore.” It is also translated as “crossing over.” It speaks of the great practice by which a bodhisattva both cultivates himself and transforms others: riding this great practice, one can go from this shore of birth-and-death to the other shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called “reaching the other shore.”
[Mount Sumeru, the great seas and mountains, the islands and sandbars and the land of realms, the stars and sun and moon, the heterodox, the gods, and the asuras.]

Mount Sumeru, the four great seas, the four great continents, and the lands of realms, the stars and the sun and moon, the heterodox, the gods and humans, and the asuras, and so on — ultimately all are without self-nature.

[Mount Sumeru] Translated into Chinese as “Wondrous High Mountain”; it is the center of a small world. This mountain is formed of the four treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; no other mountain can compare with its height, and it is the king of mountains. [Islands and sandbars (
zhǔ

)] Small pieces of land in the water. Here it refers to the four great continents. [The four great seas and the four great continents] Mount Sumeru stands at the center of the world; around it are four great seas, and in each of the four great seas is a great continent; beyond the four great seas is the Iron Ring Mountain. These four great continents are called the “four great continents”: the eastern one is called Pūrvavideha, the southern one is called Jambudvīpa (which is where we now dwell), the western one is called Aparagodānīya, and the northern one is called Uttarakuru. [Land of a realm] One great chiliocosm is one land of a realm. [Great chiliocosm] The region taught and transformed by one Buddha is one great chiliocosm. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called one small world. One thousand small worlds gathered together are called one “small chiliocosm”; one thousand small chiliocosms gathered together are called one “middle chiliocosm”; one thousand middle chiliocosms gathered together are called one “great chiliocosm.” Because “thousand” is spoken three times, one great chiliocosm is also called a “thousand-thousand-thousand world.” [Asura] One of the six paths; translated into Chinese as “non-god.” Because they have the blessings of gods but not the virtue of gods, they are like gods yet not gods. They are fond of fighting and often battle with Indra; among them the men are ugly and the women beautiful; their palaces are north of Mount Sumeru, beneath the great sea. [Indra] The lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

[Liberation, sovereign power, and the penetrations; the powers, dhyāna, and samādhi; cessation and the bases of miraculous power; the factors of enlightenment and the requisites of the path; the immeasurable dhyānas; the coming and going of the aggregate-bodies; the cessation samādhi of right reception; and the arising of mind and speech within samādhi.]

Liberation, sovereign power, and the penetrations; the ten powers, dhyāna, and the cessation samādhi; and the four bases of miraculous power; the seven factors of enlightenment and the thirty-seven requisites of the path; the immeasurable dhyānas; the coming and going in birth-and-death of the intermediate-state body; the cessation samādhi within right reception; and the arising of mind and speech while dwelling in samādhi — all these, and so on, are ultimately without self-nature.

[Samādhi] That is, samādhi. [Samādhi] Also written samādhi, samāpatti, and so on; translated into Chinese as “concentration.” It means dwelling the mind on a single object without distraction. [Right reception] The dhyāna in which thought and mind are both stilled and all discursive deliberation has perished, and which accords with samādhi, is called “right reception.”

[Mind, mentation, and consciousness; the five dharmas of selflessness; self-nature, thought, and what is thought; and the two views that appear. The vehicles and the various lineages; gold, silver, and maṇi jewels; the icchantika, the great elements, chaos, and the one Buddha; wisdom and the object of wisdom, attainment and direction; the existence and non-existence of beings?]

Mind, mentation, and consciousness; the two selflessnesses; the five dharmas; the three self-natures; and the capable thinking and the thought, the capable seeing and the seen. The lineages of the various vehicles of the Buddha-dharma; gold, silver, and jewels; the icchantika, the great elements, the chaos of lands, and the one Buddha; wisdom and the sphere of wisdom (the object of wisdom); the existence and non-existence of beings, and so on — ultimately all are without self-nature.
The Tang translation says:

“Mind, consciousness, and no-self; the five dharmas and self-nature; the discerning and the discerned; the two views of the capable and the object. In the lineages and places of the various vehicles; gold, maṇi, and true pearl; the icchantika and the great elements; chaos and the one Buddha. The wisdom and the known, the teaching and the attainment; the existence and non-existence of beings?”

[Mind, mentation, and consciousness] Mind has the meaning of gathering and arousing, that is, the eighth consciousness (the ālaya-consciousness); mentation has the meaning of deliberation, that is, the seventh consciousness (the manas); consciousness has the meaning of distinguishing, that is, the first six consciousnesses. The Sutra of the Six Pāramitās says:
“Gathering and arousing is called mind; the nature of deliberation is named mentation; the meaning of distinguishing is consciousness.”

[Great elements] That is, earth, water, fire, and wind. Because these four pervade all dharmas they are named “great,” and because they can produce form-dharmas they are named “elements.” All material things in the world are produced from the four great elements and cannot exist apart from them, and so they are called the “great elements.” [One Buddha] This responds to the bodhisattva Mahāmati’s earlier question: “Why does the Great Muni proclaim such words as, ‘Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are myself’?” [The object of wisdom] This responds to the bodhisattva Mahāmati’s earlier question: “How is the object of wisdom purified?”

[Elephants, horses, and the birds and beasts — why are they captured? How do simile and cause perfect the siddhanta, together with the doer and the deed? The thickets, the bewilderment, and the six superknowledges — the mind's measure that does not appear, the grounds that never reach one another, the hundred changes, the hundred non-receptions; the art of medicine, works of craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places.]

Why are elephants, horses, and the various birds and beasts captured? How is it that, relying on simile, the siddhanta is brought to accord? And what of the doer and the deed? The thicket, the bewilderment, the six superknowledges, the mind's measure that does not appear, the grounds that do not reach one another, the hundred changes, the hundred non-receptions; the art of medicine, treatises on craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places — all of these, in the end, are devoid of self-nature.
The Tang translation says:

“Of what cause are elephants and horses? How are they taken? How, relying on simile, is the siddhanta brought to accord? The deed and the doer, the many groves and bewilderment. Such is the principle of reality: mind only, without realms, the grounds without sequence, the signless turning-grounds. The art of medicine, works of craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places.”

blocks.text: The World-Honored One Rebuts

inline.s: Above,
the World-Honored One repeated the various names and marks that Mahamati had asked about,
and pointed out that these
are all illusions devoid of self-nature (“
arriving at self-naturelessness
”). Below, in order to further rouse the
Great

assembly so that they would not squander time and energy entangling themselves in these endless vine-tangles, he answered Mahamati's question in turn with even deeper and finer questions, saying: Why do you not ask about such things?

[Vine-tangles] Vines wrap around a tree until it withers. In the lineages (the Chan school), 'vine-tangles' refers to delighting in verbal language and intellectual analysis, leading people to busy themselves with the karmic consciousness; just as vines spread and interweave, so those who hear are instead bound. Those harmed either waste their time at best or go astray at worst.

[Mountains, the earth, Mount Sumeru, the vast seas, the measure of sun and moon — the beings low, middling, and high: how many particles of dust are in each body? And in each land, how many particles?]

Taking a particle of dust as the unit of volume, measure the mountains, Mount Sumeru, the great seas, the sun and moon, and the beings below, middling, and above: how many particles make up each? And how many particles are there in each land (the great chiliocosm)?

[Particles of dust] The subtlest thing visible to the naked eye. [Beings below, middling, and above] The lower beings are those of the three evil paths — hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; the middling beings are those of the three wholesome paths — devas, humans, and asuras; the higher beings are those of the three noble paths — sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
[How many in a bow? How many in an elbow, a pace, a krosa, a half-yojana, a yojana?]
Taking the diameter of a particle of dust as the unit of length, measure each bow, elbow, krosa, and yojana: how many particles make up each?
An old commentary says: two feet make one cubit, four cubits make one bow, five hundred bows make one krosa, and ten krosas make one yojana. The yojana is the same as the yojana (a distance measure).
[Yojana] The unit of distance in India. It has three sizes — great, middling, and small: the great yojana is about eighty li, the middling about sixty li, and the small about forty li.
[How many [dust-particles] in a hare's hair, in a window-dust, in a nit, in a sheep's hair, in a grain of barley?]
Taking a particle of dust as the unit of volume, measure each hare's-hair tip, window-dust, nit, sheep's-hair tip, and grain of barley: how many particles make up each?
[Ji (
jǐ
)] is the egg of the louse [shi (
shī
)]. [Barley (
kuàng
)] is the barley grain.

An old commentary says: seven particles of dust make one window-dust; seven window-dusts make one hare's-hair-tip dust; seven hare's-hair-tip dusts make one sheep's-hair-tip dust; seven sheep's-hair-tip dusts make one ox's-hair-tip dust; seven ox's-hair-tip dusts make one nit; seven nits make one louse; seven lice make one mustard seed; and seven mustard seeds make one grain of barley.
[How many barley grains in a prastha? How many barley grains in an adhaka? In a drona, a nadika, a laksa, and a koti — and down to a vimbaka — how many are in each?]

How many grains of barley are in one prastha (half a dou)? How many in one adhaka (one dou)? In one drona (one hu), one nadika (ten hu), one laksa (a hundred thousand hu), one koti (a hundred million hu), and down to one vimbaka (one zhao hu) — how many grains of barley are in each?
[Hu (
hú
