[How many anu make one sarshapa (mustard seed)? How many sarshapa make one laja? How many laja make one masha (bean)? How many masha make one dana? How many dana make one karshapana? How many karshapana make one pala (pound)? These successive aggregates — how many pala make one Sumeru?]

Taking a particle's weight as the unit of weight: how many anu (particles) make one sarshapa (mustard seed)? How many sarshapa make one laja (grass seed)? How many laja make one masha (bean)? How many masha make one dana (zhu)? How many dana make one karshapana (liang)? How many karshapana make one pala (jin)? These successive aggregates — how many pala make one Mount Sumeru? (The Tang translation says:
“How many jin make one Sumeru?”
[Anu (
nóu
)] a particle of dust.
[These are exactly what you should have asked — why need you ask about other things?]
All of these are what you should have asked; why need you ask about other matters?
[The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, the Buddha and his most victorious sons — how many in each body? Why do you not ask about this!]
The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, the Buddha and the bodhisattvas — how many are there in all? And how many particles of dust are in each of their bodies? Why do you not ask about these?

[Sravaka] One who attains awakening by hearing the sound of the Buddha's teaching of the Four Noble Truths. [Pratyekabuddha] Also called the independently awakened one: one who, in the Buddha's time, hears the Buddha teach the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby awakens, and is called a 'pratyekabuddha'; one who, born in a world without a Buddha, contemplates the arising and ceasing of all dharmas through dependent origination and awakens on his own is called a 'solitary awakened one.'
[How many anu in a flame? How many anu again in the wind? How many anu in each of the senses? How many in the pores and the eyebrows?]
How many dust-particles in a blossom of flame
How many in a gust of wind
How many in each hair of the body
And the pores and eyebrows, how many dust-particles
These too are questions
why do you not ask?
Above,
from
Mountains, the earth, Mount Sumeru
” to “how many in the pores and the eyebrows”
, there are thirty-eight lines in all,
asking about
thirty-two
items
of matters,
all of which
Mahamati
had not asked about,
and therefore
the World-Honored One
raises them to ask,
reproaching him: Why do you not ask about these questions?

In fact, the World-Honored One used these questions — utterly unrelated to the self-awakened noble wisdom — to show from the opposite side that everything Mahamati had asked above was idle talk. Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way says:
“All number-sayings and not-number-sayings — what have they to do with my spirit's awareness?”
The realm of the self-awakened noble wisdom realized by the Buddhas is indeed not to be reached by deluded discrimination.

[Idle talk] Speech without practical substance. [All number-sayings and not-number-sayings — what have they to do with my spirit's awareness?] All discrimination of names and marks — what has it to do with the awareness of my own nature? 'Number-sayings, not-number-sayings' here is a metaphor for the discrimination of names and marks. [Discrimination] Attempting to derive reality out of concepts.

blocks.text: The World-Honored One Continues to Answer

inline.s: Below, the World-Honored One again continues to repeat
the remaining part of what Mahamati had asked,
showing even more clearly that, with respect to entering the self-awakened noble wisdom, they are all idle talk.

[Guardian of wealth, the sovereign king, the wheel-turning universal monarch — how does the king protect? What is liberation? The expanded teaching and the pithy saying, as you have asked. The manifold desires of beings, and their manifold foods and drinks. How the grove of men and women, the adamantine mountain? How the illusion-like dream, the wild-deer's simile of craving? How the mountain devas and rishis, adorned by the gandharvas? To where does liberation go? Who is bound, who liberated? How the dhyana realms, the transformations and the non-Buddhist sects? How what is made without a cause, how what is made with a cause? Made with a cause and made without a cause, and the neither-having-nor-not-having cause? How what has now ceased? How to purify the consciousnesses? How the consciousnesses turn, and how they turn the various deeds? How to cut off the notions? How samadhi arises? Who destroys the three realms of existence? In what place, for what body? How, when there is no being, does one speak of 'I' and 'self'? How the worldly speech? I pray you, expound in detail. What is the mark of what is asked, and the non-self of what is asked? How the embryo, and the various other bodies? How to cut off the views of permanence and annihilation? How does the mind attain stillness — speech and the various wisdoms, the precepts, the lineage, the Buddha's sons? How the attainment and the treatise? How the teacher and the disciple? The various beings — how are these? How the food and drink? The wise one, Mara's arrangements? How the trees and the vine-tangles? Asked by the most victorious son. How the various lands? The immortals' long ascetic practice? How the clan names? From what teacher do they receive instruction? How the ugly? How do people cultivate? In the realm of desire, what is not comprehended — the Akanistha accomplished? How the mundane psychic powers? What is a bhikshu? How the nirmana-buddha (the transformation Buddha)? How the sambhoga-buddha (the reward Buddha)? How the tathata-buddha? The Buddha of equality and wisdom? How the assembly (the sangha)? Thus asks the Buddha's son. The harp and the waist-drum, the flower, the lands beyond light. The mind-ground has seven.]

[Akanistha] That is, the Akanistha heaven, translated into Chinese as the Heaven of Ultimate Form. It is one of the eighteen heavens of the realm of form, the very summit of the realm of form, and so is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form. [The mind-ground has seven] The Tang translation says: 'How to cause his mind to dwell in the seven grounds?'

What do these questions above have to do with entering the self-awakened noble wisdom? Answering them is of no benefit. Therefore the World-Honored One merely repeats these questions so that everyone may understand that they are but idle talk.
[All that you have asked is as it truly is — these and the many others that the Buddha's son should ask!]

What you have asked is all that worldly people ponder over. If that is so, then apart from the questions you asked above, there are still a great many others that you too should ask! (This is ironic: if one is still sunk in thought and reckoning, the questions that could be asked are still countless! To count the sands of the sea — how could one hope to gain the treasure?)

blocks.text: The Meaning of the One Hundred Eight Phrases

inline.s: Below, the World-Honored One formally answers the 'one hundred eight meanings' that the bodhisattva Mahamati asked.

[Each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views, the siddhanta beyond words. Now I shall display, establishing the phrases in due order; the Buddha's sons, listen well! These one hundred eight phrases above, as the Buddhas have spoken.]

As to the vast array of all phenomena, one should bring each mark into accord with its real nature (returning the marks to the essence), and so be far from the faults of the views of the two extremes (clearly indicating that what was asked above is the fault of views), because the all-bestowing dharma (the siddhanta of the first meaning) is beyond words. Now I, at the place of wordlessness, will display through words, establishing phrases in due order. O Buddha's sons, listen well and carefully! These one hundred eight phrases below are, as the Buddhas have spoken.

[Each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views] As to the vast array of all phenomena, one should bring each mark into accord with its real nature, and so be far from the faults of the views of the two extremes. This is the signless dharma: returning the marks to the essence, apart from marks within the marks — within all marks, apart from all marks. [The faults of views] The various questions above are all views of the two extremes; with respect to entering the self-awakened noble wisdom they are all not right views, and so are called faults. The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
“The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is without thought and without thought-moment.”
Again it says:
“Pulling out the very root of all idle talk, eternally separated from all of it, cool and smokeless.”
The Essential of the Mind-Seal says:
“When thoughts cease and one forgets
(through 'forget' we take the meaning of 'extinguish')
worry, the Buddha appears of itself.”

[The siddhanta of the first meaning] The fourth of the four siddhantas; this is the ultimate siddhanta. The Buddha, seeing that the faculties and conditions of beings are ripe, speaks to them of the real nature of all dharmas, so that beings may together awaken into the path of the noble ones.
[These one hundred eight phrases, as the Buddhas have spoken] The Tang translation says:
(The World-Honored One then addressed him:)

'As the former Buddhas have said, the one hundred eight phrases, each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views, also apart from the worldly dharmas made of words. I shall speak them for you; the Buddha's sons should listen and receive.' At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, what are the one hundred eight phrases?' The Buddha said to Mahamati: 'What is called the birth-phrase, the not-birth phrase; the eternal phrase, the not-eternal phrase......'

From this we know that the one hundred eight phrases 'as the Buddhas have spoken' refer to the great section below, 'the not-born phrase, the born phrase; the eternal phrase, the impermanent phrase.' [Establishing the phrases in due order] The dharma is, in its essence, beyond words; now the World-Honored One, at the place of wordlessness, displays through words, and so it is called 'establishing in due order.'

blocks.text: Five. The Store Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousness
The Two Kinds of Arising, Abiding, and Ceasing

inline.s: [At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the consciousnesses have?]
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the consciousnesses have?
[Again said to the Buddha] Respectfully spoke again to the Buddha. Here 'to report to' (bai) is how the lower reports to the higher.

[The various consciousnesses] The eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness, alaya-consciousness). Here the eight consciousnesses are taken as a whole, referring to 'consciousness.' [Arising, abiding, and ceasing] Arising: the arising; abiding: the dwelling; ceasing: the extinction.

[The Buddha told Mahamati: The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, not to be known by thought. The consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, namely the flowing-arising and the characteristic-arising; two kinds of abiding, namely the flowing-abiding and the characteristic-abiding; and two kinds of ceasing, namely the flowing-ceasing and the characteristic-ceasing.]

The Buddha told Mahamati: the consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which are not to be known through reckoning. They are the flowing arising-abiding-ceasing and the characteristic arising-abiding-ceasing. (That is, there are: flowing-arising, flowing-abiding, flowing-ceasing; characteristic-arising, characteristic-abiding, characteristic-ceasing.)

[Flowing arising-abiding-ceasing] The arising, abiding, and ceasing of a thought. Because it continues unbroken like the flowing stream of water, it is called the flowing arising-abiding-ceasing. [Thought] The stirring of the mind, flowing across the three times (past, present, future), is called a thought; the former thought, the later thought, thought after thought, and so on. [Characteristic arising-abiding-ceasing] The arising, abiding, and ceasing of the characteristics produced by the six senses conditioning on the six sense-objects.
The Tang translation says:

“The Buddha said: Mahamati, the consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, not to be known by those who conjecture; namely the continuous-arising and the characteristic-arising, the continuous-abiding and the characteristic-abiding, the continuous-ceasing and the characteristic-ceasing.”

blocks.text: The True Aspect, the Transforming Aspect, and the Karmic Aspect

inline.s: [The consciousnesses have three kinds of aspects, namely the transforming aspect, the karmic aspect, and the true aspect.]
The consciousnesses have three kinds of aspects: the true aspect, the transforming aspect, and the karmic aspect.

[The three kinds of aspects] Before a single thought of unmindfulness arises, it is the true aspect; when a single thought has just arisen, it is the transforming aspect; when thought succeeds thought and becomes thinking, it is the karmic aspect. [The true aspect] The aspect apart from arising and ceasing, that is, the store consciousness spoken of below. [The transforming aspect] The aspect of passing from awareness into delusion, that is, the manifest consciousness spoken of below, that is, the 'three subtle' among the three subtle and six coarse. [The karmic aspect] The aspect of karma-creation, that is, the consciousness that discriminates particular things spoken of below, that is, the 'six coarse' among the three subtle and six coarse. These two (the transforming aspect and the karmic aspect) together are called the evolving consciousness.
A verse says:
“From a single thought of unmindfulness
(fundamental ignorance)
the three subtle arise; with objects as conditions, the six coarse grow.”

This describes the process in which self-nature (consciousness), because of fundamental ignorance, passes from awareness (the store consciousness) into delusion (the evolving consciousness), and so arouses delusion, creates karma, and receives retribution. The 'three subtle and six coarse' are the nine false aspects of the flow of arising and ceasing that self-nature manifests when it falls into delusion: the karmic aspect of ignorance, the seeing aspect, and the object aspect (the seen aspect); the wisdom aspect, the continuous aspect, the grasping aspect, the name-reckoning aspect, the karma-arising aspect, and the karma-bound-suffering aspect. Of these, the first three are born of fundamental ignorance ('from a single thought of unmindfulness the three subtle arise'), and their aspects are subtle, so they are called the 'three subtle'; the last six are nourished by the object aspect as condition ('with objects as conditions the six coarse grow'), and their aspects are coarse and manifest, so they are called the 'six coarse.'

[Fundamental ignorance] Fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of a thought. Because of this single stirring of thought, self-nature is benighted through the long night, not comprehending the true principle, and so gives rise to all the delusions and afflictions.
The process of the 'three subtle and six coarse' is:
the three subtle”:
One: the karmic aspect of ignorance. The stirring of the mind is karma, so 'unmindful stirring of the mind (the very first stirring of thought)' is called the karmic aspect of ignorance.
Two: the seeing aspect. Relying on the previous 'karmic aspect of ignorance,' when the mind stirs it can see.
Three: the object aspect (the seen aspect). Relying on the previous 'seeing aspect,' because of seeing, the objects falsely appear.
These three subtle take ignorance as their cause, and so it is also said: 'With ignorance as cause, the three subtle arise.'
the six coarse”:
One: the wisdom aspect. Relying on the previous 'object aspect,' it falsely produces deliberation and discriminates favorable and adverse, beautiful and ugly, loved and hated.
Two: the continuous aspect. Relying on the previous 'wisdom aspect,' toward the discrimination of objects it reflects and reckons, thought succeeding thought in continuity.

Three: the grasping aspect. Relying on the previous 'continuous aspect,' toward the continuous thoughts that turn ever deeper, it produces self and what belongs to self, thus forming the grasping aspect.
Four: the name-reckoning aspect. Relying on the previous 'grasping aspect,' it names the various environments, affairs, and things, forming concepts and language.
Five: the karma-arising aspect. Relying on the previous 'name-reckoning aspect,' it reflects and reckons and so creates various bodily, verbal, and mental karma.

Six: the karma-bound suffering aspect. Relying on the previous 'karma-arising aspect,' it is bound by the bodily, verbal, and mental karma it created and so experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.
These six coarse are nourished by the object aspect as condition, and so it is said: 'With objects as conditions, the six coarse grow.'
In
the nine false aspects
, the first seven (
the karmic aspect of ignorance
the seeing aspect
the object aspect
the wisdom aspect
the continuous aspect
the grasping aspect
the name-reckoning aspect
) are delusion,
the eighth (
the karma-arising aspect

the karma-bound suffering aspect

The sutra says:
“From delusion one creates karma; from karma one experiences suffering.”
This is the process of passing from awareness into delusion.

Thus the process by which self-nature passes from awareness into delusion, until one is bound by karma and suffers, is: unmindful stirring of the mind (arising of thought) → the senses and consciousness arising so as to see → manifestation of objects → discrimination → deluded thinking (reflection and reckoning, thought succeeding thought) → grasping (running after desires and thoughts) → creating karma → being bound by karma and suffering.

Returning to the source, on the other hand, is to reverse the above process, passing from delusion to awareness: being bound by karma and suffering → not creating karma → not grasping (not running after desires and thoughts) → not deluded thinking →
not discriminating
→ objects ceasing → transforming consciousness into wisdom so that the senses and consciousness cease → the subtle flowing ceasing.
In this process of returning to the source,
not discriminating
is an extremely crucial link; therefore this sutra devotes a great many pages to explaining why one should not discriminate and how to accomplish not discriminating.

[Transforming consciousness into wisdom] To transform the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms: transform the first five consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness), which are tainted, into the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, which is undefiled; transform the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness), which is tainted, into the wisdom of wondrous observation, which is undefiled; transform the seventh consciousness (manas-consciousness), which is tainted, into the wisdom of universal equality, which is undefiled; transform the eighth consciousness (alaya-consciousness), which is tainted, into the wisdom of the great perfect mirror, which is undefiled. [Outflow] An alias for afflictions, carrying the two meanings of leaking out and falling away. The afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion leak and flow out unceasingly day and night through the gates of the six senses; hence they are called outflow. Moreover, afflictions can cause one to fall away among the three evil realms; hence they are also called outflow. All dharmas with afflictions are called “dharmas with outflow”; dharmas without afflictions are called “dharmas without outflow.” [The four wisdoms] The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of universal equality, and the wisdom of the great perfect mirror. “The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done” is the wisdom that accomplishes all deeds that universally benefit sentient beings. “The wisdom of wondrous observation” is the wisdom that observes all dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings, prescribing medicine according to the illness and turning the ordinary into the sage. “The wisdom of universal equality” is the wisdom that penetrates the principle of no-self and universal equality and so arouses unconditional great compassion toward all sentient beings. “The wisdom of the great perfect mirror” is the wisdom that contemplates all phenomena and all principles with nothing unclear; this wisdom is pure and perfectly bright, seeing through within and without, like a great perfect mirror that illumines all things.

blocks.text: True Consciousness, Manifest Consciousness, and the Consciousness That Discriminates Particular Things

inline.s: [Mahamati, briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness; extensively stated, there are eight aspects. What are the three? They are the true consciousness, the manifest consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates particular things.]

Mahamati, consciousness, briefly stated, has three kinds; extensively stated, it has eight aspects (the eight consciousnesses). What are the three? They are the true consciousness, the manifest consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates particular things.

[The three kinds of consciousness] When not a single thing exists, it is the true consciousness; when it reflects objects like a mirror, it is the manifest consciousness; when it discriminates good and bad, it is the consciousness that discriminates particular things. [Extensively stated, eight aspects] Extensively stated, consciousness is composed of eight component consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness, and alaya-consciousness. [Manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things] The manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things are two states of consciousness. The sense-objects manifested by the manifest consciousness are like the images reflected by a flat mirror. The sense-objects manifested by the consciousness that discriminates particular things are like the images reflected by a distorting mirror, which are bent out of shape. The consciousness that discriminates particular things is also called the crooked mind or the fawning and crooked mind. In ordinary terms, the manifest consciousness looks at things without subjective coloring (discrimination and reckoning), while the consciousness that discriminates particular things looks at things with subjective coloring (discrimination and reckoning). The manifest consciousness is also called the upright mind. The Vimalakirti Sutra says:
“The upright mind is the bodhisattva's Pure Land.”
It also says:
“The upright mind is the place of practice.”
[Mahamati, it is like a bright mirror holding all the images of form; the manifest consciousness, as it manifests objects, is likewise.]
Mahamati, just as a bright mirror reflects all the images of form, so the manifest consciousness, as it reflects objects, is like this
, reflecting the sense-objects as a mirror reflects things.
[Mahamati, the manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things, these two in their ceasing and not ceasing, are mutually conditional causes.]

Mahamati, the ceasing (extinction) and not ceasing (arising and abiding) of these two consciousnesses — the manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things — are mutually causal.

This means: the manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things are two states of the evolving consciousness, mutually transforming. When the manifest consciousness transforms into the consciousness that discriminates particular things, the manifest consciousness ceases while the consciousness that discriminates particular things arises and abides; when the consciousness that discriminates particular things transforms into the manifest consciousness, the consciousness that discriminates particular things ceases while the manifest consciousness arises and abides. The Tang translation says: “The manifest consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates particular things — these two consciousnesses are not different; they are mutually causal.”

[Mahamati, the inconceivable perfuming, and the inconceivable transformation, are the causes of the manifest consciousness. Mahamati, the grasping of various sense-objects, and the perfuming of beginningless deluded thinking, are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates particular things.]

Mahamati, the inconceivable perfuming and cultivation, and the inconceivable transformation, are the causes of the true consciousness transforming into the manifest consciousness. Mahamati, the clinging and discriminating of various sense-objects, along with the perfuming of beginningless deluded thinking, are the causes of the manifest consciousness transforming into the consciousness that discriminates particular things.

[Inconceivable] Beyond thought and discussion. A profound principle that transcends thinking and discussion is called “inconceivable.” [Inconceivable perfuming] The Record of the Meaning of the Awakening of Faith says:

“Inconceivable perfuming means that ignorance can perfume Suchness; it can perfume even where there is nothing to perfume, hence it is called inconceivable perfuming. Moreover, perfuming is itself non-perfuming; the perfume that is not perfuming is called inconceivable perfuming.”

[The manifest consciousness, with inconceivable perfuming and transformation as its cause; the consciousness that discriminates particular things, with the discriminating of sense-objects and the dispositions of beginningless deluded thinking as its cause] Because of the inconceivable perfuming of ignorance, the true consciousness transforms into the manifest consciousness; because of the discriminating of objects and the dispositions of beginningless deluded thinking, the manifest consciousness transforms into the consciousness that discriminates particular things. Thus the path of returning to the source is: keeping away from discrimination and deluded thinking, then the consciousness that discriminates particular things transforms into the manifest consciousness (without love, hatred, grasping, or rejecting), thereby ending the deluded birth-and-death and emerging from the cycle; then, eradicating ignorance, the manifest consciousness transforms into the true consciousness (the subtle flowing forever extinguished), thereby ending the transformative birth-and-death and realizing Buddhahood.

blocks.text: The Cessation of Characteristics and the Cessation of the Flowing

inline.s: Below we discuss the cessation of characteristics among the two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
[Mahamati, if one turns back to
(in the sense of “returns to”)
the true consciousness, and the various unreal and delusory [perfumings] cease, then all the sense-based consciousnesses cease. Mahamati, this is called the cessation of characteristics.]

Mahamati, if the evolving consciousness returns and restores [itself] to the true consciousness, then the various dispositions of false discrimination cease. Thus all the sense-based consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness) cease. Mahamati, this is called the cessation of characteristics.

[If one turns back to the true consciousness] In classical Chinese “fu” is interchangeable with “fu” (return), meaning: to return, to turn back. [Sense-based consciousnesses] The six consciousnesses corresponding to the six senses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind): eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness.
The Tang translation says:

“Mahamati, when the various dispositions of false discrimination in the alaya-consciousness cease, then all the sense-based consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness) cease; this is called the cessation of characteristics.”
Below we discuss the cessation of the flowing among the two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

[Mahamati, as for the cessation of continuity, when the cause of continuity ceases, then continuity ceases; when that from which it arises ceases, and when what it relies upon ceases, then continuity ceases. Mahamati, why is this so? Because these are what continuity depends upon. The support is the perfuming of beginningless deluded thinking; the condition is the discrimination of the objects seen by one's own mind.]

Mahamati, as for the cessation of continuity (the cessation of the flowing), it is because the cause of continuity ceases that continuity ceases; because the support of continuity ceases and that which it relies upon ceases, continuity ceases. Mahamati, why is this so? Because these are what continuity relies upon. The support is the perfuming of beginningless deluded thinking; the condition is the discriminations of the objects seen by one's own mind.

[The cessation of continuity] That is, the cessation of the flowing. Here “continuity” and “flowing” are synonyms, because the flowing is uninterrupted continuity. [The condition is the discrimination of the objects seen by one's own mind] The Tang translation says: “The condition is the discriminations of the objects seen by one's own mind.”
The Tang translation says:

“Mahamati, as for the cessation of continuity, when the support-cause ceases and the condition ceases, then continuity ceases. The support-cause is the beginningless false dispositions of frivolous speculation; the condition is the discriminations of the objects seen by one's own mind.”

blocks.text: The Store Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousness

inline.s: The following passage discusses that the store consciousness and the evolving consciousness are one substance in two states, mutually transforming. The store consciousness is the true aspect of consciousness; the evolving consciousness is the karmic aspect of consciousness.

[Mahamati, it is like a lump of clay and the atoms of dust: they are neither different nor not different. Gold and the ornament made of it are likewise. Mahamati, if the lump of clay and the atoms of dust were different, then the lump would not be made of them, yet it is indeed made of them; hence they are not different. If they were not different, then the lump of clay and the atoms of dust would be indistinguishable.]

Mahamati, it is like the lump of clay and the atoms of dust: these two are neither different nor not different. The gold ingot and the gold vessel (the ornament) are likewise. Mahamati, if one says the lump of clay and the atoms of dust are different, then the lump is not made of the atoms, yet in reality the lump is made of the atoms; hence they are not different. If one says they are not different, then the lump of clay and the atoms of dust would be indistinguishable, yet in reality they are distinguishable.

[Thus, Mahamati, if the true aspect of the evolving consciousness and the store consciousness were different, the store consciousness would not be their cause. If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousness ceases, the store consciousness would also have to cease, yet its own true aspect in reality does not cease. Therefore, Mahamati, it is not the consciousness of one's own true aspect that ceases, only the karmic aspect ceases. If one's own true aspect ceased, then the store consciousness would cease.]

By the same reasoning, Mahamati: if the karmic aspect of the evolving consciousness and the true aspect of the store consciousness were different, the store consciousness would not be the cause of the evolving consciousness. If the two were not different, then when the evolving consciousness ceases, the store consciousness would also have to cease; yet in reality when the evolving consciousness ceases, the store consciousness does not. Therefore, Mahamati, when the evolving consciousness ceases it is not the true aspect of consciousness (the store consciousness) that ceases, only the karmic aspect of consciousness (the evolving consciousness) that ceases. If the true aspect of consciousness ceased, the store consciousness would cease.

[Neither different nor not different] This refers to the case of one substance in two states. Not different, because the substance is the same; not not-different, because the two states are different.
[Store consciousness] This is the Tathagata-garbha. (Regarding the Tathagata-garbha, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-Garbha
The Tang translation says:

“Mahamati, if the evolving consciousness and the store consciousness were different, the store consciousness would not be their cause; if they were not different, when the evolving consciousness ceases the store consciousness would also have to cease, yet its true aspect does not cease. Mahamati, the true aspect of consciousness does not cease; only the karmic aspect ceases.”

This passage discusses that the store consciousness and the evolving consciousness are one substance in two states, mutually transforming one into the other, like the gold ingot and the gold vessel (ornament) made from it. The craftsman makes the gold ingot into a gold vessel; at that moment the ingot transforms into the vessel. After the vessel melts and solidifies, the vessel transforms back into the ingot. The ancients also illustrated this with water and ice: the store consciousness is like
H
O
appearing as water, while the evolving consciousness is like
H
O

appearing as ice. The store consciousness is the true aspect of consciousness (which is the self-nature of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) (the state of not a single thought arising); if the store consciousness gives rise to reflection, then it becomes the evolving consciousness. The evolving consciousness is the transforming aspect (a single thought just arising) or the karmic aspect (thought succeeding thought, becoming thinking) that is transformed from this true aspect, the store consciousness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Self-nature can contain all dharmas, hence it is called the containing store consciousness; if it gives rise to reflection, it is the evolving consciousness. It produces the six consciousnesses, goes out the six gates, and sees the six sense-objects; thus the eighteen realms all function from self-nature. If self-nature is evil, it produces the eighteen evils. If self-nature is good, it produces the eighteen goods. If used evilly, it is the use of sentient beings; if used well, it is the use of the Buddha. What is the use conditioned upon? It is conditioned upon self-nature having them.”

(Translation: Self-nature can contain all dharmas, hence it is named the containing store consciousness (fundamental nature). If self-nature gives rise to reflection, it is the evolving consciousness (the nature of consciousness), producing the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out the six gates (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) and see the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental objects). Thus the eighteen realms (six consciousnesses, six senses, and six sense-objects) all function from self-nature.) This means: if the store consciousness gives rise to discrimination (reflection), it transforms into the evolving consciousness and produces the first six consciousnesses; then objects appear.

[Mahamati, one who says that the store consciousness ceases is not different from the annihilationist discussions of the heterodox. Mahamati, these heterodox argue thus: when the grasped objects cease, the flowing of consciousness also ceases; if the flowing of consciousness ceases, then the beginningless flowing should be cut off. Mahamati, the heterodox say that the cause of the arising of the flowing is not the eye-consciousness arising from the gathering of form and light, but another, different cause. Mahamati, as for that cause, they speak of the supremely wondrous, or a person, or the sovereign, or time, or the atoms.]

Mahamati, one who says that the store consciousness ceases is the same as the annihilationist discussions of the heterodox. Mahamati, those heterodox argue thus: “When the grasped objects cease, the flowing of consciousness also ceases; if the flowing of consciousness ceases, then the beginningless flowing should be cut off and extinguished.” Mahamati, the heterodox say that the cause of the arising of the flowing is not the eye-consciousness arising from the gathering of the sense-object form and light, but rather another, different cause. Mahamati, they hold the supremely wondrous, a person, the sovereign, time, or the atoms to be the cause of the arising of the flowing.

[Supremely wondrous] The lord of the Brahma heaven. [Person] Also called the husband, one of the sixteen views, an alias for the spirit-self. [The sixteen views] Also called the sixteen spirit-selves. Those who have not seen the Way, forcibly establishing a sovereign within the dharmas of the five aggregates, falsely assume a self and that which belongs to self, and so have sixteen views: 1. Self: within the five aggregates, falsely assume a self and that which belongs to self. 2. Beings: within the five aggregates, falsely assume a real being. 3. Life: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that one's life-span in this life has length and shortness. 4. Vitality: falsely assume that one's life-root continues without interruption. 5. One born: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I can bring forth various matters, and that I am born among humans. 6. Nurtured: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I am born, nurtured by my parents, and can nurture others. 7. Multitude: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I have the five aggregates, the twelve entrances (six senses and six sense-objects), the eighteen realms (six senses, six sense-objects, and six consciousnesses), as the number of various dharmas. 8. Person: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I am one who can cultivate, unlike one who cannot cultivate. 9. Doer: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I have the ability to do various things. 10. Causing to act: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I can cause others to act. 11. Raiser: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I can raise future karma of merit and demerit. 12. Causing to raise: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I can cause others to raise future karma of merit and demerit. 13. Receiver: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that my future body will receive the retribution of merit and demerit. 14. Causing to receive: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I can cause others to receive the retribution of future merit and demerit. 15. Knower: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I have the five senses and can know the five sense-objects. 16. Seer: within the five aggregates, falsely assume that I have the eye sense and can see all forms. The above sixteen views are all aliases of “self.” [Sovereign] The great sovereign heaven.
The Tang translation says:

“Mahamati, these heterodox say thus: ‘When the continuous consciousness that grasps objects ceases, then the beginningless continuous consciousness ceases.’ Mahamati, these heterodox say that the continuous consciousness arises from a creator; they do not say that the eye-consciousness arises from the union of form and light, but only that the creator is the cause of arising. What is the creator? They falsely hold
(they falsely suppose)
the supreme nature, the husband, the sovereign, time, and the atoms, to be the creator.”

blocks.text: A Brief Summary on Consciousness

inline.s: Consciousness has three situations: the true consciousness, the manifest consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates particular things. When not a single thing exists, it is the true consciousness; when it reflects objects like a mirror, it is the manifest consciousness; when it discriminates good and bad, it is the consciousness that discriminates particular things.

Consciousness has three aspects: the true aspect, the transforming aspect, and the karmic aspect. Before a single thought arises, it is the true aspect. When a single thought has just arisen, it is the transforming aspect. When thought succeeds thought, becoming thinking, it is the karmic aspect.

The process of consciousness passing from awareness (the store consciousness) into delusion (the evolving consciousness), so as to arouse delusion, create karma, and receive retribution: “From a single thought of unmindfulness (fundamental ignorance), the three subtle [aspects] arise; with objects as conditions, the six coarse [aspects] grow.”
Their relationship is tabulated as follows:

rows.s: The awareness and delusion of consciousness
Consciousness passing from awareness into delusion

inline.s: The store consciousness is a single entity, while the evolving consciousness is composed of eight consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness, and alaya-consciousness. Master Hanshan's Record on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra says:
“Deluded by a single mind
(the store consciousness)
and [transformed] into eight consciousnesses.”

Of the eight consciousnesses, the alaya-consciousness is the main entity; it gives rise to the other seven consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, and manas-consciousness.
Question: What is the relationship between “consciousness” in this sutra and “self-nature” in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch?

Answer: “Consciousness” in this sutra is precisely what the sutras and treatises commonly call “self-nature.” The store consciousness is the primordial state of consciousness, i.e., the fundamental nature (Tathagata-garbha); the evolving consciousness is the deluded state of consciousness, i.e., the nature of consciousness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is sentient beings; when self-nature is aware, that is the Buddha.”
