Question: What is the consciousness store?
Answer: The consciousness store is the alaya-consciousness. This sutra says:

“Mahamati, when false thinking manifests from one's own mind, there are eight kinds of discrimination: the consciousness store, the mind, the mental consciousness, and the five consciousness bodies — because [they arise from] the false thinking of unreal characteristics.”

(Translation: Mahamati, when false thinking manifests from one's own mind, then the Tathagata-garbha transforms into eight different consciousnesses: the consciousness store (alaya-consciousness), the mind (manas-consciousness), the mental consciousness (the sixth consciousness), and the five consciousnesses (the first five consciousnesses: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness). This is all because of the false thinking of unreal characteristics.) This means: when false thinking manifests from one's own mind, the Tathagata-garbha (store consciousness) transforms into eight consciousnesses — the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness, and the consciousness store (alaya-consciousness) — collectively called the evolving consciousness.

However, because the first seven consciousnesses are derived from the consciousness store (alaya-consciousness), [the sutras] often also use the consciousness store as a representative term for the whole of the eight consciousnesses, and place it alongside the Tathagata-garbha. At that point, the consciousness store and the evolving consciousness are synonyms. This sutra says:
(the Tathagata-garbha)
perfumed by the false evil habits of beginningless [time], is named the consciousness store.”
It also says:
“The consciousness store manifests sentient beings.”
It also says:
“Therefore, you and the other bodhisattva-mahasattvas should diligently cultivate and study the Tathagata-garbha and the consciousness store.”
Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra, Treasury of Jewels, says:

“Because this sutra directly points out that the sentient being's consciousness store is the Tathagata-garbha, revealing the objects before one in daily life, and causes them to conform and observe the present state of their own mind, suddenly realizing the self-realized holy wisdom of the Buddhas, it is named the ‘Buddha-Word-Mind.’”
Master Hanshan's Direct Explanation of the Mahayana Awakening of Faith says:
“The sutra says: ‘The Tathagata-garbha transforms the thirty-two marks and enters the bodies of all sentient beings.’ Thus, deluded by the Tathagata-garbha, it becomes the consciousness store.”
Master Yongming Yanshou's Mirror of the Ancestral Record says:
“The Tathagata-garbha, perfumed by the false evil habits of beginningless [time], is named the consciousness store.”

Therefore, when reading the sutras and treatises and encountering the two terms “consciousness store” and “alaya-consciousness,” one should judge from the context whether they refer to the whole of the eight consciousnesses or only to the eighth consciousness.

In the sutras and treatises, the great ocean is usually used as a simile: the great ocean stands for consciousness; its tranquil, still state stands for the store consciousness; and its state of rising waves and surging billows stands for the evolving consciousness. In the great ocean of the evolving consciousness, the surging waves above stand for the first seven consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness, manas-consciousness), and the calm part below stands for the alaya-consciousness.

blocks.text: Six. The Realm of the Store Consciousness

inline.s: [At that time the bodhisattva Mahamati again addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, regarding what you have spoken — mind, will, consciousness, the five dharmas, and self-nature characteristics — as practiced by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the views of one's own mind and so forth are not conjoined with the objects. Displaying all teachings, [they] become the real characteristic,
the Buddha-Word-Mind
. For the great bodhisattvas dwelling within the sea on Mount Malaya of the Lanka country, speak the ocean-wave store-consciousness realm and the Dharma-body, which the Tathagatas praise.]

At that time the bodhisattva Mahamati again asked the Buddha: World-Honored One, I pray you teach me the various wondrous Dharma gates of mind, will, consciousness, the five dharmas, and the three self-natures. As practiced by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the views of one's own mind and the objects one encounters are not conjoined (not mixed together). Displaying all teachings, [they] all become the real characteristic — the Buddhas teach sentient beings by the mind (the Buddha-Word-Mind of all Buddhas). I pray the Tathagata, for these bodhisattvas in this mountain, following the Buddhas of the past, speak the ocean-wave store-consciousness realm and the Dharma-body realm.

[As practiced by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the views of one's own mind and the objects encountered are not conjoined] As practiced by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the views of one's own mind and the objects one encounters are not conjoined (not mixed together). This says that mind and objects each go their own way: the mind abides in the mind's position, and objects abide in the objects' position; in the midst of seeming arising and ceasing, one sees only non-arising. As the saying goes: “When the whole world praises him, he is not thereby encouraged; when the whole world censures him, he is not thereby discouraged. He is fixed in the distinction between the inner and the outer, and distinguishes the realms of glory and disgrace.” (See the Zhuangzi

Free Wandering.) Translation: When the whole society praises him, he is not gladdened by it; when the whole society censures him, he is not dejected by it. He can fix the boundary between inner mind and outer objects, and clearly knows that outer objects such as glory and disgrace are but illusions. (The “encouraged” (quan) in the sentence is interchangeable with “rejoiced” (huan), meaning joy. For example, the Hanfeizi
Eight Traitorous [Perspectives] says: “To encourage (quan) his mind so as to make him offend his lord.”) To this, the Lotus Sutra says:
“This Dharma abides in the Dharma-position; the characteristics of the world abide permanently.”

[This Dharma abides in the Dharma-position; the characteristics of the world abide permanently] This Dharma should abide in the Dharma-position (not entering the mind); thus the characteristics of the world are the permanent real characteristic — in the midst of seeming arising and ceasing (the characteristics of the world), one sees only non-arising (the real characteristic).
[The Buddha-Word-Mind] The Tang translation says:
“The teaching mind of the Buddhas.”

[Mount Malaya] The Buddha spoke this sutra in the city of Lanka atop Mount Malaya in the Lanka country. [The Dharma-body realm] That is, the realm of the Dharma-body. [To speak the ocean-wave store-consciousness realm and the Dharma-body realm] The ocean-wave store-consciousness is the one mind deluded into eight consciousnesses — this is the realm of arising and ceasing. The Dharma-body realm is the eight consciousnesses returning into the one mind — this is the realm of Suchness. The bodhisattva Mahamati's question respectfully asks the World-Honored One to teach how to leave arising and ceasing and realize Suchness.
The Tang translation says:

“At that time the bodhisattva-mahasattva Mahamati again addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, I pray you teach me the various wondrous Dharma gates of mind, will, consciousness, the five dharmas, and self-nature characteristics. This is the realm of mind entered by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, free from the characteristics of their practice. It accords with the real meaning, the teaching mind of the Buddhas. I pray the Tathagata, for these bodhisattvas in this mountain, following the Buddhas of the past, speak of the store-consciousness ocean-waves and the Dharma-body realm.”

blocks.text: The Translocation of the First Six Consciousnesses

inline.s: [At that time the World-Honored One told the bodhisattva Mahamati: Because of four causes, the eye-consciousness turns. What are the four? Namely: not being aware of the grasping of what one's own mind manifests; the beginningless false dispositions toward form-excess; one's clinging to the self-nature of the consciousness-nature; and the desire to see various forms. Mahamati, these are named the four causes: where the water flows, the store consciousness turns and the waves of the evolving consciousness arise.]

At that time the World-Honored One told the bodhisattva Mahamati: Because of four causes, the eye-consciousness is caused to turn. What are the four? One: not being aware that all dharmas are manifested from one's own mind, and so grasping at them. Two: the beginningless false dispositions of clinging to the sense-object form. Three: the nature of the eye-consciousness's condition on the sense-object form. Four: delighting in seeing various forms. Mahamati, with these four causes, the water of the store consciousness (the tranquil, serene ocean of mind) becomes the waves of the evolving consciousness (the surging ocean of mind).

[Mahamati, like the eye-consciousness, all the sense faculties arise together in the atom-like pores; [the consciousnesses] arising successively with objects are likewise. It is like a bright mirror manifesting various images of form.]

Mahamati, the other consciousnesses, like the eye-consciousness, arise together with objects in the atom-like pores of all the sense faculties. It is like a bright mirror (which stands for the mind) manifesting various images of form (which stand for the characteristics of objects).
[Atom-like number] A metaphor for a great quantity; when a thing is crushed into atoms, the number is great. The Lotus Sutra says: “Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of the great-thousand world.”

[Mahamati, it is like a fierce wind blowing on the water of the great sea; the wind of external objects stirs the ocean of mind, and the waves of consciousness are unceasing. Cause and the characteristics produced, both different and not different. Combined with karma and the arising characteristics, deeply entering into clinging, one cannot know the self-nature of form and so forth; hence the five consciousness bodies turn.]

Mahamati, it is like a fierce wind blowing on the water of the great sea; the wind of external objects stirs the serene ocean of mind (the store consciousness), causing it to become the turbulent ocean of mind (the evolving consciousness), and the waves of consciousness are unceasing. The cause (the store consciousness) and the characteristics produced (the evolving consciousness) are both different and not different. Karma and the arising characteristics oscillate with one another, like rolling a snowball, and deeply enter into clinging; one cannot know that the sense-objects such as form and sound have no self-nature, and so the first five consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness) translocate as a single body.

[Cause and the characteristics produced, both different and not different] The cause and the characteristics produced are both different and not different. The cause is the store consciousness (the serene ocean of mind); the characteristics produced are the evolving consciousness (the turbulent ocean of mind). The two are both different and not different. Different: one is serene, the other turbulent. Not different: whether the serene ocean of mind or the turbulent ocean of mind, they are both the same seawater. Therefore “different and not different” is used to describe the situation of one substance in two states. One substance: the two are the same seawater. Two states: the states of the two are different — one serene, the other turbulent. [Combined with karma and the arising characteristics] The Tang translation says:
“Karma and the arising characteristics are bound together in deep entanglement.”

[Cannot know the self-nature of form and so forth] Cannot know that the self-nature of the sense-objects such as form and sound is truly nonexistent. [The five consciousness bodies turn] When the store consciousness transforms into the evolving consciousness, the first five consciousnesses translocate as a single body.

[Mahamati, together with those five consciousness bodies, the knowing of the differentiated and distinguished characteristics — know that this is the cause of the mental consciousness. That body turns, yet it has no such thought: ‘I am mutually causal in succession.’ From one's own mind manifesting, false thinking and clinging turn. And those each turn with their ceasing characteristics, discriminating objects, with the distinctions and separations — this is called their turning.]

Mahamati, together with the first five consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness), the distinguishing of the differing objects is the cause of the mental consciousness (the sixth consciousness), and so the mental consciousness arises. Yet these consciousnesses have no such thought: “We are mutually causal in succession.” Rather, toward the objects manifested from one's own mind, false thinking and clinging turn and are turned by them. The consciousnesses turn with the various characteristics of objects from arising to disintegration, and so discriminate the divisions and differences of objects — this is what is called being turned by objects.

blocks.text: The Quelling of Consciousness

inline.s: [It is like a practitioner entering the meditative samadhi: the subtle dispositions turn without the practitioner being aware of it, and he thinks: ‘Consciousness ceases, and then one enters the meditative right attainment.’ In reality, it is not that consciousness ceases and then one enters the right attainment. Because the seeds of the dispositions do not cease, [consciousness] does not cease. Because objects turn and the grasping is incomplete, [the coarse consciousness] ceases.]

For example, when a practitioner enters samādhi, the habitual tendencies flow on so subtly that he is unaware of them, and so he thinks: ‘I have extinguished the consciousnesses and entered samādhi.’ In truth, without truly extinguishing the consciousnesses (merely subduing them), he enters samādhi. Because the seeds of tendency have not been destroyed, the consciousnesses are not annihilated. Yet since he no longer grasps at sense objects, this is called ‘the ceasing of consciousness.’

[Subtle turning of tendency] The subtle streaming flow of habitual tendencies. [Turning with sense-objects, grasping being incomplete, therefore ‘ceasing’] Because sense-objects cause consciousness to arise again, and since the grasping is incomplete (he no longer grasps at the sense-objects), consciousness ‘ceases’ (this is called the ceasing of consciousness). Here ‘ceasing’ means suppressed cessation, not cut-off extinction. Hence the ancients said: ‘Do not suppose that a mind without thought is itself Buddhahood; a mind without thought still lies beyond one more barrier.’
The Tang translation says:

“Mahāmati, when practitioners enter samādhi, the power of habit arises so subtly that they do not perceive it, but only form the thought: ‘I have extinguished consciousness and entered samādhi.’ In truth, they do not extinguish consciousness yet still enter samādhi. Because their seeds of tendency are not destroyed, they merely no longer grasp at sense-objects, and this is called the ceasing of consciousness.”

blocks.text: Abilities to See the Streaming of One’s Own Mind’s Delusions

inline.s: Mahāmati, such is the subtle ultimate extent of the store consciousness, which none can fathom or determine — not the power of samādhi and wisdom gained through their practice by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists. Those who possess the wisdom of the ground realms, who skillfully discriminate and determine the meaning of terms, supreme and boundless, whose roots of goodness are matured, and who are free of the falseness of the delusions presented by their own minds, may know it.

Mahāmati, the working of the store consciousness is so subtle that only the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas abiding on the grounds can know it. The power of samādhi and wisdom attained through the practice of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the non-Buddhists alike cannot know it. Only those who practice in accordance with reality, who with the power of wisdom understand the characteristics of the grounds and master the meanings of phrases (deeply comprehending the sūtra), whose roots of goodness are matured in the presence of countless Buddhas, and who are free of the false views of their own minds, are able to know it.
The Tang translation says:

“Mahāmati, the working of the store consciousness is so subtle that only the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas abiding on the grounds can know it; all the power of concentration and wisdom of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists cannot know it. Only those who practice in accordance with reality, who with the power of wisdom understand the characteristics of the grounds, master the meanings of phrases, and have widely gathered roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas without falsely discriminating what their own minds see, are able to know it!”

Dwelling in meditation amid the mountains and forests and practicing at the lower, middle, and higher levels, they can see the streaming of their own minds’ delusions. The Buddhas of countless lands pour the consecration upon them; they gain the power of freedom, spiritual powers, and samādhi, and are surrounded by good friends and the retinue of the Buddha’s children. What mind, intention, and consciousness present as the realms of self-nature are mere vain imaginings. The ocean of birth and death in the three realms, with its karma, craving, and ignorance — all such causes they entirely transcend. Therefore, Mahāmati, practitioners should draw near to the supreme good friends.

These who practice in accordance with reality, dwelling in meditation amid the mountains and forests, practicing at the lower, middle, or higher level, can see the streaming of their own minds’ delusions. The Buddhas of countless lands pour the consecration upon them, and they gain the power of freedom, spiritual powers, and samādhi, surrounded by bodhisattvas. They understand that what mind, intention, and consciousness course through are but vain imaginings, and so they entirely transcend such causes as the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance. Therefore, Mahāmati, practitioners should draw near to such supreme good friends.

[Dwelling in meditation (yànzuò)] Sitting silently in stillness. [Ocean of existence (yǒuhǎi)] This refers to birth and death. ‘Existence’ (yǒu) is the three realms of existence; ‘ocean’ is a metaphor for the boundless extent of birth and death. The Ratnakūṭa Sūtra says: ‘The ocean of existence in birth and death — how bitter, how painful!’ The Treasury of Abhidharma says: ‘Through delusion, the world drifts upon the ocean of existence.’ The verse commentary of the Treasury of Abhidharma says: ‘Through the deluding defilements, the world of sentient beings drifts in the sea of death within the three realms of existence.’
The Tang translation says:

“Mahāmati, practitioners who dwell in meditation amid the mountains and forests and practice at the highest, middle, and lowest levels can see the streaming of their own minds’ discriminations, gain the freedom and powers of the various samādhis, receive the consecration of the Buddhas, and are surrounded by bodhisattvas. They know the realms traversed by mind, intention, and consciousness, and transcend the great ocean of birth and death, with its craving, karma, and ignorance. Therefore you should draw near to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and practice in accordance with reality under great good friends.”

blocks.text: The Store Consciousness Turns into the Eight Consciousnesses

inline.s: At that time the Blessed One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again in verse, spoke: Like a vast ocean’s swelling waves, raised by the force of a fierce wind, whose billows heave against the dark abyss and never find a moment’s rest; so the sea of the store consciousness, ever abiding, is stirred by the winds of objects, and the waves of the manifold consciousnesses leap up and turn into being. Blue and red and manifold hues, conch-shell, milk, and rock sugar, faint flavors, blooms and fruits, the sun and moon and their light — none of these is other, and none is not other.

At that time the Blessed One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again in verse, spoke: just as the great ocean’s waves are raised by a fierce wind, and its billows heave against the dark abyss without ever ceasing, so the sea of the store consciousness, calm and still, is stirred by the winds of objects, and the waves of the manifold consciousnesses leap up and turn into being. For example, the manifold hues of blue and red, the jade ornaments, fragrant milk, and rock sugar, faint flavors, blooms and fruits, the sun and moon with their light — all these are the winds of objects that whip up the waves of consciousness in the sea of the mind, and all of them are neither identical nor not identical.

[Blue and red and manifold hues, conch-shell, milk, and rock sugar, faint flavors, blooms and fruits] Blue and red are form-objects that give rise to the eye consciousness; the sound of the jade ornaments (as an ancient poem says: ‘Noble scions of the five mausolea, in pairs they sound their jade tinklers’) is a sound-object that gives rise to the ear consciousness; fragrant milk is a scent-object that gives rise to the nose consciousness; rock sugar and faint flavors are taste-objects that give rise to the tongue consciousness; the jade ornaments are also touch-objects that give rise to the body consciousness; and the present blossoms, the future fruits, and the sun and moon with their light are mental objects that give rise to the mind consciousness. All these are the winds of objects that whip up the waves of consciousness in the sea of the mind. The Tang translation says:
“Blue and red and other hues, salt, conch, milk, and rock sugar, blooms and fruits, sun, moon, and light — none is other, and none is not other.”
[Jade ornament (kēpèi)] A pendant made of shell. [Shell (
kē

)] A fine stone resembling jade. [Rock sugar] That is, crystal sugar. [Neither identical nor not identical] From the standpoint of the true nature of all dharmas, all things are the same (not different). The Heart Sūtra says:
“The empty characteristic of all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
Yet with respect to their characteristics, the myriad things are infinitely varied (not without difference). (For the details of the true nature of all dharmas, see the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”

Just as the sea water gives rise to waves, so too the seven consciousnesses, arising together with the mind, are born in combination with it. Just as the sea water changes and the manifold waves turn about, so too the seven consciousnesses, arising together with the mind, are born in combination with it. This means that from that place of the store consciousness, the manifold consciousnesses turn forth.

The tranquil, still ocean of the store consciousness, stirred by the winds of objects, gives rise to the waves of the seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), which together with the mind (the ālaya consciousness) arise in combination as the evolving consciousnesses. Just as the still sea water suddenly surges into billows, the waves of the seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and the manas) together with the mind (the ālaya) arise in combination as the evolving consciousnesses. This is to say that from the store consciousness the manifold consciousnesses (the eight) turn forth into being.

[Just as the sea water gives rise to waves, so the seven consciousnesses (the first seven) arise together with the mind (ālaya) in combination] The still ocean of the store consciousness, stirred by the winds of objects, becomes the ocean of evolving consciousnesses surging with waves. The waves of the ocean of evolving consciousnesses are a metaphor for the first seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), while the sea water beneath the waves is a metaphor for the ālaya consciousness. The store consciousness is a single unity, while the evolving consciousnesses are composed of eight (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, manas, and ālaya). Master Hanshan’s Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“Deluded, the one mind becomes the eight consciousnesses.”

Here the still, tranquil ocean is a metaphor for the store consciousness, and the surging, billowing ocean is a metaphor for the evolving consciousnesses. The store consciousness is a single unity; when it transforms into the evolving consciousnesses, it gives rise to the first seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and manas), while the remaining portion becomes the ālaya consciousness. Thus the evolving consciousnesses are composed of these eight consciousnesses.
The Tang translation says:

“The seven consciousnesses, beginning with the manas, should be known to be the same — like the sea together with its waves, they arise with the mind in combination. Just as the sea water moves and the manifold waves turn about, so the store consciousness likewise gives rise to the manifold consciousnesses.”

(Translation: the seven consciousnesses beginning with the manas (the intention), namely the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and manas consciousnesses, should be known to be likewise — just as the waves with the sea water beneath them, these seven consciousnesses arise with the ālaya consciousness (the mind) in combination as the evolving consciousnesses. Just as the calm sea water moves and the manifold waves arise, so the store consciousness likewise is deluded by the winds of objects, and the manifold consciousnesses (the eight) turn forth into being.)

It is said that by that mind, intention, and consciousness, one thinks upon the meanings of characteristics. In the undivided characteristic, there are eight; without characteristics, there is likewise no characteristic. Just as the sea and its waves are without distinction, so too the consciousnesses and the mind; difference likewise cannot be attained. The mind is called ‘gathering karma’; the intention is called ‘broad gathering’; the consciousnesses are what is cognized by consciousness; and as for the manifest equal objects, five are spoken of.

Because there come to be the mind (ālaya consciousness), the intention (manas), and the consciousnesses (the first six: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), one thinks upon the meanings of the various characteristics. In the ‘undivided characteristic’ there is the eighth consciousness (ālaya), which has neither an active characteristic nor an objective characteristic. Just as the still sea and the surging sea are not two different things (both being the manifestation of one body), so too the store consciousness and the evolving consciousnesses: they are one body in two states, and in essence they are not different. The mind (ālaya) is able to store karma; the intention (manas) broadly gathers karma and feeds it into the ālaya consciousness; because it discriminates, it is called consciousness (the sixth); and what truly mirrors the sense-objects (form, sound, scent, taste, and touch) are the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body).

[In the undivided characteristic there are eight] In the undivided characteristic there is the eighth consciousness (ālaya), which is the substance of the first seven consciousnesses. When the evolving consciousnesses are restored to the store consciousness, the first seven consciousnesses cease, while the eighth (ālaya) does not cease, and it becomes the store consciousness.
The Tang translation says:

“Mind, intention, and consciousness are spoken for the sake of the various characteristics; the eight consciousnesses have no distinct characteristic, neither active nor objective. Just as the sea and its waves are then without distinction, so too the consciousnesses and the mind; difference likewise cannot be attained. The mind
(ālaya)
is able to gather karma; the intention
(manas)
is able to gather broadly; because it discriminates, it is called consciousness
(the sixth)
; with respect to the manifest present objects, five are spoken
(the first five)

blocks.text: 7. The Selfless Tathāgatagarbha

inline.s: [The selfless Tathāgatagarbha] The Tathāgatagarbha, like all dharmas, is selfless; all of it is the stuff of the dream of ignorance, an illusion. (For the dream of ignorance, see the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”

At that time the great bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: ‘O Blessed One, the Blessed One’s sūtra says: “The Tathāgatagarbha is pure in its own nature, and the thirty-two marks enter into the bodies of all sentient beings. Like a jewel of great price wrapped in a soiled garment, so too the Tathāgatagarbha, eternal and unchanging, is wrapped in the soiled garment of the aggregates, realms, and sense-fields, and is defiled by the false imaginings and defilements of greed, anger, and delusion.” This is what all the Buddhas proclaim. How then, O Blessed One, speaking of a self as the non-Buddhists do, does the Blessed One say that there is a Tathāgatagarbha? O Blessed One, the non-Buddhists also speak of an eternal agent, free from the guṇa-support, all-pervading and unceasing. O Blessed One, they teach a self.’

At that time the great bodhisattva Mahāmati respectfully said to the Buddha: ‘O Blessed One, the Blessed One’s teaching says: “The Tathāgatagarbha is pure in its own nature, and the thirty-two marks enter into the bodies of all sentient beings. Like a most precious jewel wrapped in a filthy rag, so too the Tathāgatagarbha, eternal and unchanging, is wrapped in the filthy rag of the aggregates, realms, and sense-fields, and is defiled by the false imaginings and defilements of greed, anger, and delusion.” This is what all the Buddhas proclaim. Why then, O Blessed One, does the Blessed One, speaking of a “self” as the non-Buddhists do, say there is a Tathāgatagarbha? O Blessed One, the non-Buddhists also speak of an eternal agent, free from the guṇa-support, all-pervading and unceasing. O Blessed One, they teach a “self.”’

The bodhisattva Mahāmati, out of compassion lest sentient beings misconstrue the Tathāgatagarbha as bearing merely a different name but the same meaning as the substantial self asserted by the non-Buddhists, raised this question to clarify the matter.

[Sūtra (xiūduōluó)] The Chinese rendering is ‘qìjīng’ (concordant scripture). ‘Concord’ means that above, it accords with the wondrous principle of the Buddhas, and below, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings; ‘scripture’ has the sense of a thread, stringing together the meaning of the Dharma so that it is not scattered or lost. [Tathāgatagarbha] See
“Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha”

article. [Thirty-two marks] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great man, namely: 1. the feet at rest and even; 2. a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles; 3. long and slender fingers; 4. soft hands and feet; 5. webs like a net between the fingers and toes; 6. perfectly rounded heels; 7. ankles raised and full; 8. calves like those of a deer; 9. arms long enough to reach the knees; 10. the male organ concealed; 11. the body’s height and breadth equal; 12. blue-black pores; 13. body hairs upturned; 14. a body radiant with golden light; 15. a constant halo one fathom wide; 16. smooth and delicate skin; 17. seven places full and even; 18. both armpits full; 19. a body like a lion’s; 20. a well-formed body; 21. rounded shoulders; 22. forty teeth in the mouth; 23. white teeth even and compact; 24. four fangs bright and pure; 25. jawbones like a lion’s; 26. the throat’s saliva having the finest flavor; 27. a long and broad tongue; 28. a Brahmā-sound clear and far-reaching; 29. eyes of deep blue hue; 30. eyelashes like those of a bull; 31. a white hair between the brows; 32. a fleshy uṣṇīṣa atop the crown. [Aggregates, realms, sense-fields (yīn jiè rù)] The five aggregates (skandhas), the eighteen elements, and the twelve sense-fields (āyatanas), also called aggregates, elements, and fields. [Aggregates, elements, and fields] The five aggregates, eighteen elements, and twelve sense-fields. [Five aggregates] The aggregates of form, feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness — the five great constituents of the human person. [Eighteen elements] The six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), the six objects (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and mental objects), and the six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness) united as the ‘eighteen elements.’ [Twelve sense-fields] The six faculties plus the six objects together are the twelve sense-fields. ‘Field’ means the place of arising, for from the six faculties and six objects the six consciousnesses are born. Then the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses together form the eighteen elements. [Defilement (chénláo)] Wearied by objects in the mind, a synonym for afflictions. [Guṇa (qiúnà)] A Sanskrit transliteration, meaning a primary substance. [Free from the guṇa-support] The Wei translation says:
“Without relying on any conditions, it exists of itself.”

The Buddha told Mahāmati: The Tathāgatagarbha I speak of is not the same as the self the non-Buddhists speak of. Mahāmati, sometimes I speak of emptiness, the signless, the wishless, thusness, reality, dharmahood, the Dharma body, nirvāṇa, freedom from self-nature, non-arising and non-ceasing, primordial stillness, and intrinsic nirvāṇa — with such phrases I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha. The Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Perfectly Enlightened One, out of a wish to cut off the fear of the phrase ‘selfless’ in foolish beings, speaks of the door of the Tathāgatagarbha, the realm free of delusion and possessing nothing at all.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: The Tathāgatagarbha I speak of is not the same as the ‘self’ the non-Buddhists speak of. Mahāmati, sometimes I speak of emptiness, the signless, the wishless, thusness, reality, dharmahood, the Dharma body, nirvāṇa, freedom from self-nature, non-arising and non-ceasing, primordial stillness, and intrinsic nirvāṇa — with such phrases I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha. Because foolish beings of nihilistic views are afraid of the phrase ‘selfless,’ the Buddhas speak of the Dharma-door of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the realm free of delusion, possessing nothing at all.

[Selfless] An entity having the function of a sovereign master is a self. Selfless means that there is no such entity having the function of a sovereign master. [Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One] These are three of the Buddha’s ten titles. ‘Tathāgata’ — riding the road of Suchness, he comes from cause to fruit and attains perfect enlightenment; ‘Worthy of Offerings’ — he is worthy of the offerings of gods and humans; ‘Perfectly Enlightened One’ — the genuine, universal, and equal enlightenment, that is, the Buddha’s own enlightenment.

The Tathāgatagarbha is the mind of the ultimate meaning that the Buddhas themselves realize, beyond words and beyond thought. Because sentient beings falsely cling to the five aggregates as self and turn in the round of birth and death, and because when they hear the phrase ‘selfless’ they suppose it means annihilation and so become afraid, the Buddhas proclaim the Dharma-door of the Tathāgatagarbha, the realm free of delusion and possessing nothing at all, causing sentient beings to distance themselves from the five aggregates, gradually to penetrate what the Buddhas have realized, and to awaken from the dream of ignorance.

Mahāmati, the great bodhisattvas of the future and the present should not form the view of self or cling to it. For example, as a potter takes a single lump of clay and by the craft of human labor, water, the wooden wheel, and a cord makes it into various vessels, so too the Tathāgata, selfless with regard to all dharmas and free of all deluded characteristics, by various skillful means of wisdom sometimes speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha and sometimes speaks of selflessness. By reason of this, when I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is not the same as the self the non-Buddhists speak of; this is called speaking of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Mahāmati, the great bodhisattvas of the future and the present should not regard the Tathāgatagarbha as a self and cling to it. For example, as a potter takes a lump of clay and by the craft of human labor, water, the wooden wheel, and a cord skillfully makes it into various vessels, so too the Tathāgata, selfless with regard to all dharmas and free of all deluded characteristics, by various skillful means of wisdom sometimes speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha and sometimes speaks of selflessness. By reason of this, when he speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is not the same as the ‘self’ the non-Buddhists speak of; this is called speaking of the Tathāgatagarbha.

For the sake of leading and guiding the non-Buddhists who cling to a self, I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, causing them to leave the false imagination of the view of self, to enter the realm of the three gates of liberation, and in the hope of swiftly attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore the Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Perfectly Enlightened One, speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha in this way. If it were not so, it would be the same as the self the non-Buddhists speak of. Therefore, Mahāmati, in order to be free of the views of the non-Buddhists, one should rely on the selfless Tathāgatagarbha.

I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha for the sake of leading and guiding the non-Buddhists who cling to a self, causing them to leave the false imagination of the view of self and to enter the realm of the three gates of liberation, in the hope that they may swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore the Buddhas proclaim the Tathāgatagarbha in this way. If it were not spoken thus, it would be the same as the ‘self’ the non-Buddhists speak of. Therefore, Mahāmati, to be free of the wrong views of the non-Buddhists, one should rely on the meaning of the selfless Tathāgatagarbha.
The Tang translation says:

“Mahāmati, I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha in order to gather the hosts of non-Buddhists who cling to a self, causing them to leave false views, to enter the three liberations, and swiftly to realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore the Buddhas speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is not the same as the self the non-Buddhists speak of. If one wishes to be free of the views of the non-Buddhists, one should know the meaning of the selfless Tathāgatagarbha.”

[Three gates of liberation] Three gates of wisdom for entering the realm of liberation. First, the gate of emptiness: to realize that all dharmas are originally empty without clinging to emptiness; second, the gate of the wishless: to know that all dharmas exist as illusions and therefore to have no wish or seeking; third, the gate of the signless: to know that all dharmas are without signs yet not devoid of signs, and to enter the middle way. [If it were not so, it would be the same as the self the non-Buddhists speak of] If one merely speaks of the existence of the Tathāgatagarbha without speaking of its selfless meaning, then the Tathāgatagarbha would be the same as the ‘self’ the non-Buddhists speak of. [The selfless Tathāgatagarbha] The Tathāgatagarbha, like all dharmas, is selfless; all of it is the stuff of the dream of ignorance, an illusion. (For the dream of ignorance, see the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
Question: If the Tathāgatagarbha is an illusion, does this mean that the Dharma body is also an illusion?
Answer: This sūtra says:
“In all things there is no nirvāṇa; there is no Buddha who attains nirvāṇa; there is no Buddha who is without nirvāṇa.”
In the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Within it, the Buddha-worlds countless as hundreds of millions of billions of asamkhyeyas, beyond expression, like the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, arising in confusion and ceasing in confusion.” ‘Originally there is no enlightenment and no nirvāṇa, no becoming a Buddha and no not-becoming, no deluded transmigration and no non-transmigration.’ ‘Birth and death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all the Buddhas, are alike the marks of flowers in the sky.’
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground, on the Roots of Goodness, says:
“Ever contemplate the wondrous Dharma body of the Buddhas; its nature is like empty space, unattainable.”
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“The Dharma body is like an illusion or a dream — how can it be praised? Knowing it to be without self-nature and without arising, one then truly praises the Buddha.”
Regarding the meaning of the selfless Tathāgatagarbha, the Chan school has two famous gong’an (public cases):
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records:
A monk asked: ‘Venerable, why do you say that
this very mind is Buddha
?’ The master
(Mazu)
replied: ‘To stop a child from crying
(this is an expedient teaching for beginning students)
.’ The monk asked: ‘When the crying has stopped, what then?’ The master said: ‘
neither mind nor Buddha
.’ The monk asked: ‘For one who has gone beyond these two kinds of people, how would you point?’ The master said: ‘Tell him
(him)
to say
it is not a thing

[To stop a child from crying] A metaphor for an expedient teaching (not the ultimate teaching). When a child cries, an adult gives him a yellow leaf from a poplar, saying: ‘This is a piece of gold; take it and buy some candy.’ The child, taking it, stops crying. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
Volume Twenty says:

“As when a baby is crying, the parents give it a yellow leaf of the poplar and say: ‘Do not cry! Do not cry! I will give you gold.’ The baby, seeing it, thinks it is real gold and so stops crying. Yet that poplar leaf is in truth not gold.”
The Compendium of the Five Lamps further says:

The Chan master Zizai of Funiu Mountain at Yique, a son of the Li clan of Wuxing. At first he attended on the Chan master Guoyi, and after receiving the full precepts he went to call on Mazu and awakened to the ground of mind
(enlightenment)
. The patriarch bade him carry a letter to the National Master Zhong
(the National Master Huizhong)
. The National Master asked: ‘By what Dharma does Great Master Ma instruct his disciples?’ He replied: ‘
This very mind is Buddha
.’ The National Master said: ‘What kind of talk is that
(he strongly disapproved)
!’ After a long while
(after a long time)
he asked again: ‘Apart from this, is there any other teaching?’ The master said: ‘
Neither mind, nor Buddha
. Or again, one may say:
It is not mind; it is not Buddha; it is not a thing.
.’ The National Master said: ‘Now that is a bit closer
(that is more like it)
In the gong’ans above, three levels are set forth:
“This very mind is Buddha”
“Neither mind nor Buddha”
“It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing”

. The ‘mind’ spoken of here refers to self-nature. ‘This very mind is Buddha’ means that the Buddha is nothing other than this: the fully awakened self-nature is itself the Buddha. ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ means that self-nature and the Buddha are both illusions, the stuff of the dream of ignorance. ‘It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing’ speaks of the ‘that’ which dreams the dream of ignorance.

blocks.text: 8. Realizing the Immediate Perception of One’s Own Mind

inline.s: But realize the immediate perception of one’s own mind, and delusive thinking does not arise,
peaceful
and happy, and the affairs of the world are forever stilled.
Moreover, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the immediate perception of his own mind — the realm of delusion of the grasping and the grasped
he should abandon crowds, worldly conventions, and sleep; through the first, middle, and last watches of the night, ever wakeful in self-realization
and skillful in practice
he should abandon the scriptures of wrong views and their pronouncements, and the characteristics of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas
and penetrate the characteristics of the delusions presented by his own mind.
Moreover, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know
the immediate perception of his own mind

— that the characteristics of the grasping and the grasped are all realms presented by his own mind — he should abandon clamor, drowsiness, and sleep; through the first, middle, and last watches of the night, ever wakeful in self-realization, he should diligently and skillfully practice; he should be far from the wrong views of non-Buddhists and their scriptural pronouncements, and from the characteristics of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and penetrate the characteristics of the discriminations presented by his own mind.
The Tang translation says:

“Moreover, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know that the discriminated realms of the grasping and the grasped are all presented by his own mind, he should abandon clamor, drowsiness, and sleep, diligently practice through the first, middle, and last watches of the night, be far from the wrong treatises of the non-Buddhists he has heard and the dharma of the two vehicles, and penetrate the characteristics of his own mind’s discriminations.”
immediate perception (pratyakṣa)
” means: without adding

thought, one directly intuits its presence — that is, direct knowledge. To know by reasoning is inferential knowledge. [Realizing the immediate perception of one’s own mind] To be aware of what the senses — eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body — convey without adding thought. That is, of the four stages of the mind’s functioning — feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness — one has only the feeling, without the later three stages of conception, volition, and consciousness. (For the functioning of the mind, see
“Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgata”
Realizing the immediate perception of one’s own mind is like a mirror reflecting an object: one is aware of the realms presented by one’s own mind without thought or calculation.
To see
is merely to see; to hear is merely to hear; to smell is merely to smell; to taste is merely to taste; to touch is merely to touch. This sūtra says:
“But realize the immediate perception of one’s own mind, and delusive thinking does not arise; peaceful
(the same as ‘secure’)
and happy, the affairs of the world are forever stilled.”
The Record of the Mirror of the School says:

“The Buddha said: ‘But realize the immediate perception of one’s own mind, and delusive thinking does not arise; peaceful and happy, the affairs of the world are forever stilled.’ As for ‘peaceful and happy’ — this is the still, wondrous, and eternal; as for ‘the affairs of the world are forever stilled’ — this is the severing of all clinging and pursuit. One may say that one has met the perfect treasure and at once put an end to all seeking; one has arrived at the nirvāṇa of eternal bliss, and there is nowhere further to go. This is the boundary of the ordinary and the noble, as if one had reached one’s own native home; it is the support of delusion and of awakening, and one has exhausted its very root. The Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: ‘The diamond treasure is without lack or diminution.’”
Master Hanshan’s Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“Because
(by virtue of)
the immediate perception of one’s own mind, the holy and the ordinary are not established, and all things are negated — thereby revealing the meaning of ultimate awakening within birth and death.”
The Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Gate of Pacifying the Mind says:

“As soon as there is a mind that discriminates and reckons about the immediate perception of one’s own mind, all of it is a dream; if one knows the mind to be stilled and extinguished, with no place where any thought arises, this is called right enlightenment.”
[On ‘to see
is merely to see; to hear is merely to hear

’ Once there was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long and wearying journey, arrived at Śrāvastī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. He found the Buddha going from house to house collecting alms in the city, his every gesture graceful and wonderful, his six senses fully tamed and guarded, tranquil and serene. Bāhiya came forward, bowed, and asked the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to teach him a way of boundless benefit and peace. The Buddha said that he was going from door to door for alms just then, and it was not a fitting time to teach. But Bāhiya asked again and again, and so the Buddha taught him on the spot:

“Bāhiya! You should practice thus: in the seen, let there be only what is seen; in the heard, only what is heard; in the sensed, only what is sensed; in the cognized, only what is cognized. Bāhiya! When you are able, in the seen, to have only what is seen, in the heard, only what is heard, in the sensed, only what is sensed, in the cognized, only what is cognized, then you will be free of clinging and obstruction. When you are free of clinging and obstruction, then you have no past, and no future. Since you have no past and no future
(but only the present)
, all your sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering will vanish utterly.”
(The original is found in the Theravāda Udāna.)

[Three times] The past, present, and future times. Dharmas that have already arisen and ceased are called ‘past’; dharmas that have arisen but not yet ceased are called ‘present’; dharmas not yet arisen are called ‘future.’ [But only the present] The scripture says:
“In the seen, only what is seen; in the heard, only what is heard; in the sensed, only what is sensed; in the cognized, only what is cognized.”
This is without any delusive thought about the past or the future. In fact, people’s unease, anxiety, and suffering all arise from delusions about the past or the future.

[First, middle, and last watches of the night] The first, middle, and last divisions of the night. Ancient India divided a day into six periods: three by day and three by night. The three by day are morning, noon, and sunset; the three by night are the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. One ancient Indian period equals four modern hours, so six periods make twenty-four hours. [Skillful practice (xíng fāngbiàn)] This is a literal rendering of one Sanskrit word order, meaning ‘to practice by skillful means.’ The sense is to practice diligently and skillfully. Here ‘expedient’ (fāngbiàn) means skillful and diligent.

[Penetrate the characteristics of the delusions presented by one’s own mind] This is to give not a single thought a free pass, and to see through every single thought. [Not letting a single thought slip] Do not let any delusive thought slide past (do not be deceived by it). [Seeing through every thought] Do not be shrouded by any delusive thought, do not follow it as it manipulates, and do not take it as real.
The state of realizing the immediate perception of one’s own mind is called presence (also called clear awareness).
Presence — be aware of that presence.

blocks.text: 9. The Great Dharma-Door of Skillful Means

inline.s: At that time the great bodhisattva Mahāmati, observing the sentient beings of the future, again besought the Blessed One: May the Blessed One be pleased to teach the uninterrupted practice, and, as for the bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas, the great skillful means of the practitioner.

At that time the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati, perceiving the capacities of beings in the future, again asked the World-Honored One: “I pray you, for the sake of beings in the future, tell us how one may practice without admixture and without interruption, so that they may, like all great bodhisattvas, attain the great skillful means of practitioners.”

[Perceiving beings in the future] The bodhisattva Mahāmati perceived that among the capacities of beings in the future there would also be those of sudden faculties who could be brought to maturity, and so he especially besought the World-Honored One to reveal to them the great skillful means of practitioners. [Without interval] Without admixture and without interruption. [Great skillful means] Bodhi is the fruit of the path; the fruit is accomplished through practice, and practice rides upon skillful means (expedient wisdom). Therefore the bodhisattva Mahāmati, for the sake of beings of future ages, besought the World-Honored One to reveal the great skillful means of practitioners.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who accomplishes four dharmas attains the great skillful means of practitioners. What are the four? They are: skillfully discerning what appears as one’s own mind; observing that the nature of external things is no nature; being free from the view of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and attaining the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas, by which he attains the great skillful means of practitioners.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: A great bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas attains the great skillful means of practitioners. What are the four? They are: 1. skillfully observing what appears as one’s own mind; 2. observing external dharmas as illusory (the nature of external things is no nature); 3. being free from the view of arising, abiding, and ceasing; 4. attaining the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas, by which he attains the great skillful means of practitioners.

[As for ‘skillfully discerning what appears as one’s own mind’] Here the word ‘discern’ means to distinguish that what appears as one’s own mind is false and not real. But taken literally it is easily confused with the ‘discernment’ that this sutra repeatedly stresses one must be free from. Therefore this annotation, following the Tang translation, renders it: skillfully observing what appears as one’s own mind. The Tang translation says:

“What are the four? They are: observing what appears as one’s own mind; being far from the view of arising, abiding, and ceasing; skillfully knowing that external dharmas have no nature; and single-mindedly seeking the wisdom of self-realization.”
[External dharmas] Dharmas produced by the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are called internal dharmas; all other dharmas are called external dharmas. The Tang translation says:

“King of Lanka, just as a single seed produces sprouts, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits in immeasurable variety, so it is with external dharmas, and so too with internal dharmas: with ignorance as condition, all dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields arise, and within the three realms one receives birth in the various destinies, with all their distinctions of suffering and pleasure, fair and foul, speech and silence, movement and rest.”
How does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully discern what appears as his own mind? He observes thus: the three realms are but distinctions of mind only
apart from self and what belongs to self, without wavering, apart from coming and going
Perfumed by beginningless habits of falsehood
bound by the various forms and formations of the three realms
the establishments of body and wealth arise as imagination enters in. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what appears as his own mind.

What is the great bodhisattva’s skillful observation of what appears as his own mind? He observes thus: the three realms are fundamentally empty and still, and their distinctions exist only as mind; therefore he knows that they are fundamentally unborn, and is apart from self and what belongs to self, without wavering, apart from coming and going. He realizes that, perfumed by the beginningless habits of falsehood that mistake the illusory for the real, one is bound in saṃsāra by the various bonds of the five aggregates, body, and mind within the three realms, so that there arise the various establishments of body, family, and wealth; all such dharmas appear only as the imaginations of the mind follow along. This is called the great bodhisattva’s skillful observation of what appears as his own mind.
[Distinctions] Differences. [Perfumed by beginningless habits of falsehood] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time all sentient beings have been subject to various inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the directions of the four quarters

, falsely taking the four great elements as the marks of his own body and the reflections of the six dusts as the marks of his own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! The sky truly has no flowers; it is the sick person who falsely grasps at them. Because of that false grasping, he is deluded not only about the nature of space itself, but also about where those flowers truly arise. From this false grasping comes the turning round in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: What is ignorance? Good man! From beginningless time all sentient beings have been subject to various inversions, taking the false as real — this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the body of flesh formed by the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own self, and the thoughts arising when the six faculties come into contact with the six dusts as the mark of his own mind. It is like eyes afflicted with cataracts that falsely see flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; this is an illusion falsely grasped by the diseased eye. Because of that false grasping, one is deluded not only into thinking space itself real, but also into believing that flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings, deluded and inverted, falsely take the illusory body and mind as real and cling to them as self, they turn round in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.) [Four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, and wind has motion. All material forms in the world possess these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, and so they are called ‘great.’ [Reflections of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six dusts; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the reflections of the six dusts — the illusory reflections of the six dusts.

[Three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sex and food, and includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still have a body of form, and includes the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas; the formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who have no body of form but dwell with their consciousness in profound and wondrous samādhi, and includes the four heavens of emptiness (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of the birth-and-death turning of ordinary beings. [Form and formations] The aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations — these two are mentioned briefly to represent the five aggregates. Because there is the body and mind of the five aggregates, there arise the various establishments of body, family, and wealth. [Five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five arise from accumulation, and so are called the ‘five aggregates’; they can also cover over people’s true nature, causing them to become deluded and inverted and to create all kinds of karma, and so they are also named the ‘five yin’ (wǔ yīn). Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called ‘form-dharma’; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called ‘mind-dharma.’ These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, the aggregate of form is the physical body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness) are mind.

How does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully observe that the nature of external things is no nature? He observes that all natures are like a mirage, a dream, and so forth, and that beginningless habits of false imagination are their cause; he observes the self-nature of all natures. When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus skillfully observes that the nature of external things is no nature, this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful observation that the nature of external things is no nature.

What is the great bodhisattva’s skillful observation that external dharmas are illusory (the nature of external things is no nature)? He observes that all dharmas are like a mirage, like a dream; that beginningless habits of false imagination are the cause of all dharmas; and he observes the essential nature of all dharmas (the reality of all dharmas). When the great bodhisattva thus skillfully observes that external dharmas are illusory, this is called the great bodhisattva’s skillful observation that external dharmas are illusory.

How does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully become free from the view of arising, abiding, and ceasing? He observes that all natures are like illusions and dreams, that they are unborn whether by self, by other, or by both together, and that they follow along as distinctions of one’s own mind; therefore he sees that the nature of external things is no nature
he sees that consciousness is unborn and that conditions do not accumulate
he sees that, with imagination as condition, birth takes place in the three realms
Within and without, all dharmas are unobtainable

he sees that they are apart from self-nature, the view of arising is utterly extinguished, and knowing the self-nature of all dharmas to be like an illusion, he attains the patient acceptance of the unborn

Having attained the patient acceptance of the unborn, he is free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful discernment and freedom from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

What is the great bodhisattva’s skill in becoming free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing? He observes that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams: they are unborn by self, unborn by other, and dharmas arising from both together are likewise unborn; all are what one’s own mind distinguishes and manifests. Therefore he sees that there are no external dharmas, and so sees that consciousness is unborn, that the multitude of conditions does not accumulate, and understands that, with imagination as condition, birth takes place in the three realms. Within and without, all dharmas are unobtainable; he sees that they are apart from the self-nature of perceived forms, the view of arising is utterly extinguished, and knowing the self-nature of all dharmas — that they are like illusions — to be fundamentally unborn, he attains the patient acceptance of the unborn. Having attained the patient acceptance of the unborn, he is free from the view of arising, the view of abiding, and the view of ceasing. This is called the great bodhisattva’s skill in becoming free from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
This means: directly beholding that all dharmas are only what one’s own mind manifests, that they arise from conditions and are without nature, one suddenly realizes the unborn.

[The view of arising is utterly extinguished] One awakens to the fact that dharmas are fundamentally unborn. Since dharmas are unborn, they do not abide and do not cease; thus the view of abiding and the view of ceasing are utterly extinguished.
Whether it be saṃsāra or nirvāṇa depends entirely on the turning about of a single mind; there is no other dharma. Therefore the Buddha’s teaching takes mind as its cardinal principle.

How does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom? He attains the patient acceptance of the unborn, dwells on the eighth bodhisattva ground, becomes free from mind, manas, and consciousness, from the five dharmas, from self-nature, and from the marks of the two kinds of selflessness, and attains the mind-made body.

What is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s attainment of the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom? It is attaining the patient acceptance of the unborn, dwelling on the eighth bodhisattva ground, becoming free from mind, manas, and consciousness, from the five dharmas, from the three self-natures, and from the marks of the two kinds of selflessness, and attaining the mind-made body.

[Patient acceptance of the unborn] Abbreviated as the acceptance of the unborn; true wisdom settles upon the principle that ‘all dharmas were never born, and therefore do not cease,’ and never again falls back. [Mind, manas, consciousness] Mind means the act of gathering and arising, that is, the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna); manas means the act of thinking and measuring, that is, the seventh consciousness (mano-vijñāna); consciousness means the act of distinguishing, that is, the sixth consciousness. [Free from mind, manas, and consciousness] Free from the workings of consciousness. (For the workings of consciousness, see in detail the article
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
, the section ‘The Workings of Consciousness.’) [Mind-made body] The body obtained by bodhisattvas above the first ground, who, in order to save sentient beings, receive birth as they wish.
[World-Honored One, what is the cause and condition of the mind-made body?

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: The mind-made is so called because it is like a thought that goes swiftly and without hindrance; therefore it is called mind-made. It is like a thought that passes through stone walls without hindrance: to another region immeasurable yojanas away, because of what was previously seen and remembered without forgetting, as the flow of one’s own mind continues without interruption, one is born there without hindrance to the body.

(The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha:) World-Honored One, by what cause and condition is it named the mind-made body? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: The mind-made is so named because it resembles a thought that comes and goes swiftly and without hindrance. Just as a thought passes through stone walls without hindrance, so the mind-made body, toward places immeasurably far away and countless yojanas distant, because of what was previously seen and remembered without forgetting — so long as the flow of one’s own mindful recollection continues uninterrupted — goes there with no hindrance at all.

[Yojana] Also called yojana (yóuyán), a unit of distance in India. There are three kinds, large, medium, and small: the large yojana is about eighty li; the medium yojana about sixty li; the small yojana about forty li.
The Tang translation says:

“Just as a thought, toward places immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas away, recollects the various things previously seen, and with thought succeeding thought swiftly reaches there, and neither its body nor mountains, rivers, or stone walls can hinder it, so it is with the mind-made body.”

Mahāmati, such a mind-made body is attained all at once. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind-made body — the power of the samādhi of illusion, sovereign spiritual powers, the adornment of wondrous marks, and a body of the noble lineage — is born all at once
Like the mind-made, without hindrance, following the sphere of his original vows wherever his recollection turns, in order to
perfect
sentient beings, he attains the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, such a mind-made body is attained all at once (
it is possessed immediately at the very moment the patient acceptance of the unborn is attained)
The great
bodhisattva’s mind-made body, together
with the power of
the samādhi of illusion, sovereign spiritual powers, the adornment of wondrous marks, and a body of the noble lineage, is born all at once
Like the mind-made, without hindrance,
the mind-made body,
following the sphere of his original vows wherever his recollection turns, in order to
perfect
sentient beings, is born among all the assemblies of noble ones, and attains the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom.
The Tang translation says:

“Mahāmati, just as a thought, toward places immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yojanas away, recollects the various things previously seen, and with thought succeeding thought swiftly reaches there, and neither its body nor mountains, rivers, or stone walls can hinder it, so it is with the mind-made body: by the samādhi of illusion, the sovereign power of spiritual penetration, and the adornment of all marks, because he recollects his original vow to accomplish sentient beings, he goes like a thought and is born among all the assemblies of noble ones.”

Thus the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the patient acceptance of the unborn, dwells on the eighth bodhisattva ground, progressively abandons the body of mind, manas, and consciousness, of the five dharmas, of self-nature, and of the marks of the two kinds of selflessness, and attains the mind-made body and the bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas, by which he attains the great skillful means of practitioners
Thus should one learn.
