blocks.text: 10. The Mark of Self-Awakened Noble Wisdom

inline.s: The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati again said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, pray speak to us of the mark of self-awakened noble wisdom and of the One Vehicle. If you speak of the mark of self-awakened noble wisdom and of the One Vehicle, I and the other bodhisattvas will be skilled in the mark of self-awakened noble wisdom and the One Vehicle, and without depending on others will penetrate the Buddha-Dharma.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati again reverently addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, pray reveal to us the mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom (the mark of practice by which one himself awakens to noble wisdom) and the mark of practice of the One Vehicle. If we hear the World-Honored One’s mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom and the mark of practice of the One Vehicle, I and the other bodhisattvas will gain this skill and, without passing through other paths, penetrate the Buddha-Dharma.

[Noble wisdom] The Tathāgata’s wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma-realm, that is, the wisdom that awakens to ‘all dharmas are fundamentally unborn’; it is also called the wisdom of the pure dharma-realm. This sutra says:

“Mahāmati! As for the ultimate mark of self-awakened noble wisdom: toward all marks of dharmas one has no calculation or attachment; one attains the body of the samādhi of illusion, and advances and proceeds to the ground of all Buddhas.”
[The mark of self-awakened noble wisdom] The mark of practice by which one himself awakens to noble wisdom. [Mark of practice] The aspect of one’s practice.
The Tang translation says:

“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati again said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, pray speak of the mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom and the mark of practice of the One Vehicle. I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, gaining this skill, will within the Buddha-Dharma awaken without depending on others.”
[Awaken without depending on others] To awaken without passing through other paths.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: Listen well, listen well! Reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: Listen attentively! Listen attentively! Reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: So be it
I receive your teaching.
Mahāmati reverently addressed the Buddha: Yes, World-Honored One. We receive your teaching with purified minds.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: What the sages of old knew has been transmitted one to another: imagination has no nature. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, observes with self-awakening, without depending on others, and is free from the imagination of views
and rising higher and higher, he enters the Tathāgata’s ground. This is called the mark of self-awakened noble wisdom.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: What the Buddhas of the past knew has been transmitted one to another: imagination has no substantial nature; it is an illusion. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, alone in a quiet place,
observes with self-awakening
, without passing through other paths,
and is free from the imagination of views
(far from all views and imaginations), rising higher and higher, he enters the Tathāgata’s ground. Such practice is called the mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom.
[Imagination has no nature] Imagination has no substantial nature; it is an illusion.
The Tang translation says:

“The Buddha said: Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, relying on the teachings of the sages, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet and stillness, he observes with self-awakening, awakens without depending on others, is free from the view of discrimination, rises higher and higher, and enters the Tathāgata’s ground. Such practice is called the mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom.”
[The view of discrimination] The various thoughts that arise from discrimination and calculation.
Therefore the core of the mark of practice of self-realized noble wisdom is:
to observe with self-awakening and be free from the imagination of views
(this is the breaking of the obstruction to the known)
The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
“Pulling out the very root of all idle talk, eternally separated from all of it, cool and smokeless.”
Again it says:
“Śāriputra, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is but one meaning: detachment. What is detachment?
Detachment from all desires and all views

. Desire is ignorance; views are recollection. Why? Because all dharmas have recollection as their root. Whatever is thought and imagined is a view, and a view is perverse. Śāriputra, even a view within wholesome dharmas I also declare to be a perverse view. Why? Śāriputra, in the detachment and stillness of desire extinguished, there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil; all such things are empty. Being far from all knots and all recollection, it is therefore called detachment. Śāriputra, in the unsurpassed path, all desires are forever stilled. What are those desires? They are perverse and unwholesome thoughts — of self, of what belongs to self, of marks of action, and marks of things. This is called the forever stilling of all desires within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

(Translation: Śāriputra, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is but one meaning: detachment. Detachment from what? From all desires and all views. Desire is ignorance; views are recollection. Why? Because all dharmas take recollection as their root. Whatever is thought and imagined is a view, and a view is perverse. Śāriputra, even a view within wholesome dharmas I also declare to be a perverse view. Why? Śāriputra, in the detachment and stillness where desire is extinguished, there is no dharma and no non-dharma, no good and no evil; all these things are utterly empty. Being far from all desires and all recollection — this is detachment. Śāriputra, in the unsurpassed path, all desires are forever stilled. What are those desires? They are perverse and unwholesome recollections, such as the view of self and the view of what belongs to self, and marks of action and marks of things. Being free from all of them is called the forever stilling of all desires within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.)

[The very root of all idle talk] The view of discrimination. [Cool and smokeless] Like a fire utterly extinguished — cooled, with no smoke left. This illustrates that detachment is most thorough. [All knots] All desires. ‘Knot’ means bondage; here it refers to ‘desire.’ Desire is the root of affliction: it binds practitioners so that they cannot attain liberation and instead sink into birth and death.
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:

“Believing firmly in one’s own nature, knowing that it is the mind’s false movement and that no object stands before one, one cultivates the dharma of detachment. Because one knows in accordance with reality that no object stands before one, by various skillful means one rouses practice in accord with it
not grasping and not thinking, even for a long, long time.
Through the power of perfuming, ignorance is extinguished.”

(Translation: Deeply believing that one’s own nature is Buddha, and knowing that this is the mind’s false movement while in truth no object stands before one, one cultivates the dharma of detachment (‘knowing the illusion, one is immediately detached, without resorting to skillful means; detached from the illusion, one is immediately awakened, with no gradual stages’). Because one knows in accordance with reality that no object stands before one, by various practicable means one rouses practice in accord with it: not grasping and not thinking, even for a long, long time. Persisting in this way, through the power of perfuming, ignorance is extinguished.)
The Essential of the Mind-Seal says:

“When an ordinary person is about to die, he need only contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty, that the four great elements are without self, and that the true mind is without marks, neither going nor coming. At birth the nature does not come; at death the nature does not go. Limpid and perfectly still, mind and object are one suchness. If one can thus directly and suddenly awaken, and is not bound by the three periods of time, then one is a person who has gone beyond the world. One must not harbor the slightest inclination. If one sees auspicious marks — Buddhas coming to welcome one — and all manner of things appearing, one’s mind does not follow them; if one sees ominous marks and all manner of things appearing, one’s mind is not afraid. One has only to forget
(through ‘forget’ we take the meaning of ‘extinguish’)
one’s own mind, and be one with the dharma-realm, then one attains freedom — this is the essential point.”

[Believing firmly in one’s own nature] Deeply believing that one’s own nature is Buddha. [Knowing the mind’s false movement] Knowing that because of the false movement of one’s own mind, the true nature turns into the nature of consciousness and one falls into the state of a sentient being (see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
). Therefore the practice now is simply to stop this false movement:
not grasping and not thinking, even for a long, long time.

Persisting in this way, through the power of perfuming, the nature of consciousness is restored to the state of the original nature. [No object stands before one] There is no present object. Objects appear as illusions produced by the mind’s false movement. [Perfuming] ‘Perfume’ means to fumigate and bring forth; ‘habit’ means doing something repeatedly over a long time until it becomes instinct (habit becoming second nature). Continuously grasping at defiled and pure conditions perfumes the essence of the mind so that it becomes defiled or pure; therefore it is called perfuming. Ignorance is the cause of defiled perfuming; clarity is the cause of pure perfuming. Giving rise to the imagination of views is ignorance; being free from the imagination of views is clarity.
In
The Essentials of the Mind of Baiyun
, the section ‘Self-Realized Noble Wisdom’ contains a detailed exposition of this passage of the sutra.

Mahāmati, what is the mark of the One Vehicle? It is the awakening that attains the path of the One Vehicle; this I call the One Vehicle. How does one attain the awakening of the path of the One Vehicle? It is when, as to grasping and the grasped, imagination does not arise in the place of reality; this is called the awakening of the One Vehicle.]

Mahāmati, what is the mark of practice of the One Vehicle? To realize the path of the One Vehicle — this is the mark of practice of the One Vehicle. Then how does one realize the path of the One Vehicle? It is to be free from the discrimination of the grasping and the grasped, to abide in accordance with reality, and not to give rise to imagination; this is called realizing the path of the One Vehicle.
The Tang translation says:

“What is called the mark of practice of the One Vehicle? It is the realizing and knowing of the path of the One Vehicle. What is called knowing the path of the One Vehicle? It is being free from the discrimination of the grasping and the grasped, and abiding in accordance with reality.”

[Grasping and the grasped] The grasping and the grasped. [One Vehicle] The sole teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. ‘Vehicle’ means a carriage or cart; it illustrates that the Buddha’s teaching can carry people across to the far shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a ‘vehicle.’ The Lotus Sutra says:
“In the buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the dharma of the One Vehicle; there is no second and no third, except as the Buddha speaks expediently.”
The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra says:
“The perfect and sudden teaching is the One Buddha Vehicle.”

[No second and no third, except as the Buddha speaks expediently] There is no second vehicle and no third vehicle; the two vehicles and the three vehicles are the Buddha’s expedient teaching. [Two vehicles] The śrāvaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle. [Three vehicles] The śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The śrāvaka vehicle is also called the small vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle the middle vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle the great vehicle.
In
The Essentials of the Mind of Baiyun
, the section ‘The Mark of Practice of the One Vehicle’ contains a detailed exposition of this passage of the sutra.

[Mahāmati, the awakening of the One Vehicle is not something that other outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Brahmā kings, and the like can attain. It is attained by the Tathāgata alone; therefore it is called the One Vehicle.]

Mahāmati, this path of the One Vehicle is realized by the Tathāgata alone, and cannot be realized by other outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, great Brahmā kings, and the like. It is realized by the Tathāgata alone; therefore it is called the One Vehicle.

[Śrāvaka] One who hears the Buddha’s vocal teaching and, relying on the Four Noble Truths, cultivates and realizes true emptiness; his final fruit is that of the arhat. [Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path (abbreviated as suffering, origin, cessation, and path). ‘Truth’ here means reality. The truth of suffering explains the reality that life is full of suffering; in the truth of origin, ‘origin’ means the arising and gathering together, and it explains the reality of how life’s suffering comes about; the truth of cessation explains the reality that only the state of nirvāṇa is the ultimate cessation of suffering; the truth of the path explains the reality of how one must cultivate the path in order to realize nirvāṇa. These Four Noble Truths fully include the two layers of cause and effect of the mundane and the supramundane: origin is the cause and suffering the effect — this is the cause and effect of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation the effect — this is the cause and effect of the awakened realm.

[Pratyekabuddha] One who receives the Buddha’s teaching, contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, and awakens to the principle of true emptiness; his final fruit is that of the pratyekabuddha. [Twelve links of dependent origination] This explains the process by which sentient beings turn round in birth and death. The twelve links are: ignorance (the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, which are the root of birth and death); formations (the creating of various karmas); consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering a womb); name-and-form (having only the fetal form, the six faculties not yet complete); the six sense-fields (the fetus growing into human form with the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind); contact (being born as a human and coming into contact with external objects); feeling (the sensations of pleasure and pain arising from contact with external objects); craving (desire and love arising toward objects); grasping (seeking and creating); becoming (the forming of karmic causes that can bring about future retribution); birth (again receiving a future body of the five aggregates); and old age and death (the future body gradually aging and dying). These twelve links describe how all the cause and effect of delusion, karma, rebirth, aging, and death in the three periods of past, present, and future revolve without beginning and continue without end. Among them, ignorance and formations are the karmic causes created in the past life; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-fields, contact, and feeling are the retributions experienced in the present life; craving, grasping, and becoming are the karmic causes created in the present life; and from receiving birth through old age and death are the retributions experienced in the future life.

[Brahmā kings] In the first dhyāna heaven of the realm of form there are three heavens: the heaven of Brahmā’s retinue, the heaven of Brahmā’s ministers, and the heaven of Great Brahmā. The lord of the heaven of Great Brahmā is called the Brahmā king, and his name is Śikhin.

The state of the two-vehicle practitioners who have realized the fruit (arhats and pratyekabuddhas) is this: they have broken the attachment to a self in persons, removed the obstruction of afflictions, and ended segmentary birth and death. If they are to become Buddhas, they must further break the attachment to a self in dharmas, remove the obstruction to the known, and end transformational birth and death.
[The two obstructions]

The obstruction of afflictions and the obstruction to the known. The obstruction of afflictions is also called the obstruction of delusion; it is the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, which cause sentient beings to turn round in birth and death within the three realms and thus obstruct liberation, and so it is called the ‘obstruction of afflictions.’ The obstruction to the known is also called the obstruction of wisdom; because sentient beings do not know the emptiness of dharmas (the non-self of dharmas) and cling to all dharmas, producing all kinds of erroneous views, they obstruct bodhi, and so it is called the ‘obstruction to the known.’ The sutra says:
“If the attachment to dharmas is not removed, the obstruction to the known arises and obstructs bodhi.”

[Segmentary birth and death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six destinies, because of the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have divisions; therefore their birth and death is called ‘segmentary birth and death.’ One who ends segmentary birth and death escapes the turning round and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth and death] For the sages among the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusion of views and thoughts and ended segmentary birth and death: in the course of cultivating the path, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases, and this transition of delusion and awakening differs in each period. The passing from one period into the next is just like undergoing one birth and death, and so it is called ‘transformational birth and death.’ One who ends transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, why do you speak of three vehicles and not of the One Vehicle?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, then why is it said that there are three vehicles, and not that there is the One Vehicle?

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: Because they have no dharma of parinirvāṇa of their own, I do not speak of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the One Vehicle. Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are tamed by the Tathāgata and, given the expedient teaching of stillness, attain liberation — not by their own power — therefore I do not speak of the One Vehicle. Furthermore, Mahāmati, because their afflictions, obstructive karma, and latent tendencies are not cut off, I do not speak of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the One Vehicle; because they do not awaken to the non-self of dharmas and do not transcend segmentary birth and death, I speak of three vehicles.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati: Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot attain the dharma of nirvāṇa by themselves, I do not speak of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the One Vehicle. Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are tamed by the Tathāgata and, given the expedient teaching of stillness, attain the liberation of emptiness and stillness — not attaining ultimate liberation by their own power — I do not speak of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the One Vehicle. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have cut off only the delusion of views and thoughts, while the delusion of dust and sand and the delusion of ignorance are not yet cut off; they have removed only the obstruction of afflictions, not yet the obstruction to the known, and their karmic latent tendencies remain; therefore I do not speak of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as the One Vehicle. They have broken only the attachment to a self in persons, not yet the attachment to a self in dharmas, and still have transformational birth and death; therefore I speak of them as the three vehicles.

[Parinirvāṇa] Abbreviated as ‘nirvāṇa’; in Chinese it is rendered as ‘perfect stillness’ (yuánjì). ‘Perfect’ means the perfection of all the virtues of wisdom; ‘stillness’ means the stilling of all delusion and karma. It is also translated as ‘extinction and crossing over’ (mièdù): ‘extinction’ means extinguishing the three delusions — the delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance; ‘crossing over’ means crossing over the two kinds of birth and death, segmentary and transformational. Taken together, when a person’s wisdom and virtue have reached the realm of ultimate perfection, and both birth and death and afflictions have been transcended and cut off, this is called ‘nirvāṇa.’ This is also the true-suchness realm, neither arising nor ceasing and beyond time and space, realized by the sages; it is likewise the most ideal and most beautiful destination of the myriad sentient beings. [The three delusions] The delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of dust and sand, and the delusion of ignorance. Among the three delusions, the delusion of views and thoughts is coarse, the delusion of dust and sand is middling, and the delusion of ignorance is subtle. [The delusion of views and thoughts] The delusion of ordinary beings. Within the delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of views is confusion and error in knowledge and views, such as the five false views — the view of a self in the body, the view of extremes, and so forth; the delusion of thoughts is confusion and error in thought, such as the five afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. If practitioners of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha paths cut off this delusion of views and thoughts, they can realize the fruit of arhatship and leave the three realms. [The delusion of dust and sand] The delusion of bodhisattvas. If a bodhisattva who transforms and saves sentient beings does not penetrate the immeasurable dharma-gates numerous as dust and sand, he cannot accomplish the work of teaching sentient beings; therefore it is called the delusion of dust and sand. [The delusion of ignorance] Fundamental ignorance, which obscures the principle of the middle way and true reality; when it is utterly cut off, one becomes a Buddha. [Not awakening to the non-self of dharmas, not transcending segmentary birth and death] The Wei translation says:
“Not yet realizing the non-self of dharmas, they have not yet escaped inconceivable transformational birth.”

“Mahāmati, once the latent tendencies of all arising afflictions are cut off and the non-self of dharmas is realized — one sees that the flavor of samādhi is without real nature, and attains the unconditioned realm. Having attained it, one enters the supreme, supramundane unconditioned realm, perfects all the requisites, and will attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, sovereign dharmakāya.”

Mahāmati, once they (the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) cut off the latent tendencies of all arising afflictions and wrongdoings, and eradicate the attachment to a self in dharmas, they are able to realize that samādhi too is an illusion, and no longer cling to its blissful flavor; thus they attain the realization of the unconditioned realm. Having attained it, they enter the Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance (the supreme, supramundane unconditioned realm), fully perfect all the virtues, and will attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, sovereign dharmakāya.

[Non-substantiality] Having no essential nature; an illusion. [Unconditioned realm] The sphere in which no afflictions arise. [Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance] One of the four lands. Eternal refers to the dharmakāya, which is forever beyond arising and ceasing; stillness refers to liberation, in which all afflictions are forever stilled; radiance refers to prajñā, the wisdom that illuminates reality. These three virtues — dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā — are the abode of all Buddhas, and so it is called the Land of Eternal Stillness and Radiance. [Four Lands] The land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together; the land of expedient remainder; the land of true reward and adornment; and the land of eternal stillness and radiance. The land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together is where common people dwell alongside the sages who manifest bodies and teach the Dharma in order to guide beings; the land of expedient remainder is where the two vehicles and those bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the dharmakāya dwell; the land of true reward and adornment is where the Buddha’s reward body and the bodhisattvas of the stages dwell; the land of eternal stillness and radiance is the land that appears as tranquility from the Buddha’s pure dharmakāya.

At that time the Bhagavān, wishing to restate this meaning in verse, declared: The vehicle of the gods and the vehicle of Brahmā, the vehicle of śrāvakas and of pratyekabuddhas, the vehicle of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas — these vehicles I have spoken. As long as the mind still turns, these vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind is utterly extinguished, there is no vehicle and no rider
no vehicle is established, and I declare it the One Vehicle
Only for the sake of guiding sentient beings do I teach the vehicles in their distinctions.
At this time
the Bhagavān, wishing
to restate this
meaning, spoke in
verse: the vehicle
of the gods,
the bodhisattva vehicle,
the śrāvaka vehicle,
the pratyekabuddha vehicle,
the Tathāgata
vehicle —
I have
explained these
vehicles. If
the mind
turns (gives
rise to
thought), then
all vehicles
are not
ultimate; if
the mind
is extinguished,
then there
is no
vehicle and
no rider,
and there
is no
vehicle that
is established;
I call
this the
One Vehicle.
Only for
the sake
of leading
sentient beings,
therefore, I
teach the
vehicles distinctly
(hence the
vehicles are
expedient teachings).
[Brahmā vehicle] That is, the bodhisattva vehicle. Brahmā means pure. The bodhisattvas, through the four immeasurable
minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, carry sentient beings across the sea of birth and
death; this is called the Brahmā vehicle. [Four immeasurable minds] The immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, the
immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Giving
pleasure to all sentient beings is called the mind of loving-kindness; removing suffering from all sentient
beings is called the mind of compassion; rejoicing deeply when others do good or are
freed from suffering is called the mind of joy; and letting go of these three
without attachment, or treating enemy and kin alike without rising partiality, is called the mind
of equanimity. Because these four minds are universally directed to immeasurable sentient beings and give
rise to immeasurable merit, they are called the immeasurable minds. [The vehicles of gods, śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas] The vehicle of the gods is riding the teaching of the ten
wholesome deeds to be reborn in heaven; the vehicle of the śrāvakas is riding the
teaching of the four noble truths to realize the fruit of arhatship; the vehicle of
the pratyekabuddhas is riding the teaching of the twelve links of dependent origination to realize
the fruit of the pratyekabuddha; and the bodhisattva vehicle is riding the teaching of the
six perfections to realize the supreme, unsurpassed buddhahood. [No vehicle, no rider; no vehicle is
established] If the workings of the mind are utterly extinguished, then there is no one
who rides, and there is no vehicle ridden; moreover all vehicles are no longer established.
The Tang translation says:

“The vehicle of the gods and of Brahmā, the vehicles of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the vehicles of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas — all these I have spoken. As long as the mind arises, these vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind has turned and ceased, there is no vehicle and no rider, no vehicle is established, and I declare it the One Vehicle. For the sake of gathering the foolish, I teach the distinctions among the vehicles.”
Liberation is threefold: the non-self of dharmas, liberation from afflictions and from clinging to wisdom
There are three liberations
separation from all afflictions
, destroying
the attachment to a self in dharmas
, and gaining
the equality
wisdom
The Tang translation says:
“Liberation is threefold: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality.”
[Liberation threefold]
This scripture says:

“For the sake of guiding the outsiders who grasp at a self, I speak of the tathāgatagarbha, that they may be free from the false views of an unreal self and enter the sphere of the three doors of liberation, in the hope of quickly attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The three doors of liberation
are

three gates of wisdom that lead into liberation: first, the door of emptiness, which realizes that all dharmas are fundamentally empty without clinging to emptiness; second, the door of wishlessness, which knows that all dharmas are illusorily existent and so has nothing to seek; third, the door of signlessness, which knows that all dharmas are without marks yet not without marks, and enters the middle way.
However, the Tang translation says:
“Liberation is threefold: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality.”

This indicates that the three liberations spoken of here are: separation from all afflictions, the non-self of dharmas, and liberation through the wisdom of equality. This is likewise what the scripture’s passage and its context suggest, and so the annotation’s rendering follows it.

[Wisdom of equality] This is the wisdom of equality — the wisdom of the perfect equality of nature — one of the four wisdoms of the Tathāgata. [Four wisdoms] The Tathāgata’s four kinds of wisdom: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of the equality of nature, and the wisdom of the great mirror. The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is produced from the transformation of the five defiled sense-consciousnesses, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha accomplishes all beneficent deeds for sentient beings; the wisdom of wondrous observation is produced from the transformation of the sixth defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha observes dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings to prescribe the remedy suited to the illness and to turn the ordinary to the holy; the wisdom of the equality of nature is produced from the transformation of the seventh defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha penetrates the principle of selflessness and equality and rouses unconditional great compassion toward all sentient beings; the wisdom of the great mirror is produced from the transformation of the eighth defiled consciousness, and is the wisdom with which the Buddha contemplates all phenomena and principles without anything left unclear — pure, luminous, seeing within and without, like a great mirror that illuminates all things.

It is like a floating log on the sea, ever turning with the waves; the śrāvakas in their folly are likewise, blown about by the wind of marks. Their arising afflictions are destroyed, yet the folly of residual tendencies remains; they delight in the bliss of samādhi and abide in the unconditioned realm, with no destination that is final

Yet they do not fall back; they acquire the bodies of samādhi and do not awaken for eons. It is like a drunken man who, when the wine wears off, then becomes aware; so too, when they awaken to the Dharma, they obtain the supreme body of the Buddha.
It is like a
floating log on the
sea, ever turning
with the waves;
so too are
the śrāvakas and
pratyekabuddhas, foolishly attached
to the marks
of dharmas, drifting
with the wind
of marks. Although
they have destroyed
their afflictions, they
are still bound
by residual tendencies,
and delight in
the bliss of

the unconditioned realm
of emptiness of
persons, and take
this to be

truth they have
not reached the
Buddha’s final ground
(the ultimate destination).
Even so, they
will not fall
back, for they
have obtained the

Going on like
this, even after
many eons they
do not awaken.
It is like
a drunken man
who, when the

they turn their

to the fact

are without a

[Wind of marks] The two-vehicle practitioners have already left the mark
of a self in persons, but still cling to the mark
of a self in dharmas. The wind of marks here is
the wind of the marks of dharmas that causes them to
drift. The Diamond Sutra says: “Dwelling on no mark, thus does
one remain unmoved.” The practice of the One Vehicle is to
be unmoved by the wind of marks. [Mark of dharmas] Falsely
grasping that the method of practice really exists. [Method of practice]
The Dharma of cultivation — the means of ending birth and
death and realizing nirvāṇa. [Like a floating log on the sea,
ever turning with the waves; so are the foolish śrāvakas, blown
about by the wind of marks] This illustrates that the two
vehicles, not having cut off the obstruction to the known, still
take the marks of dharmas to be real, and so are
tossed about by the wind of marks, just as a
floating log is turned by the waves on the sea.
The Tang translation says:

“It is like a log in the sea, ever turning with the waves; the mind of the śrāvaka is likewise, tossed about by the wind of marks. Though their arising afflictions are destroyed, they are still bound by residual tendencies, intoxicated by the wine of samādhi, dwelling in the unconditioned realm. This is not the final goal, yet they do not regress, for they have obtained the body of samādhi, and do not awaken for eons. It is like a drunken man who becomes aware when the wine wears off; so too the śrāvakas, who will become Buddhas after they awaken.”

inline.s: Question: Many treatises speak of dharmas as having no self-nature, so why does the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra say
“as a cow has no horse-nature and a horse has no cow-nature, yet it is not that there is no self-nature”
Answer: The word self-nature has three meanings: first, the essential nature of a thing (its substance), namely the reality of all dharmas (see
The Reality of All Dharmas
); second, the innate spiritual faculty within sentient beings (see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
); and third, the characteristic attributes of a thing.
[Attributes] The properties intrinsic to a thing itself — the necessary, fundamental, and inseparable characteristics of a thing.

Polysemous words in language satisfy the principle of linguistic economy — using a limited vocabulary to reflect the boundless objective world — but they also create a certain difficulty for our understanding. Therefore, when reading, one must always determine the meaning of a polysemous word in a given context.
The passage you ask about comes from the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:

“Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without self, because there is no self-nature within those dharmas I declare them selfless; yet it is not that dharmas are without their own nature — the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words should be known likewise. Mahāmati! Just as a cow has no horse-nature and a horse has no cow-nature, so dharmas are not without their own nature.”

Its meaning is: Mahāmati! As I have said that all dharmas are without a self, it is because there is no self-nature within dharmas that I declare them selfless (that is, dharmas are illusions), not that dharmas are without their respective attributes; the meaning of the words taught by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas should be known likewise. Mahāmati! Just as a cow lacks the attribute of a horse and a horse lacks the attribute of a cow, dharmas are not without their respective attributes.
In the passage above, the meaning of self-nature is the characteristic attributes of a thing.

In this passage, “all dharmas are without self” is spoken in terms of the reality of dharmas, meaning that dharmas are illusions. And “dharmas are not without self-nature (dharmas are not without their respective attributes)” is spoken in terms of the respective attributes of the myriad phenomena within the dream of ignorance. The central idea of this passage is: fundamentally, dharmas do not exist (“all dharmas are without self”); but within the world of forms in the dream of ignorance, they each have their own attributes (“dharmas are not without self-nature”). The former is spoken of the essence of dharmas, the latter of the marks of dharmas.

All dharmas are without self,” is also often expressed in the scriptures and treatises as “all dharmas are without self-nature (dharmas have no self-substance),” meaning that all dharmas have no real entity, are all illusions, like things in a dream. For example, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:

“For this reason, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of prajñā, if toward all dharmas he grasps existence, or non-existence, or both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, or even non-grasping itself, then he is not practicing the perfection of prajñā. Why? Because
(since)
all dharmas are without self-nature and cannot be grasped.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the essential nature
(substance)
of a thing, namely the reality of all dharmas.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Ancestor says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is the ordinary being; when self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the innate spiritual faculty within sentient beings.

The Reality of All Dharmas
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
